VS.

full_judgment:
This Rule on an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure at the instance of the plaintiff-petitioner was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-5 to show cause as to why the order dated 22-3-1998 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Fultala, Khulna in Title suit No. 35 of 1997 should not be set-aside and or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule, in short, is that the present petitioner as plaintiff instituted Title Suit being No. 25 of 1995 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Fultala, Khulna for specific performance of contract against the opposite party Nos. 6-11 contending, inter alia, that late Abdur Rashid Molla, the predecessor in interest of the opposite party Nos. 6-10 being owner and possessor of 0.73 acres of land appertaining to CS plot Nos. 1939 and 1940 recorded in CS khatian Nos. 1996 and 1998 of Baniakhamar mouza of Khulna Police Station had entered into an agreement to sale 0.085 acres of land to the plaintiff at a consideration of Taka 50,000 and on receipt of an advance of Taka 20,000 executed a bainaparta on 8-2-1986 and thereafter took Taka 25,000 on 13-4-1986 and extended the time for execution and registration of the sale deed for a long period on the ground of pendency of a title suit. Subsequently Abdur Rashid Molla died leaving the present opposite party Nos. 6-10 as his heirs who ultimately refused to execute and register the sale deed on 20-3-1995.

3. The said suit was transferred in the Court of Assistant Judge, Fultala and renumbered as Title Suit No. 35 of 1997. On 11-2-1998 the opposite party Nos. 1-5 appearing in the Court below filed an application for impleading them as defendants in the suit averring inter-alia that the suit land originally belonged to one Girl. Bala Debi who got decree in Title Appeal No. 6 of 1958 arising out of Title Suit No. 342 of 1956. Giri Bala died leaving her brother Horimohan as her only heir and Horimohan while was in possession of the said land sold the same to them and 4 others by registered kabala deeds keeping a small portion in his khash. The petitioners and Horimohan jointly filed Title suit No. 701 of 1979 against Abdur Rashid Molla and the said suit was decreed on 30-7-1994. Abdur Rashid Molla had no title and possession in the suit land as such his heirs inherited nothing from him. Abdur Rashid Molla did not execute any bainapatra in favour of the plaintiff and after the death of Abdur Rashid Molla, the plaintiff in collusion with some other interested quarters created ante dated bainaparta with the forged signature. The petitioners having title into the suit land are the necessary party in the suit to protect their interest.

4. The said application for adding party was heard on contest by the Court below and passed the impugned order on 22-3-1998 allowing the same. The plaintiff petitioner being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said impugned order moved this Court amongst with some other grounds and obtained the present Rule.

5. Mr AKM Alamgir Parvez Bhuiyan for Mrs Purabi Rani Sharma, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner supports the Rule. He submits that the original suit being a suit for specific performance of contract on the basis of a bainapatra dated 8-2-1986 taken place between Abdur Rashid Mollah and the plaintiff, the executant Abdur Rashid Molla or his heirs are the only necessary party in such a suit. He further submits that in a suit like this the only point for determination, is that whether the executant executed the bainapatra in favour of the plaintiff, so other than the executant of the bainapatra no other is necessary party but the Court below ignoring the cardinal principle of such a suit very illegally added the opposite party Nos. 1-5 in the suit as defendants. So, the impugned order is liable to be set-aside making the Rule absolute.

6. Mr Probir Haider, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party Nos. 1-5 opposing the Rule strenuously submits that it is fact that in a suit for specific performance of contract generally the necessary parties are those who executed the bainapatra or his heirs in interest as the case may be and though in this particular case the opposite party Nos. 1-5 are not the executants of the bainapatra dated 8-2-1986 but Abdur Rashid Molla who executed the bainapatra in favour of the plaintiff claiming the ownership in the land in question had no title and possession into the suit land. In a former Title Suit being No. 701 of 1979, the title of the present opposite party No. 1-5 along with Horimohan was declared against Abdur Rashid Molla in his presence. So, under the above facts and circumstances the presence of the present petitioners in the present suit was inevitable for an effective and complete justice in the suit and the Court below considering the said facts and circumstances allowed the petitioners to be added as defendants in the suit. So, the impugned order does not call for interference from this Court and the Court below did not commit any illegality occasioning failure of justice to the plaintiff-petitioner. So, the Rule is liable to be discharged with costs.

7. I have considered the above submissions of the learned Advocates of both the parties with anxious consideration and perused the materials on record.

8. On going to the materials on record it appears that Abdur Rashid Molla claiming title and possession into the suit land had entered into a bainapatra to sell 0.085 acres of land to the plaintiff and after his death his heirs the present opposite party Nos. 6-10 denied to exe-cute and register a sale deed pursuant to the said bainapatra and ultimately the said fact rises the present suit. From the impugned order of the Court below it appears that the trial Court was very much conscious and aware about the scope and limit of a suit for specific performance of contract. The Court below categorically observed that in a suit for specific performance of contract, the prime duty of the Court to scrutinize whether there was a contract between the plaintiff and the defendants but even then since the petitioners got a decree for the suit land before filing of the present suit, the presence of the petitioners will facilitate the scope to have an effective and complete justice in the suit and he also observed that if the opposite party Nos. 1-5 are not allowed to be added as defendants in the original suit that may be the cause of more suit among the par-ties. I find it difficult to show any disagreement with the findings and observations of the Court below.

<u>9. It is fact that in a suit for specific performance of contract normally the parties to the contract are necessary parties but there may be case and exception to this normal principle that where the persons claim title over the suit land backed by strong instruments are considered as necessary parties to the suit. The case in my hands go to show that the title of the opposite party Nos. 1-5 were declared by a competent civil Court before filing of the present suit. Having regards to those facts, the opposite party Nos. 1-5 appears to be necessary parties in the suit for an effective and complete justice in the litigation among the parties. The Court below considering these all aspects of the suit allowed the petition of opposite party Nos. 1-5 with the following observations:</u>

<u>“ এক্ষেত্রে চুক্তি প্রবলের মোকদ্দমায় বাদী ও বিবাদী পক্ষের মধ্যে নালিশী চুক্তি সম্পাদিত হইয়াছিল কি না তাহাই মুখ্য বিচার্য বিষয় হইলেও যেহেতু নালিশী সম্পত্তি সংক্রান্ত দরখাস্তকারী পক্ষ পূর্বেই ডিক্রি প্রাপ্ত হইয়াছে সেক্ষেত্রে উক্ত ডিক্রি ভুক্ত সম্পত্তি সংক্রান্ত বাদীও বিবাদীদের মধ্যে অত্র মোকদ্দমা দায়ের হইলেও  দরখাস্তকারী পক্ষের উপস্থিতিতে অত্র মোকদ্দমার বিচার সমাপ্ত হইলে তাহাতে পক্ষগনের ক্ষতিগ্রস্ত হওয়ার কোন সম্ভাবনা নাই বরং দরখাস্তকারী পক্ষের অনুপস্থিতিতে অত্র মোকদ্দমার বিচার সমাপ্ত হইলে পক্ষগনের মধ্যে অধিকতর আইনগত জটিলতার সৃস্টি হইবে এবং অধিক সংখ্যক মামলার উদ্ভব হইতে পারে বিবেচনায় দরখাস্তকারী পক্ষের ইং ১১-২-৯৮ তারিখের দেঃ কাঃ বিধি আইনের ১ আদেশের ১০ বিধি মতে আনীত পক্ষভুক্তির দরখাস্ত ন্যায় বিচারের স্বার্থে মঞ্জুর করা হইল।”</u>

10. From the above observations of the Court below I find that the Court below considering the pros and cons of the suit and the other relevant facts particularly the decree in a former Title Suit being No. 701 of 1979 between the opposite party Nos. 1-5 and Abdur Rashid Mollah from whom the plaintiff has been claiming the suit land passed the very considerate, thoughtful and rational order giving chance to the opposite party Nos. 1-5 to contest in the suit. Since in a former suit the title of the opposite party Nos. 1-5 was declared such parties cannot be kept away from a subsequent suit where their question of title and interest are also involved. If the opposite party Nos. 1-5 are devoiced now from the suit how they will protect their interest in respect of the suit land.

<u>11. More so, Rule 10(2) of Order 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that Court can add persons whose presence before the Court may be necessary in order to enable the Court effectively and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit. Considering the facts and circumstances of the suit and the case of the opposite party Nos. 1-5, their adding as defendants in the suit is very much consistent and harmonical with the provisions of Rule 10(2) of Order No. 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

12. So, under the above facts and circumstances, I find no the illegality in the impugned order of the Court below dated 22-3-1998.

13. By the Rule issuing order dated 19-7-1998, the further proceeding of Title Suit No. 35 of 1997 was stayed till disposal of First Appeal No. 129 of 1997 pending before this Court, arising out of Title Suit No. 701 of 1979. From the record of First Appeal No. 129 of 1997 it appears that the appeal has been dismissed on non prosecution on 26-2-2006. So there appears no impediment to vacate the stay order of this Rule.

14. In the result, the Rule is discharged. The stay order passed in this Rule on 19-7-1998 is hereby vacated. The Court below is directed to dispose of the suit within 6(six) calendar months from the date of receipt of the judgment and order of this Court.

Let a copy of this judgment and order be sent down to the concerned Court for information and necessary action.

End.

full_judgment:
The Rule issued calling upon the opposite party No.1 to show cause as, to why the judgment and decree dated 27-3-2007 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No.250 of 2005 allowing the appeal reversing those of dated 19-4-2005 and 26-4-2005 respectively passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 352 of 2004 rejecting the plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, the present opposite party No.1 as plaintiff filed the original suit being Title Suit No. 352 of 2004 in the 1 St court of learned Assistant Judge, Dhaka for a declaration that the appointment of the defendant No. 1 as Headmistress of Hazrat Shah Ali High School is illegal contending inter-alia that the son of the plaintiff is a student of the High School and being the guardian and a local elite person the plaintiff is a voter from the guardian category in the school. The defendant No. 1 was an illegally appointed Head-mistress of the School having no required qualification for the post and practicing fraud sup-pressing the defendant No.1 has been appointed as Headmistress of the School and with-drawing the salary of the post. During pendency of the original suit the defendant No.1 filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejecting the plaint and after hearing the learned trial court allowed the application and rejected the plaint of the suit vide order dated 19-4-2005.

3. Being aggrieved the plaintiff preferred an appeal being Other Class Appeal No. 250 of 2005 in the court of learned District Judge, Dhaka which was heard and disposed of by the learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka and the learned appellate court below by the impugned judgment and order dated 27-3-2007 allowed the appeal reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial court.

4. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and decree the defendant-respondent-petitioner has preferred this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule with an interim order of stay.

5. Mr. Kazi Akhtar Hosain, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the petitioner while Mrs Shaheen Akther, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the opposite party No.1.

6. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the learned court of appeal below during disposal of the appeal committed illegality and that the impugned judgment and decree is not a proper judgment and decree of reversal. The learned Advocate further submits that the appointment of the defendant-petitioner is legal and on compliance of the Rules of Non-Government Institution Instruction Manual issued from the ministry of education the appointment was completed. The learned Advocate also submits that the plaintiff-opposite party has no locus standi to institute the original suit under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and secondly the plaintiff before institution of the suit without exhausting the proper forum to seek redress of his grievances filed the original suit and as a result of which the learned trial court was quite justified to reject the plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Advocate lastly submits that no fruitful result can be given from a decree by a civil court in the instant nature of suit and the learned appellate court without proper appreciation of law decided the merit of the appeal illegally which deserve interference of this court.

7. As against the aforesaid submissions of the learned counsel for the petitioner the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party opposing the Rule controverted the arguments advanced from the side of the learned Advocate for the petitioner and submits that there is no ingredient for rejection of the plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the learned appellate court below rightly after proper appreciation of law and materials on record reversed the judgment and decree passed by the trial court rebutting the findings of the trial court adverting the relevant provisions of law in consultation with the pleadings of the plaintiff. The learned Advocate further submits that the plaintiff-opposite-party have every locus standi to institute the suit under the purview of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and if the relief is granted by the civil court that would be a fruitful result for the plaintiff-opposite party. The plaintiff after exhausting the legal requirements for filing a civil suit before a competent court of law instituted the suit. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party in this context pointed out the facts of the case and content of the pleading which was brought by the plaintiff. Learned Advocate has drawn the notice of the court in paragraph Nos. 2, 3, 8, 9 and 11 of the plaint which are related with the locus-standi of the plaintiff and the cause of action of the suit. The learned Advocate lastly submits that after serving legal notice upon the defendants while the plaintiff did not obtain any relief he was constrained to file the original suit. The learned trial court misconstrued the actual position of law as well as the content of the pleadings in its true perspective and subsequently the appellate court below rightly appreciated the law and acted under the provisions laid down in Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in compliance of that reversed the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge and there is nothing to interfere with the impugned judgment and decree.

8. Heard the learned Advocates of both sides, perused the case records, connected papers, impugned judgment and decree along with the judgment and decree passed by the trial court in Title Suit No. 352 of 2004.

9. On perusal of the connected papers it transpires that during pendency of the original suit the defendant-petitioner submitted an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint. In the said application the defendant No.1 states that her appointment in the post of Headmistress of the institution is legal and after compliance of all legal formalities and fulfillment of requirements she has been appointed as Headmistress of the school but the plaintiff in collusion with the interested corner instituted the suit on false allegation having no locus-standi to file the suit. The learned trial court being satisfied rejected the plaint vide judgment and order dated 19-4-2005.

10. Being aggrieved the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No.250 of 2005 and the appellate court below at the time of disposal of the appeal finding the status of the plaintiff and locus standi to prefer civil suit under the purview of section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure in a civil court reversed the judgment and decree of the trial court by the impugned judgment and decree dated 27-3-2007.

11. Having gone through the certified copy of the plaint marked Annexure-"A" I find that in paragraph Nos.2 and 3 of the plaint there is a clear contention of the plaintiff that he has locus standi as well as legal status i.e. to institute the suit under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Being a guardian of a ward of the institution and having vote casting authority in the governing body of the institution he felt aggrieved by the misdeed of the defendants and in the appointment of the Headmistress of the institution, which was done in collusion and practicing fraud. Paragraph Nos.8 and 9 of the plaint disclosed the specific allegation against the defendant No.1 who is admittedly holding the post of Headmistress of the institution and there is an allegation on violation of the government Rules for the post. Paragraph No. 11 of the plaint speaks about the cause of action which was acquired after serving legal notice upon the defendants. Besides this; there is an allegation on the defendants that they have practiced fraud as well as unholy alliance in the appointment of the defendant No. 1 to the post of Headmistress of the institution.

Under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 any person entitled to any legal character, or to any right as to any property, may institute a suit against any person denying, or interested to deny, his title to such character or right, and the court may in its discretion make therein a declaration that he is so entitled, and the plaintiff need not in such suit ask for any further relief.

<u>12. Under the purview of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act i.e. Act I of 1877 the spirit of the section contemplates that any member of a institution having a right to the properties of the institution has right to sue for proper relief under section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. A person can enforce his substantive right, even though time barred, it there are other legal remedies available for the enforcement of the same. Our Apex court in the case of Divisional Forest Officer vs Md Shahabuddin reported in 12 BLC (AD) 138 held:</u>

<u>"A suit for declaration is maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as to any legal character or to any right as to any property of the plaintiff if the defendant denies or is interested to deny his title to such character or right. If the above conditions are satisfied, the plaintiff need not ask for any further relief than a mere declaration."</u>

<u>13. It is a fact that section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure confer jurisdiction of the Civil court to entertain all civil suit in civil nature excepting the suit which is expressly or impliedly barred under law. Ouster of jurisdiction of civil court cannot be readily inferred unless expressly taken away and "impliedly barred" means barred by General Principles of law or equity of public policy. In our instant suit there is no baring clause by which it can be held by any means that civil suit is barred either expressly or impliedly.</u>

14. In view of the above discussions and findings I have every reason to draw such inference that the lower appellate court is quite justified in holding that the trial court committed gross illegality in rejecting the plaint under the ambit of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

15. Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure can be invoked only—

(a) where the plaint does not disclose a cause of action;

(b) where the relief claimed is undervalued, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the Court fails to do so;

(c) where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a lime to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so;

(d) Where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law.

16. The learned trial court misconstrued the law in its total approach and the appellate court below deserve appreciation of this court in passing the impugned judgment and decree after correct findings of law.

17. In the result the Rule having no merit is discharged without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree dated 27-3-2007 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 250 of 2005 reversing those of dated 19-4-2005 and 26-4-2005 respectively passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 352 of 2004 is hereby affirmed.

18. The order of stay granted earlier by court at the time of issuance of the Rule stands (b)vacated.

Communicate the judgment and order at once and send back the lower court's records immediately.

End.

full_judgment:
Sharif Uddin Chaklader J : This appeal by plaintiff directed against judgment and decree dated 1-12-2009 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Chandpur, dismissing Title Suit No. 5 of 2006.

2. Plaintiff instituted the aforesaid suit for following declaration :—

“সে মতে বাদীপক্ষের বিনীত প্রার্থনা-

(ক) আরজির বর্ণিত অবস্থাধীনে ও প্রমানিকৃত অবস্থায় নালিশী ১নং তপছিল বর্ণিত ভূমিতে বাদীগনের খরিদা রায়তীস্বত্ব ঘোষনা দিতে,

(খ) বাদীগনের নামীয় ১৩২/৮৩-৮৪ ও ২৩৩/৮৩-৮৪ নং জমা খারিজ মোকদ্দমা বাতিল করা সম্পর্কিত পুনঃ বিচার মোকদ্দমা ১৭/২০০০-২৮৮১ইং নং মোকদ্দমায় ৪নং বিবাদী কর্তৃক দেওয়া বিগত ৩০-১০-২০০১ ইং তারিখের আদেশ একদা বেআইনী তনচকতামূলক ও এখতিয়ার বর্হিভূত বাদীপক্ষের প্রতি অবাধ্যকর হওয়া মর্মে ঘোষনা প্রচারের ডিক্রি দিতে,

(গ) নালিশী ভূমি সম্পর্কে ২নং বিবাদী কর্তৃক বাদীগনের বরাবরে বিগত ১৫-৭-২০০২ ইং তারিখের ৬৬/ভি,পি নং স্মারক মূলে ইস্যুকৃত উচ্ছেদের নোটিশ একদা বে আইনী, বেদাড়া, তনচকতামূলক, এখতিয়ার বর্হিভূত বাদীপক্ষের প্রতি অবাধ্যকর হওয়া মর্মে ঘোষনা প্রচারের ডিক্রি দিতে।”

3. Plaintiff's case, in short, is that, suit land was originally belong to Raj Kumar Chandra who transferred 591/2 decimals of land from dag No 1688 by registered saf kabala dated 24-2-14 to Chandra Mohan and Jogendra Chandra. Raj Kumar on the same date by another registered saf kabala No. 1702 transferred 29 1/2 decimals of land from dag No. 1688 and 11 decimals of land from dag No. 1684, totaling 40/2 decimals of land to Brojo Mohan and become titleless inspite of that CS Khatian was prepared in his name. But SA khatian No. 548 was prepared in the name of Chandra Mohan, Jogendra Mohan and Brojo Mohan. The sons of Ram Dayal by registered deed No. 9571 dated 23-10-1948 sold their share to Horihor Chandra. The heirs of recorded tenant of CS and SA khatian were in possession and while they were in peaceful possession by power of attorney to plaintiff, Arman Ali Sarker exchange the entire land and by giving delivery of possession to Arman Ali Sarker, having title less, left the suit premises. Annan Ali Sarker having possession enjoyed the suit land for more than 12 years, died leaving only son, Munnaf Sarker who by registred saf kabala deed No. 13130 dated 11-7-1967 transferred 5.50 acres of land to Abdul Khalek Kha and Omar Kha, by registered deed No. 9996 dated 16-11-1967 sold 1.73 acres of land to Idris Mollah. Abdul Khalek Kha and Omar Kha by registered deed dated 16-11-1967 sold 5.50 acres of land to 18 persons. One Harunur Rashid obtained lease in respect of 2.54 acres of land in EP Case No. 50/67-68 from schedule to the suit land. Objection was raised and lease was cancelled. Thereafter, aforesaid purchaser through different deeds transferred quantum of certain land to different persons. Omar Kha and Abdul Khalek Kha, later on, by registered saf kabala deed Nos. 2311, 2312, 2313, 2544 and 2545 dated 22-1-1975 and 27-1-1975 transferred the suit land to plaintiffs. After purchase, plaintiffs mutated their names and sold some land to some other persons. Defendant No. 1-5 treat the suit property as enemy property, served notice for eviction, whereupon plaintiff filed Writ Petition No. 5509 of 2002. A Division bench of this Court on 28-8-2005 opined to file suit and this suit was filed.

4. Defendant No. 1-5, 33-39 and 6-31 field three separate sets of written statements and contested the suit.

5. It is the Case of defendant No. 1-5 that suit land recorded in CS and SA khatian in the name of Horihor who having left this country, as such, the suit land has been vested in the government as enemy property. One Harunur Rashid was given lease of certain quantum of land in EP Case No. 50/67-68. The case of plaintiffs that plaintiffs purchased the suit land from Arman Ali Sarker who is an imaginary, fictitious person and there is no exchange of the suit land with Arman Ali Sarker with recorded tenants of CS and SA khatian and deeds showing Omar Kha and Abdul Khalek Kha as vendors are all false, fabricated without any consideration. Plaintiffs filed the suit on false averments, is liable to be dismissed.

6. The case of defendant No. 6-31 is that they after the suit land release from enemy property cell, they purchased the suit land and they divided the suit land in 26 plots and are possessing the same. After release of the suit land, defendant No. 2 has no authority to issue eviction notice under Memo No. 66 DP dated 15-7-2002.

7. The case of defendant Nos. 33-39 is that they are heirs of Abdul Khaleque who purchased the suit land form its original owner and the suit is liable to be dismissed as it is not filed as per Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

8. Learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Chandpur framed 3 issues and for the plaintiff's 3 witnesses were examined and for the defendants. 4 witnesses were examined. In the suit plaintiff Exhibited as many as 38 Exhibits. No one of the defendants Exhibited any document.

9. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, along with Mr Mahbub Ali and Mr Md Ziaul Hoque, learned Advocates, appearing for the plaintiffs appellants, submits that, plaintiffs through registered instrument purchased the suit property before liberation of Bangladesh and chain of title having not been broken at any point of time, trial court ought to have decreed the suit. Learned Advocate. further submits that, it is admitted position that plaintiffs are in possession for more than 40 years and this possession is by registered document which has presumptive value and defendant entry to the suit land having not been through legal process trial court ought to have decreed the suit. Learned Advocate further submits that plaintiffs possession of the suit land from CS recorded owner is enough to bestow title as possession follows title, is one part and in the other part, by purchase from CS recorded owner, as such, the suit ought to have decreed. Learned Advocate further submits that no property can be taken over by the Government as enemy property unless there is formation of opinion to that effect, as such, the impugned judgment and order passed by the learned Joint District Judge without consultation of law, is liable to be set-aside.

10. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, learned Advocate, relied on the case of Abul Hossain vs Amjad Hossain, 62 DLR (AD) 436 wherein it is held that :—

"Section 110 of the Evidence Act provides for a presumption of ownership in favour of the person who is in possession of the property. A person in possession of land however imperfect his title may be, has a good title against whole world except the true owner and until the true owner comes in Court to assert a claim to the property. Possession is evidence of title, and gives a good title as against wrongdoer. The High Court Division, in the premises, fell in an error in reversing the judgment of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge without adverting to the findings arrived at as regards acquisition of title and possession of the suit lands by the appellants. On consideration of the fact and circumstances of the matter, we are of view that the. High Court Division erred in law in disbelieving the appellants title in the suit lands."

11. Learned Advocate next relied on the case of Shishir Kanti Pal vs Nur Muhammad, 55 DLR (AD) 39 wherein it is held as "A registered document carries presumption of correctness of the endorsement made therein one who disputes this presumption is required to dislodge the correctness of the endorsement."

12. When the PW 1 (witness examined by the defendant No; 1 Government of Bangladesh) has expressed his lack of knowledge about the possession of the land in suit or, in other word, has not denied the claim of plaintiff's possession in the land suit and that dW 2 (defendant No. 5) has not specifically denied the claim of possession of the plaintiffs in the land in suit, nor was there any case from the side of the defendants in their pleadings as well as in the court that plaintiffs went into possession of the land in suit forcibly ousting the defendants from the properties described in schedule 'A' to the plaint and, as such, in that state or the matter plaintiffs claim of coming into possession of the land in suit in year 1963 on the basis of exchange being an admitted fact from the side of the defendants and that also fact of possession having been established by the plaintiffs by reliable and credible evidence and consequent thereupon having had acquired right and interest of unassailable character the High Court Division and the appellate Court were not in error or any kind in decreeing the suit. In the background of the materials on record the High Court Division has not committed any error in holding that there, was exchange of the 'A' schedule properties with the 'B' schedule properties by the Exhibit I and on the basis of exchange between the plaintiffs and the defendants No. 5-12, the plaintiffs went into possession of the land 30 years back.

13. Learned Advocate next relied not he case of Benoy Bhusan Bardhan being dead, his heirs Pronoy Bhusan Bardhan vs The Sub-Divisional Officer, Brahmanbaria, 30 DLR (SC) 139 wherein it is held as:—

"The Dacca High Court examined the position of a co-sharer in possession of a joint property, of which another co-sharer was an enemy, in the case of Anil Kumar Datta Chowdhury vs Province of East Pakistan (1971) 23 DLR 108 and expressed the view that a co-sharer how was presumed to have right title and was in exclusive possession of a joint property could not be said to be in unlawful possession within the meaning of the Enemy Property laws and was not therefore liable to be ousted from the said property without bringing a suit for partition in a civil court according to law."

"The said view of the Dacca High Court is in consonance with the well-established principle that if a co-sharer was in occupation of a common land without objection from his sharer and with their express or implied consent and if the co-shares out of possession are dissatisfied with the manner in which the said common land was being used by the said co-sharer in possession, their remedy or separate possession of their share of the common land it to bring a suit for partition. If, however, such sole occupation of the common land being in denial of rights of the co-sharers out of possession constitutes ouster, the ousted co-shares may also bring a suit for joint possession and compensation. In one of the early decisions of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, Sir Earnest Peacock, in delivering the judgment of the Judicial Committee, laid down the law in this regard, in well-known case of Watson and Company vs Ramchand Dutta and others LR 17 IA 110 ILR -18 Cal, 10, in the following words:—

"It seems to their Lordships that if there be two or more tenants is common, and one (A) be in actual occupation of a part of the estate and is engaged in cultivating that part in a proper course of cultivation, as if it were his separate property, and another tenant in common (B) attempts to come upon the said part for the purpose of carrying on operation there inconsistent with the course of cultivation in which A is engaged and the profitable use by him of the said part, and A resists and prevents such entry, not in denial of B's title but simple with the object of protecting himself in the profitable enjoyment of the land, such conduct on the part of A would not entitle B to a decree for joint possession."

"A co-owner of an undivided share of the joint land has his right, title and interest in every grain of the soil constituting the joint land and cannot therefore be said to be in unlawful possession of such land, even if he is in exclusive possession thereof. Only when there has been separation of a co-sharer's share of land as a result of the partition of the joint land by metes and bounds, either through. Court or amicably, the possession of the co-owner, after such separation, beyond his separated share of the land without the consent of the owner of such land may be is to be not lawful. Until such separation has been effected, the exclusive possession of a co-owner is not presumed to be hostile or advise to other co-sharers who are deemed to be in constructive possession of the said land through the co-sharer in possession. In the instant case, 7.51 acres of land said to be belonging to one Nirmal Kanti Bardhan, who had left Pakistan in 1951, were declared to be leased out to certain  "landless refugees." The appellants contention in regard to the said land is that the said lands were ejmali lands, belonging to the appellant in 8 annas share and to Nirmal Kanti, Amal Kanti and Shyamal Kanti in the remaining 8 annas share all of whom, excepting Nirmal Kanti, were Pakistani nationals, having been in possession of the said lands including the in divided share of the said Ninnal Kanti Bardhan, who relinquished his interest in favour of his Pakistani co-sharers, the said lands cannot be treated as enemy properties. The appellants contention as to the relinquishment of the interest of Nirmal Kanti Bardhan in favour of the appellant and his co-sharers in Pakistan cannot, of course, be accepted in the absence of the necessary registered instrument evidencing such relinquishment and the share of the said co-sharer residing in India court very well be enemy property within the meaning of rule 165 of the defence of Pakistan Rules, 1965 and may be deemed to have vested in the Deputy Custodian or Assistant Custodian by virtue of the Notification dated 3-12-1965, but having regard to the principle of a co-sharer's possession stated above, the possession of the absentee co-sharer's undivided sharer of the land by the appellant and his co-sharers cannot be said to be unlawful and consequently the provisions of The Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order, 1966 are not attracted to the facts of the instant case. The Custodian of Enemy Property representing the share of the enemy owner cannot go into possession of the joint land by dispossessing the co-sharers in possession of the said land without partitioning the same according to law nor can be arbitrarily specify certain area representing the share of the enemy owner and lease out the same to others. It is therefore, abundantly clear that the notice dated 30-5-67 asking the appellant to show cause as to why he should not be made liable to pay compensation for use and occupation of the enemy property as well as the order dated 29-7-67 approving of the lease of the said property to landless refugee, so far as the lands measuring 7.51 acres, in which the appellant was in possession as a co-sharer, were concerted, were without lawful authority.

14. Mr. Shashank Shekhor Sarker, learned Deputy Attorney-General, appearing for the defendant-respondents, on the other hand, submits that, the impugned notice as issued and served was as per law and, as such, learned Judge committed no illegality in dismissing the suit. Learned Deputy Attorney-general elaborately submits that plaintiffs entry to the suit land having not been on proper basis without legal document, their possession over the suit land being defective, the Deputy Commissioner committed no illegality in issuing eviction notice and the learned Judge committed no illegality in dismissing the suit.

15. Let us proceed with our judgment.

16. It is the case of plaintiffs that after acquiring title of the suit property form power of attorney holder, Arman Ali Sarker, who got one schedule land by way of exchange, and thereafter died, plaintiffs purchased the suit property from the successive purchaser from Abdul Khalek Kha, Munnaf Sarker. Plaintiff got remaining schedule land by way of purchase from original owner. From Exhibit 33-39 it appears that plaintiffs purchased the suit land from Ashwani Chandra. Exhibit 32, shows plaintiffs purchase portion of the suit land from Horihor Chandra, who was admittedly owner of the suit property. Plaintiffs mutated their names and possessing the same. The Government issued eviction notice on 15-7-2002 as per provision of section 5(2) and (8) of Bangladesh Government and Local Authority. Lands and Building (recovery of possession) Order 1972 (PO 85 of 1972) directing plaintiffs to give delivery of possession within 30 days of receipt of this notice. Plaintiff challenged this notice by filing Writ Petition No. 45 09 of 2002 and a Division bench of this Court was of the opinion that dispute should be settled in suit. It is the case of plaintiff that earlier Omar Kha and Abdul Khalek Kha was give lease of the property in EP Case No. 50/67-68, Comilla wherein objection raised. Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) on 27-3-1969 ordered that case land does not appear to be government property; Harunur Rashid having tireless again moved for enlisted the property before Enemy Property Department, Comilla in revision whereupon on 5-5-1969 following order was passed "The light of this order of the Deputy Custodian the Property involved in EPL Case No. 50/67-68 at Flag D may be exempted from the management as enemy property. Harunur Rashid being a man of active habit again moved the Assistant Custodian on 27-4-1970 wherein Harunur Rashid stated as :—

“ বর্তমানে উক্ত সম্পত্তি Enemy Property Management List  হইতে উপরোক্ত মতে dropped  হওয়ায়  উহা আর Enemy  সম্পত্তি নাই। তাই উক্ত সম্পত্তি Enemy  সম্পত্তি না হওয়ায় দরখাস্তকারী আইন মতে উহা পাইতে স্বত্ববান নহে। হুজুরের বর্ণিত Lease Renewal  আদেশ অকার্যকরী হওয়ায় দরখাস্তকারী বর্ণিত অবস্থাধীনে উহা নিতে আর ইচ্ছুক নহে। তদুপরি আপত্তিকারীর ভূমি লীজ সূত্রে প্রাপ্ত হইয়া বসত ভিটি গৃহাদি নির্মানে পরিবার পরিজন নিয়া এবং নাল ভূমিতে চাষাবাদ ক্রমে ভোগ দখল করিতেছে।

উপরোক্ত অবস্থাধীনে হুজুরে বিনীত নিবেদন এই হুজুরের বিগত ২৭-৪-৭৪ ইং তারিখের আদেশ বাতিল করিতে মর্জি হয়।”

17. It appears from different registered deeds particularly Exhibit 33-39 that plaintiff purchased the suit land from its original owner. It appears that from eviction notice that it was issued on 15-7-2002. Here we may refer to the law itself. The aforesaid Ordinance, Ordinance No. XXIV of 1979 in the preamble it is stated as "An Ordinance to repeal and with certain amendment re-enact the East Bengal which include Government Lands and Buildings (Recovery of Possession) Act, 1952 and the East Pakistan Government land (Unauthorised occupation) Ordinance, 1960 and to consolidate the law relating to recovery of possession and assessment and recovery of compensation and arrear rents vested from unauthorized occupant of Government and Local Authority Lands and Buildings and section 2(f) given definition of unauthorized occupation of the Government property as "unauthorized occupant" means a person who is in occupation of any land or building or part thereof without having obtained expressed permission or authority of the Government or the Local Authority concerned, as the case may be, and without executing, where necessary, legal documents, and includes.

(I) a person unlawfully inducted into any land or building or part thereof by the lessee; and

(II) a lessee who continues in possession of the land or building or part thereof after expiry of term Or determination of lease."

<u>18. Unauthorized occupation as per law is a person who is unauthorizedly inducted into any land or building or part thereof by lessee or the lessee and who unauthorizedly in occupation after expiry of term or determination of lease. Laws lays that notice for eviction under this law (Ordinance No. XXIV of 1970) is to be served on a person who has been inducted into possession by the Government as lessee and continue in possession even after expiry of period of lease or determination of lease or to a person who has been inducted, into possession by the lessee. Excepting these two categories of unauthorized occupant under this ordinance, Government has no authority to issue any-letter or notice of eviction to anybody. When law does not permit Government to evict excepting these two sections of unauthorized person the notice itself is nothing but illegal as when plaintiffs, claim title and plaintiffs  are in possession and claim of title of plaintiffs are through  registered deed, which has presumptive value, as such, plaintiffs are in possession. On the suit land under  legal authority In such situation, until and unless the Government declared the property of the plaintiff  as vested in the Government, Government has no legal authority to issue such notice. Since notice itself is illegal, question to settle whether the deeds of the plaintiffs are genuine are not required. If Government want to evict plaintiffs from suit land, Government should at first start proceeding claiming the property as abandoned property; government if so advice can initiate but for that government cannot throttle, the plaintiffs by issuing notice which itself is illegal Judgment as passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Chandpur is without any consultation of law itself We find substance in the appeal.</u>

19. In the result, the appeal is allowed without any order as to cost.

20. The judgment and decreed dated 1-12-2009 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Chandpur in Title Suit No. 5 of 2006 is Set-aside. Title Suit No 5 of 2006 is decreed.

21. Send down the lower court records Communicate this judgment at once.

End.

full_judgment:
This is an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

2. In this application, the legality of the Order dated 15-3-2001, passed by the Artha Rin Court, Comilla, in Artha Execution Case No.339 of 2004, rejecting the prayer for amendment of an earlier petition for compromise (solenama) (Annexure-D), has been challenged.

3. It appears from the application that Pubali Bank Ltd, the respondent No. 1, obtained an ex parte decree on 30-1-2000, for an amount of Taka 4,44,68,232.46 (Annexure-A) in Artha Rin Suit No. 66 of 1995, in the Artha Rin Court, Comilla. In due course, the execution case being Artha Rin Execution Case No. 52 of 2002, was filed on 4-7-2002, which was later renumbered as Artha Rin Execution Case No. 339 of 2004.

4. Thereafter, the decree holder and judgment debtors both jointly filed an application on 5-6-2006 under section 38 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 (the 'Act') in three execution cases, namely, Artha Rin Execution Case Nos. 337 of 2004, 338 of 2004 and 339 of 2004 arising out of 3 separate Artha Rin suits, namely, Artha Rin Suit Nos. 39 of 1995, 67 of 1995 and 66 of 1995, respectively (Annexure-B). It is stated in the said petition that in pursuance of an earlier decision of the Board of Directors of the Bank, held on 13-1-2003, it was resolved that the judgment-debtor would repay Taka 3 crore in favour of the decree-holder by 31-12-2005 and accordingly, a solenama was filed in Court but the judgment debtor actually re-paid only Taka 90 lac by that date. As such, on the application of the judgment-debtors, the decree-holder bank allowed them time to repay the rest Taka 2 crore 10 lac by 31-12-2008. The judgment-debtors had by that time, re-paid a further amount of Taka 7 lac, as such, both the decree-holder and judgment debtors filed the petition dated 5-6-2006 by way of solenama, that the judgment-debtor would re-pay the rest Taka 2 crore 3 lac in four installments of Taka 50,75,000 by 31-12-2008, without any further interest. The terms and conditions of the said petition was allowed by the Artha Rin Court in Artha Rin Execution Case No. 339 of 2004 and disposed of the execution case upon full satisfaction by its order dated 5-6-2006 (Annexure-B-1).

5. It now appears that the judgment-debtors in those three execution cases and the decree-holder jointly filed another application on 15-3-2007 under section 57 of the Act read with section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure, praying for keeping the final date of payment on 31-12-2008 but deleting the terms and conditions for re-payment by installments as stated in the joint petition dated 5-6-2006, allegedly stated beyond the decision of the Board of Directors of the decree-holder bank (Annexure-C). The learned Judge by his order dated 15-3-2007, rejected the said prayer on the ground that section 49 Of the Act does not provide for re-payment of the decretal dues without installments (Annexure-D).

6. Mr Idrisur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that section 38 of the Act envisages compromise between the parties even during or subsequent to the filing of the execution case. He further submits that section 45 of the said Act also enables both the decree holder and judgment-debtor to settle the dispute amicably between the parties at any stage, as such, the learned Advocate submits that the learned Judge of the executing Court erred in law in not allowing the petition dated 15-3-2007, deleting the specific date of installments for re-payment of the decretal dues, keeping only the last date for re-payment by 31-12-2008, as resolved earlier by the Board of Directors of the decree-holder-bank and agreed to by the judgment-debtors.

7. We have heard the learned Advocate, perused the application including the order passed by the learned Judge of the executing Court on 15-3-2007.

8. It appears that the learned Judge rejected the petition on the ground that section 49 of the Act does not provide for repayment without installments. But the earlier joint petition dated 5-6-2006 (Annexure-B) which was allowed by the learned Judge, was not filed under section 49 of the Act but under section 38.

9. In this regard, the ambit of the above provisions requires examination, specially when both the decree-holder and the judgment-debtor, filed joint petitions on both the occasions, as such, while there is no dispute between them but the legality of the order dated 15-3-2007 is under challenge.

10. Section 38 of the Act provides for settlement of dispute during the pendency of the execution case and section 45 also provides for settlement of the dispute between the parties out of Court at any stage of the suit or even thereafter.

11. Section 45 of the Act reads as follows:

৪৫।মামলায় আপোষ নিস্পত্তি।–(১) ধারা ২১ বা ২২-এর বিধান সত্ত্বেও, এই আইনের কোন কিছুই, বিচার কার্যক্রমের পরবর্তী যে কোন পর্যায়ে, কোন মামলার আপোষ নিস্পত্তি করা হইতে পক্ষগণকে বারিত করিবে না।

(২)উপ-ধারা(১)-এর অধীনে প্রদত্ত মামলার আপোষ নিস্পত্তির সুযোগ এই আইনে মামলা নিস্পত্তির জন্য ব্যবস্থিত অন্যান্য পদ্ধতি এবং নির্ধারিত সময়সীমার হানি বা ব্যত্যয় ঘটাইতে পারিবে না।

12. It is true that the parties can settle their disputes out of Court at any time but within the ambit of the provisions of this Act.

13. But in this case, it appears from the order-sheet that the learned Judge after allowing the joint petition filed under section 38 of the Act, had already disposed of the execution case, by the Order No. 45 dated 5-6-2006, as such, apparently there is no scope to re-open the case.

14. But on examination of the petition dated 5-6-2006, filed on behalf of both the parties, it would appear that the said petition actually came within the ambit of section 49 of the Act.

Paragraph 3 of the petition reads as follows:

৩। ডিক্রিদার ব্যাংকের পরিচালনা পরিষদের সিদ্ধান্ত মতে ২.১০ দুই কোটি দশ লক্ষ টাকার মধ্যে ৭.০০ সাত লক্ষ টাকা পরিশোধ বাদ বাকি ২.৩ কোটি অর্থাৎ দুই কোটি তিন লক্ষ টাকা বিবাদী দায়িক পক্ষে কর্তৃক আগামী ৩১-১২-২০০৮ইং তারিখের মধ্যে বাদী ডিক্রিদার ব্যাংকে পরিশোধ করিতে হইবে অর্থাৎ আগামী ৩১-১২-২০০৬ইং তারিখের মধ্যে ১ম কিস্তি ৫০,৭৫,০০০ পঞ্চাশ লক্ষ পচাত্তর হাজার টাকা আগামী ৩১-৮-২০০৭ইং তারিখের মধ্যে ২য় কিস্তি মং-৫০,০০০ আগামী ৩০-৪-২০০৮ইং তারিখের মধ্যে ৩য় কিস্তি মং-৫০,৭৫,০০০ টাকা আগামী ৩১-১২-২০০৮ইং তারিখের মধ্যে ৪র্থ কিস্তি মং-৫০,৭৫,০০০ টাকা পরিশোধ করিতে হইবে।

15. It would appear from above that nearly 3 (three) years' time was allowed to repay the entire outstanding dues of Taka 2 crore 7 lac in 4 (four) installments within 3142-2008.

16. In this connection, the difference between section 38 and section 49 may be noted.

17. Section 38 reads as follows:

৩৮।জারীর পর্যায়ে আপোষ নিস্পত্তি।–(১)এই আইনের অধীন অর্থ ঋণ মামলায় প্রদত্ত ডিক্রির ধারাবাহিকতায় জারী কার্যক্রমে অব্যাহত থাকার যে কোন পর্যায়ে পক্ষগণ আপোষ মীমাংসার মাধ্যমে জারী মামলা নিস্পত্তি করিয়া আদালতকে অবহিত করিতে পারিবে।

(২)উপ-ধারা(১)এর অধীন আপোষ মীমাংসা ধারা ২৪-এ উল্লেখিত বিধানে নির্ধারিত পদ্ধতি অনুসরণে বৈধ হইতে হইবে।

(৩)আদালত, উপ-ধারা(১)-এর অধীন অবহিত হইলে এবং আপোষ মীমাংসার বৈধতা বিষয়ে নিশ্চিত ও সন্তুষ্ট হইলে, উক্ত জারী মোকদ্দমা চূড়ান্তভাবে নিস্পত্তি করিয়া আদেশ প্রদান করিবে।

18. This provision envisages that during the pendency of an execution case, the parties may themselves settle their disputes and apprise the Court under sub-section 1 about such settlement. This is the meaning of the words.

"পক্ষগণ আপোষ মীমাংসার মাধ্যমে জারী মামলা নিস্পত্তি করিয়া আদালতকে অবহিত করিতে পারিবে ।"

19. Under this provision, the parties can themselves settle the dispute (নিস্পত্তি করিয়া ) out of Court and then they would apprise the Court (আদালতকে অবহিত করিতে পারিবে) about such settlement.

20. Sub-section 2 describes the procedure how the parties can come to a settlement. This is provided in section 24. The said provision envisages that the settlement of dispute would be effected on the decision of the concerned authorities of the financial institution. On the basis of its such decision, necessary application, apprising such decision of the parties, can be filed jointly by both the parties in Court. The Court after being so apprised of the settlement, under sub-section 3, shall, after being satisfied about the legality of the out of Court settlement, finally dispose of the execution case.

21. On a plain reading of section 38, it would appear that this provision does not envisage filing of any petition of compromise (solenama), rather it envisages final settlement of dispute out of Court, without further claim by the decree-holder from the judgment-debtor. The provision is comparable within Order XXI, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. This provision even allows settlement of a dispute on payment of a lesser amount than the decretal dues.

22. But the ambit of section 49 of the Act is altogether different. Section 49 reads as follows:

৪৯। ঋণের কিস্তি।–(১)উপ-ধারা(৩)-এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে অর্থ ঋণ আদালত, বিবাদী-দায়িকের আবেদনের প্রেক্ষিতে বা স্বীয় উদ্যোগে উপযুক্ত মনে করিলে, ডিক্রিকৃত টাকা ১(এক) বৎসরে ৪(চার)টি সম কিস্তিতে পরিশোধের জন্য দায়িককে সুযোগ প্রদান করিতে পারিবে।

(২)বাদী ডিক্রিদার সম্মত থাকিলে, উপ-ধারা(৩)এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে, ডিক্রিকৃত টাকা ৩(তিন) বৎসরে ১২(বার)টি সম কিস্তিতে পরিশোধের জন্য আদালত, দায়িককে সুযোগ প্রদান করিতে পারিবে।

(৩)উপ-ধারা(১)বা (২)এ উল্লেখিত কোন একটি কিস্তি বকেয়া হওয়া মাত্রই সমুদয় বকেয়া তখনই পরিশোধতব্য হইবে এবং তদউদ্দেশ্যে হারী কার্যক্রম যথাবিধি অনুসৃত হইবে।

23. Sub-section 1 of this provision empowers the Court to allow on an application of a judgment-debtor in an execution case, to repay the decretal dues in 4 (four) installments, within one year, even on the face of the objection of the decree-holder. On the other hand, under sub-section 2, the Court, on the consent of the decree-holder, may allow 3 (three) years to re-pay the decretal dues, in 12 (twelve) installments.

24. But if the judgment-debtor defaults to pay even one installment under sub-section 3, the entire outstanding decretal dues would be payable at once.

25. It appears that in order to get the accommodation under this provision, no formal petition of compromise is required but an application from the judgment-debtor would suffice. If the application is allowed either under sub-section-1 or under sub-section 2, the execution case shall continue till the period allowed by the Court. If the payments are duly made, the Court, on recording its finding, shall dispose of the case, if not the procedure under Chapter-VI of the Act shall be commenced.

26. Under section 38, on allowing the joint petition of the parties, appraising the Court about their out of Court settlement, the execution comes to an end but under section 49, the proceedings of the execution case either comes to an end on satisfaction of the decree on the basis of the unilateral petition filed on behalf of the judgment-debtor with or without consent of the decree-holder or continues under section 33. Once disposed of, there is no such scope under section 38 short of filing a fresh execution case, within the stipulated period, to re-open the case, praying for enforcement of the decree.

27. Under such circumstances, in the present case the earlier joint application dated 5-6-2006, filed on behalf of the decree-holder and the judgment-debtor (Annexure-B), although purportedly filed under section 38 of the Act, but actually was within the ambit of section 49 since it was stipulated therein that the agreed amount would be paid in installments within 31-12-2008, in contradistinction to the provision of section 38 which envisages settlement out of Court and on such basis of settlement, immediate disposal of the case.

28. It appears that the petition dated 5-6-2006, although was filed purportedly under section 38 of the Act but from the language of the petition it appears that it was actually filed under section 49 of the Act. As such, although by Order No. 45 dated 5-6-2006, the execution case was shown to be disposed of but actually it could not be and it was not. It was still pending and the order dated 15-3-2007 itself shows that the learned Judge was still functioning.

29. In the present case, both the decree-holder and the judgment-debtor jointly filed an application under section 57 of the Act, praying for correction of the terms and conditions of settlement but reiterating the re-payment of the agreed amount still within the earlier agreed period of 3 (three) years, by 31-12-2008, in one installment instead of four decided earlier.

30. It is true that sub-section 2 of section 49 allows re-payment with the consent of the decree-holder, within a period of 3 (three) years in 12 equal installments. But from its language " দায়িককে সুযোগ প্রদান করিতে পারিবে it would appear that the provision with regard to the number of installments are directory and not mandatory, as such, with the consent of the decree-holder the number of installments can also be varied. If the decree-holder agrees, the judgment debtor can even repay in one installment so long it is done within the maximum period of 3 years.

<u>31. In the present case, the learned Judge by his order dated 15-3-2007, rejected the joint petition filed on behalf of the decree-holder and the judgment-debtor on the ground that without the provision for repayment in installments as envisaged in section 49 of the Act, the petition is not maintainable.</u>

<u>32. This view is not correct as explained above. The parties in their petition can provide for re-payment of the entire agreed dues in one installment. In the present case, it is agreed between the parties that the judgment-debtor would re-pay the entire agreed dues of Taka 2 crore 7 lac by 31-12-2008. The learned Judge can still consider such a prayer within the ambit of section 49.</u>

<u>33. Under such circumstances without issuing any Rule, the order dated 15-3-2007, (Annexure-D), passed by the Artha Rin Court, Comilla, in Artha Execution Case No. 339 of 7004, is declared illegal and is of no legal effect.</u>

34. The learned Judge would consider the joint application dated 15-3-2007 filed on behalf of the decree-holder and the judgment-debtor in the light of the observations made above.

In the result, the Writ petition is summarily disposed of with the above observations and direction.

End.

full_judgment:
Sheikh Hassan Arif J: Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 24-8-2010 and 7-11-2010 (Annexures-D and F) passed by the Second Court of Artha Rin Adalat, Dhaka(respondent No. 2) in Artha Execution Case No. 164 of 2010, arising out of Artha Rin Case No. 209 of 2009, should not be declared to be without lawful authority and are of no legal effect.

2. Short facts, relevant for the disposal of the Rule, are that the First Lease Finance and Investment Limited (respondent No. 3), a financial institution, filed Artha Rin Case No. 209 of 2009 against the petitioner and respondent Nos. 4 and 6 for realization of Taka 55,25,729.36 (the petitioner being impleaded as third party mortgagor). When the case was taken up for order on 24-2-2010, the defendant No. 4, the father-in-law of the petitioner, entered appearance and filed written statement along with an application for acceptance of the same, but the Adalat rejected the said application and took up the suit for ex-parte hearing and decreed the same ex-parte against the petitioner and others by judgment and decree dated 24-2-2010. The decree-holder institution, accordingly, filed execution case, being Execution Case No. 164 of 2010, before the Artha Rin Adalat for execution of the said decree through auction sale of the mortgaged properties as well as by other means in accordance with law. The decree-holder institution then took steps under section 33(1) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 ("the said Ain") for selling of the said mortgaged properties through auction, whereupon the Adalat, by the First impugned order dated 24-8-2010 fixed 3-10-2010 for auction sale of the said properties. On 3-10-2010, the decree-holder institution itself having filed an application for participation in the auction bidding, the Adalat allowed the same. Accordingly, the auction took place and the decree-holder institution turned out to be the only bidder for the purchase of the said properties with a bid money of Taka 1,63,54,677.23. However, the Adalat, by order dated 3-10-2010, refused to accept the said bid on the ground of lack of competition as the decree-holder institution was the only bidder and accordingly fixed 7-11-2010 for taking steps for further auction sale in view of Section 33(4) of the said Ain. On 7-11-2010, the decree-holder institution filed an application under Section 33(7) of the said Ain for conferring the title of the said properties in favour of it and for issuance of certificate to that effect, whereupon the Adalat, by the Second impugned order dated 7-11-2010, allowed the said application and declared and conferred title of the said mortgaged properties in favour of the decree-holder institution purportedly under Section 33(7) of the said Ain. Accordingly, by the subsequent order dated 1-12-2010, the Adalat issued certificate and disposed of the execution case in view of Section 33(9) upon sending the said certificate to the registry office for registration. Thereafter, the decree-holder institution again filed application before the executing Adalat for reviving the execution case and for an order of possession of the said properties in its favour in view of sub-section (7Ka) and (7Kha) of the said Ain, whereupon the Adalat, by different orders, issued warrant of possession in its favour. At this stage, the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the aforesaid Rule. This Court, vide Rule issuing order dated 8-6-2011, stayed operation of the said certificate.

3. The Rule is contested by the respondent No. 3 Financial Institution by filing an affidavit-in-opposition.

4. Mr Md Mozibur Rahman, learned advocate for the petitioner, submits that the relevant orders of the execution proceeding in question show that the entire proceeding was continued on the premise that the decree-holder institution would somehow grab the mortgaged properties for itself without any proper auction sale in accordance with law. Mr Rahman points out that it is apparent from the said orders that when the decree-holder institution wanted to purchase the properties for Taka 1,63,54,677.29 as a single bidder as against the total liability of the petitioner being Taka 59,65,658.93, the Adalat refused the same and by the impugned order dated 7-11-2010 transferred ownership of the said properties in favour of the said institution free of cost, thereby, depriving the petitioner from lawful adjustment of the decreetal amount out of the sale proceeds and to apply the remaining amount in order to repay the loans obtained in connection with other transactions with the same financial institution. Mr Rahman further submits that when the Adalat itself opined that the bid of Taka 1,63,54,677.23 submitted by the said institution was not enough because of the lack of competition, the same property was given to the same bidder free of cost, which is the abuse of the process of the Court and the provisions of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. This being so, he submits, this Court should interfere and knock down the certificate issued by the Adalat in favour of the decree-holder in respect of the said properties. Drawing our attention to a supplementary affidavit by the petitioner sworn on 5-3-2013, Mr Rahman submits that some flats under Schedule-Ka property had already been sold out to the bonafide buyers even before granting of credit facilities in favour of the petitioner and some other flats were sold subsequently very much within the knowledge of the decree-holder institution. This being so, he submits, unless the certificate issued by the Adalat is set-aside and an order or observation is passed by this Court for protecting the interests of those innocent purchasers, there will be great injustice.

5. Ms Rani Akhter, learned advocate for the decree-holder institution (respondent No. 3), on the other hand, submits that sub-section (7) of Section 33 clearly provides that in spite of the provisions of sub-sections (4) and (5) of Section 33, the Adalat, on the application of the decree-holder institution, can issue certificate of ownership of the mortgaged properties in favour of the decree-holder institution. This having being done in the instant case, she continues, the Adalat or the said institution committed no illegality. Considered the submissions of the learned advocates, perused the writ petition, supplementary affidavit, affidavit-in-opposition and materials on the lower court records. Section 33 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 has made provisions for selling out the mortgaged properties through auction upon following several procedures. The first step to be followed is provided under sub-Section (1) of Section 33 through which an attempt for auction sale of the said property may be taken. If the said attempt is failed for any reason or the bid in the said auction is not accepted by the Court for any reason, the procedures provided under sub-section (4) are to be adopted for the second auction attempt. If, in spite of such second attempt, the properties cannot be sold, the decree-holder, under sub-section (5), may take over the mortgaged properties through Adalat and it may attempt for selling of the same during a period of 6 (six) years. If it succeeds in selling the said properties for a price which is more than the decreetal amount, the remaining amount has to be refunded to the judgment-debtor in view of sub-Section (6). During this six years' period, the decree-holder can also file application before the Adalat for conferment of title of the said properties in its favour in view of sub-Section (6 Kha). Unless such steps are taken or failed for any reason during this six years' period, the decree-holder, with the expiry of the said six years, will get the owner-ship of the said properties on its own by operation of law. Sub-Section (7), however, has given an upper-hand to the decree-holder. It provides that notwithstanding the above provisions under sub-Sections (4) and (5), the decree-holder, after first attempt of auction sale under sub-section (1) of Section 33, under sub-section (1) of Section 33, may seek title of the said properties from the Adalat, whereupon the Adalat will issue such certificate of ownership in favour of the decree-holder.

6. Ms Rani Akhter, putting emphasis on the said provisions under sub-section (7), submits that even if no attempt is made for second auction sale under sub-section (4), the decree-holder can still avail of the opportunities given under sub-section (7) of the said Ain and, as such, the Adalat, in the instant case, has committed no illegality in granting such certificate of ownership in favour of the respondent financial institution.

7. If we read the provisions under section 33 in a mechanical way, the submissions made by Ms. Rani Akhter will sound correct. However, if we examine said provisions along with the relevant orders passed by the executing Adalat in issuing the certificate of 'ownership in favour of the respondent-institution, the impression will definitely be changed. Admittedly, at the instance of the decree-holder, an attempt for auction sale was made by the Adalat under Section 33(1). The decree-holder institution was also allowed by the Adalat to participate in the said auction as a bidder and, accordingly, it submitted its bid for Taka 1,63,54,677.23 for the purchase of the said properties, although the decree-holder filed the very execution case for recovery of a total amount of Taka 59,65,658.93. This means, the decree-holder institution was happily ready to purchase the said properties for an amount which was three times higher than the total decreetal amount for which the auction of the said properties was attempted. Order dated 3-10-2010 shows that the Adalat did not even accept this bid of the decree-holder institution on the ground of lack of competition as the decree-holder institution was the only bidder in the said attempted auction. It may very easily be understood from this order of the Adalat that the value of the properties in question was taken to be much more higher than the bid submitted by the Institution and it was expected that had there been more bidders, much more higher bids would have been submitted.

8. Upon reading the provisions under sub-sections (1), (4), (5) and (6), it appears that the intention of the Legislature in such execution sale was to get as high as possible price for the mortgaged properties so that the judgment-debtor can get some money refunded out of the sale proceeds and that no unfair practice can take place in respect of the sale of the said properties depriving the judgment-debtor from getting a competitive price. Keeping this aspect in view, the Adalat, by the said order dated 3-10-2010, observed that there were opportunities for further auction sale under Section 33(4) of the said Ain and, accordingly, refused to accept the bid submitted by the decree-holder respondent for an amount which was even three times higher than the decreetal amount. If we compare this order dated 3-10-2010 with the impugned order dated 7-11-2010, our impression changes drastically. While the Adalat did not accept a bid which was three times higher than the decreetal amount, the same Adalat, by the impugned order dated 7-11-2010, transferred the entire properties in favour of the decree-holder free of cost. When the decree-holder institution itself wanted to purchase the said properties for a price which was three times higher than the total decreetal amount, we do not see any reasonableness behind the impugned order dated 7-11-2010 through which the Adalat, by mechanical application of sub-section (7) of Section 33, passed an order for issuing certificate of ownership in favour of the same bidder followed by orders issuing the certificate and warrant of possession allowing the decree-holder institution to take possession of the said properties.

<u>9. Although, on the face of the said impugned order and the provisions under sub-section (7), if examined mechanically, there is no illegality as such, peeping behind the orders will reveal the game played by the parties and the sheer injustice done in particular by the decree-holder institution to grab the said properties without spending a single farthing. Although the provisions under sub-section (7) of Section 33 seem to be harshly imbalanced, the Legislature of a democratic country like ours cannot intend injustice to be done by application of such provisions in a mechanical way as has been done in the instant case. It is always the Court's responsibility to look into the intention of the Legislature behind the black words of the statute. The impugned order, compared with the entire proceedings and the subsequent orders, passed by the executing Adalat in the instant case reveals how a provision of law may be applied in a very harsh way and how a gross injustice can be done under the shelter of literary, mechanical and pedantic application of a particular provision.</u>

<u>10. Considering the facts in this case and comparing in particular the order dated 3.10-2010 with the impugned order dated 7-11-2010, we are of the view that the decree-holder institution, by not resorting to sub-section (4) of Section 33, has committed fraud on the Court by using the process of the same to grab the said properties free of cost. This is an ample example of the abuse of process of the Court and the spirit of law for which we have no option but to interfere to prevent such gross injustice.</u>

11. Thus, we are of the view that the impugned order dated 7-11-2010 suffers from gross illegality and injustice and the same should not sustain in law. Consequently, the subsequent orders also fall apart. However, we do not find any illegality in the earlier impugned order dated 24-8-2010 taking steps for auction sale of the properties under Section 33(1) of the said Ain.

12. Accordingly, since we find substance in the Rule in so far as the impugned order dated 7-11-2010 is concerned, the Rule is made absolute in part. Thus, the impugned order dated 7-11-2010 and the subsequent orders issuing certificates of ownership of the mortgaged properties, warrant of possession etc. in favour of the decree-holder institution are declared to have been passed without lawful authority and are of no legal effect.

13. Since it has been brought on record that some flats under Schedule-Ka properties had already been sold out to some innocent purchasers even before issuance of credit facilities and subsequently within the very knowledge of the decree-holder financial institution, we are of the view that the decree executing Adalat will take this aspect into consideration while executing the decree in particular in line with the provisions of sub-section (7 Kha) of Section 33 of the said Ain.

Send down the Lower Court records and communicate this order immediately.

End.
