full_judgment:
This Rule, calls in question the legality and property of judgment and decree dated 9-3-2006 passed by learned Additional District Judge, Third Court, Comilla, allowing Title Appeal No. 196 of 2005 and decreeing the suit by reversing the judgment and decree dated 26-6-2005 passed by learned Senior Assistant Judge, Burichang, Comilla, dismissing Title Suit No. 62 of 2002.

2. Sort facts leading to this Rule are that on 18-11-2002 opposite parties as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 62 of 2002 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, impleading the petitioners as defendants for permanent injunction restraining the defendants from evicting them illegally or leasing out suit land elsewhere or disturbing them peaceful possession in 0.21 acres of land out of 0.97 acres described in Schedule of plaint.

3. The plaintiff's case put in a nutshell are that suit land was belonged to kali Prasanna Chakraborty and others and their names were recorded in CR Khatian No. 251. Junab Ali the predecessor of plaintiffs and Kala Mia took settlement of the suit land with other lands from them through dakhila (rent receipt) dated 10-10-1950 BS. Since then they are exercising their right, title and possession in suit land by payment of rents to landlord and Government successively. Subsequently their names were recorded in SA Khatian No. 303 and mutation Khatian No. 1265 was opened in their names. Afterwards one Nurul Islam claimed title of suit land, which was challenged by Junab Ali in Title Suit No. 77 of 1980 and was decreed on compromise on 21-4-1980. Thereafter, Government enlisted the suit land as vested and non-resident property which was also challenged in Title Suit No. 1 of 1982, which decreed on contest on 30-5-1083. The plaintiffs as heirs of Junab Ali exercising their right, title and possession in suit land but Government threatening them to dispossess. Hence the suit.

4. Defendants contested the suit by filing written statement denying all material allegations made in plaint contending inter alia that the suit land was acquired by the Government in LA Case No. 11 of 1921-22 for public purpose to establish Burichang charitable dispensary, since then they are in possession by constructing a house functioning as dispensary. The suit land was wrongly recorded in the names of predecessors of plaintiffs ultimately it was corrected, now it stands in the name of Government. The plaintiffs have no right, title and possession in suit land. Thus the suit is liable to be dismissed.

5. On the pleading different issues were settled including issue of maintainability and whether plaintiffs have prima-facie title and exclusive possession in suit land.

6. Trial Court dismissed the suit and same was reversed in appeal. Hence the Rule.

7. The learned Advocate appearing for petitioners supports the Rule and submits that it was proved that there is a house in suit land which was earlier functioning as a charitable dispensary belonged to Government. So, plaintiffs exclusively possession was not proved by evidence. He adds that the suit land was acquired by. Government in 1922 but the Court of appeal below misread the entire documents furnished by Government. Thereby came into a wrong findings that the suit land beyond the acquired land of Government. The learned Counsel lastly submits that there is no correct specification of suit land for which injunction cannot be granted.

8. The learned Advocate appearing for opposite-parties opposes the Rule and submits that right, title and possession of plaintiffs were earlier determined in two separate suits. So such questions are barred by res judicata. On the question of maintainability of suit, the learned Counsel candidly submits that suit was not instituted in proper form. Therefore, he prays to send back the suit on remand.

9. In order to appreciate their submissions I have gone through the records and given my anxious consideration to their submissions.

10. The, point for consideration, whether the impugned judgment and decree, calls for interference by this Court.

11. On going to materials on record, it transpires that suit land was belonged to Kali Prasanna Chakraborty and others, plaintiffs claim that suit land was settled to their predecessor Junab Ali and Kala Miah through a rent receipt dated 10-10-1950 BS (Exhibits 2 and 6). Since then they are in possession. Defendants disowned such facts. They claim that the suit land was acquired in LA Case No. 11 of 1921-22 (Exhibits T-Y), Since then they are in possession by constructing a house functioning as Burichang Charitable Dispensary.

12. The paramount consideration in a suit for permanent injunction is whether the plaintiffs have been successful in proving his exclusive possession. The question of title may be looked into incidentally, but decision on title in such a suit is not a guiding principle. In view of the Provisions laid down in Section 54 of the Specific Relief Act perpetual injunction may be granted to prevent the breach Of an obligation in favor of the plaintiffs, whether expressly or by implication provided there exists no measure for ascertaining the actual damage or likely to be caused by threat of the defendants and Where such invasion or threat is such that pecuniary compensation would not afford adequate relief.

13. With regard to the submissions advanced as to sending back the suit on remand, I am of the view that evidences and all materials are there on record, so it is useless to send back suit on remand for causing unnecessary delay in disposal of suit. Therefore, I am inclined to dispose of the revision on merit considering the evidence and materials on record.

14. In course of trial plaintiffs examined four witnesses, of them PW 1 Serajid Islam (Plaintiff No. 1) who stated that their Predecessor got the suit land by settlement through dakhila dated 10-10-1950 BS (Exhibits 2 and 6) and they as heirs possessing the land by cultivating seasonal vegetables. In cross-examination he stated that he has no knowledge who wrote dakhila and in suit land there was a hospital and Government possessed the same but it is not acted upon, medicines were supplied from hospital. PW 2 Abdur Rahim PW 3 Shahidul Islam, PW4 Tajul Islam are local witnesses, they were examined to corroborate the evidence of PW 1. They failed to state anything regarding dakhila dated 10-10-1050 BS and failed to prove the possession of plaintiffs by corroborative evidence. Defendant examined five witnesses, of them DW 1 Shahidul Islam (defendant No. 5), local Tahsilder, who categorically stated that total area of land in plot No. 962 is 0.97 acres, which was belonged to Kali Prasanna and others while they were in possession it was acquired by Government in LA Case No. 11 of 1921-22 (Exhibit ক) Eventually they withdrew the compensation awarded to them (Exhibit খ) and same was published in official gazette (Exhibit গ) and Map (Exhibit ঘ). Now the suit land stand in the name of the Government in Khas Khatian. He added that in suit land there was a Charitable dispensary maintained by District Council. Beside, its there is a Thana Health Complex. The possession of the plaintiffs by cultivating vegetables is not correct DW 2 Md Shah Alam, DW 3 Md Abdur Rahman, DW 4 Haji Abdus Sattar, DW 5 Bishnu Kumar Bhattarcharjee are independent witnesses. They in one voice corroborated the evidence of DW 1 regarding Charitable dispensary situated in suit land.

15. On appraisal of their evidence it appears to me that evidence regarding possession of Government in suit land are consistent, uniform and corroborative with each other. There is absolutely no reason to disbelieve those competent witnesses. Therefore, I am of the view that plaintiffs failed to prove by evidence regarding their exclusive possession in suit land.

16. Moreover, I carefully examined the documents proved by both the parties. The sole basis of plaintiffs title is dakhila dated 10-10-1950 BS (Exhibits 2 and 6), which is an old document without any date and specification of land. Most of the rent receipts (Exhibits 3 and 5 series ) of plaintiffs are not relate to suit land. The documents (Exhibits) indicates that CS plot No. 962 is within the acquired land of LA Case No. 11 of 1921-22. Therefore, the observations made by Court of appeal below to that effect is not correct. It appears that earlier record of rights of plaintiffs were rescinded by Government in different Misc. cases. Now the suit land stands in the name of the Government (Exhibits Z-Z-1, Z-2)

<u>17. It is significant that the suit was instituted on 18-11-2002 but prior to that i.e. on 21-3-1992 the suit land came under Government which was not challenged by plaintiffs. However, the learned Counsel for opposite-parties candidly submits that at present record of rights stands in the name of Government which is now under challenge in a review petition before the Assistant Commissioner (Land) and to that effect I am of the view that before institution of instant suit title of plaintiffs were clouded, for which they failed to seek their redress in any manner whatsoever. So instant suit for permanent injunction is not maintainable.</u>

18. It further appears that all the issues involved in suit have rightly been framed, considered and decided by trial Court with reference to evidences and materials on record. Moreover, I do not find any misreading or non-consideration of evidence on record. The impugned judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below in its entirety are not well founded in the facts and circumstances of the case. So the ground urged and contentions advanced by learned Counsel for petitioners are correct exposition of law and facts and, as such, the legal pleas taken by him prevails and appears to have a good deal of force. On the contrary I failed to discover any merit in the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for opposite-parties.

19. Having considered the facts and circumstances of the case and foregoing narrative, I am of the view that the impugned judgment and decree suffers from legal infirmities, which calls for interference by this Court. Thus the Rule having merit succeeds.

20. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below is hereby set-aside. The order of stay and status-quo granted earlier by this Court stands vacated.

Office is directed to send down the records of the case at once with a copy of judgment for information and necessary action.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 20-2-2007 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 4308 of 2005).
full_judgment:
AHM Shamsuddin Choudhury J : This appeal, with leave, has been preferred by the person who was the auction purchaser of a property that was sold on auction by the Artharin Adalat No. 1 Thakurgaon , in execution of a decree that was earlier passed against the owner of the subject property. This appeal is geared to challenge the judgment and the order the High Court Division passed in Writ Petition No. 4308 of 2005, on 20th February 2007, making absolute the Rule it issued earlier and thereby setting the auction sale, aside.

2. Facts as appear from the writ petition, the respondent No. 1 before us filed, challenging the validity of the auction, are narrated below in succinct form.

3. The respondent No. 1, the owner of the subject property (henceforth cited as respondent No. 1) obtained a loan from the Thakoorgaon branch of Rupali Bank Ltd., a schedule bank, to the tune of Taka 3,70,000. Although he had paid a total of Taka 1,95,800 to the bank in a bid to repay the loan on different dates, yet, he failed to make the total repayment with interest by the stipulated date.

4. In view of the said default by the respondent No. 1, the lending bank initiated a suit, invoking provisions of the Artharin Adalat Ain 2003, for the realisation of the money, inclusive of interest, the said party owed the bank.

5. The suit was decreed inter partes on 31st October 2000. In the wake of the debtor's failure to act in compliance with the decree, the lending bank proceeded with an execution case, registered as, Execution Case No. 12 of 2003, to have the decree executed.

6. After hearing, the Execution Court passed an order, dated 20th April 2005, for the sale of the debtor's real property, the subject matter of the case. The decree holder bank submitted auction notice, took steps for newspaper publication of the auction notice, inviting offer from potential bidders. 30th May 2005 was fixed for the auction sale of the subject property.

7. On 20th April 2005, the judgment debtor, i.e., the respondent No. 1, placed an abortive application before the execution Court, seeking an adjournment of the execution proceeding on the plea that he needs time to pay the amount he owed.

8. The said adjournment prayer having ended in fiasco, the Court proceeded to organise the auction process, but on the scheduled date for auction, i.e., 30th May 2005, no tender was submitted. Yet, the learned Judge concerned, accepted the bid from one Md Abdul Gafur, who is none other than the appellant before us. On 30th May 2005 his bid was accompanied by no bank draft or pay order: he deposited 25% of the bid amount to the Court's sheristadar in cash. No sale took place on 30th May, 2005.

9. Abdul Gafur then submitted his bid on 31st May 2005 along with a pay order and his out of date bid was accepted by the Court concerned and the sale was concluded.

10. The respondent No. 1, the Judgment debtor, then filed an application before the execution Court, engaging Order XXI, rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure, seeking an order for setting the auction sale aside. That application was, however, rejected in limini on the ground of maintainability, not on merit.

11. The sale deed was executed and registered in favour of the decree holder bank during the intervening period.

12. In his Order XXI, rule 90 application, the judgment debtor contended that material irregularities, such as irregularity in the publication of the sale notice, auction sale itself, despite receipt of no bid on the scheduled date, irregularity by selling the property on a date other than the scheduled one and not in the open Court, rendered the auction vitiated.

13. The judgment debtor then filed the subject writ petition praying for an order to the effect that the auction sale having been vitiated for the stated reasons, the order passed by the execution Court was without lawful authority and that rejection of the Order XXI, rule 90 application, was also out Order.

14. The auction purchaser as the writ respondent, through his pleading, tried to refute the writ petitioner's , i.e., the judgment debtor's plea of irregularity by adducing Order sheets, stating that no irregularity was resorted to in the auction process or in the sale itself.

15. The High Court Division, nevertheless, made the Rule absolute, stating, "Having examined the materials on record and also the statements made in the writ petition, it is manifestly clear that the Adalat has not followed the procedure of auction as prescribed by law laid down under sub-section (1) and (2) of section 33 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003."

16. As we took up the appeal for hearing, Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, the learned Senior Counsel who appeared for the appellant, tried to have us to accept that even if any irregularity had taken place, they were neither material nor decisive and that in any event, rejection of Order XXI, rule 90 CPC application caused no loss or injury to the respondent No. 1.

17. He went on to say that in the wake of the said respondents' incessant acts of default, and in view of his failure to repay the loan even after he was allowed by the Adalat a substantial length of time and to pay the dues by 4 (four) installments, the Adalat's decision and action cannot be reckoned to be unreasonable, although it did not strictly comply with the procedure. In Mr Ali's words, it was a case of substantial compliance, which caused no prejudice to the respondent. The Judgment debtor had to honour the decree anyway and, as such, sale of the property was irresistible. Mr Ali added that the allegation of under-pricing was not supported by evidence, that it was too late during the day to erect a wall of challenge when the property has not only been sold, but the sell has already been confirmed and registered. He asked us to weigh the respondents, interest alongside the topsy turvy situation, an Order setting aside the already registered sell, would ensue.

18. Mr Qamrul Huq Siddique, the learned Senior Advocate who appeared for the respondents, on the other hand submitted that the contention of substantial compliance is a myth and the claim that no predicament has been suffered by the respondent by the impugned sale, is but, vacuous.

19. In his introspection the legislators contemplated strict compliance with all the provisions in section 33 of the Ain, as is apparent from the text therein. In his view taking away a person's property and selling it by auction to satisfy his debt is a very serious matter. It involves the question of a person's fundamental rights, which cannot be trumbled lightly. No doubt, Artha Rin Adalat Ain has empowered the Court to auction sell a judgment debtor's property in execution of a decree passed against him. But the judgment debtor is also entitled to legal redress: his property if to be sold on auction, such a sale must be materialised by strictly following all the safeguard provided by section 33. The Court has a duty, not only under the statute, but also, as inhered, to ensure that no property is sold at a throw away price and that can only be ensured if all the requirements figured in section 33 of the Ain are adhered to with comma and dot. He reminded us of even a judgment debtor's entitlement to the constitutionally guaranteed right to property. His concluding chapter of submission was based on the allegation that connivance between the Adalat's officials and the auction purchaser is so obvious and axiomatic from all the surrounding circumstances, that no adducement of evidence is needed to substantiate the same.

20. On our part, to scan the question of the validity and the propriety of the Division below's Judgment and Order, we have perused the judgment concerned, not in isolation, but also in juxtaposition with the order sheets, the execution Court below recorded, the contents in the writ petition, the affidavit in rebuttal filed by the appellant before us, who was the respondent before the Division below and, of course what the learned Advocates from both the sides had to say in their submissions before us.

21. Facts that are beyond qualm, and had  in fact been quite candidly conceded by the appellant's learned Advocate in the Division below, are that (1) 30th May was the date when the auction was fixed to be held, (2) no bid was received by that date, (3) though the respondent approached the Courts Sheristader on 30th May 2005, but he took no pay order or banker's draft, but paid 25% of the bid amount, he fixed at Taka 8,70,518, in cash to the Sheristadar, (4) the auction was not held on that date, (5) the appellant submitted a bid the following date, quite out of time with a pay order, (6) his bid was accepted, (7) the respondents' application under Order XXI, rule 90 was rejected on sight on the ground that the same was beyond maintainability.

22. To appreciate the legal position meticulously, it is incumbent upon us to see what section 33 and all the sub-sections thereto, say on auction sale of a judgment debtor's property, and hence the same are reproduced below, verbatim,

Section 33. Sale by auction.

(i) When the Artha Rin Adalat passing any decree or order for selling a property shall float a sealed press tender in newspaper at the cost of the plaintiff giving mini-mum time of 15 days and the above press tender shall be published at least in one widely circulated national Bengali daily, if the Court deems proper may order to publish in another local Bengali newspaper in addition to the same, if any for ends of justice, and the same notice shall be published hanging in the notice board of the Court and beating drums in the locality.

(ii) Every quotationer while quoting price shall deposit 25% the bidding money with the quotation in favour of the Court and deposit the same with the quotation in the form of bank draft or pay-order and drop the same in the tender box directly along with the bidding documents or the same should be sent to relevant authority by registered post within the fixed time; the tenderer, whose tender has been accepted shall deposit the money within 10 days and in case of failure to do so, shall forfeit the amount of security deposit:

Provided that, if the price so quoted under the sub-section above, if it is exorbitantly lowest, the Court shall reserve the right to cancel the proposal rate.

(iii) The security money as deposited under the provision of sub-section (ii) shall be given to the decree-holder and adjust the same with the claim of the decreetal amount and afterwards, the Court shall look into if the amount quoted by the second highest bidders and the forfeited amount is equaled to the rate of highest bidders quoted amount, then the Court shall invite the second highest bidder for buying the property under auction; if the second highest bidder fails to deposit the total amount within 10 days, the security money deposited by the second bidder, shall be forfeited and given to the decree-holder for adjustment with his claim.

(iv) Provided that, the property could not be sold in auction according to the provisions of sub-section-(i) (ii) & (iii), the Court shall publish the advertisement according to sub-section-(i) at least in two widely circulated national Bengali newspapers and in addition to that in one local newspaper if any, and hanging notice in the notice board of the Court and through beating of drums locally for ends of justice; it is noted that, while doing so, in case of forfeiting the deposited money, the Court shall follow the provisions as laid down in sub-section (ii) & (iii) above.

(v) Provided the property could not be sold in auction according to the provisions as laid down in sub-section-(i), (ii), (iii) & (iv) the property in question shall be vested in the possession of decree-holder till the realization of decreed money and the decree-holder shall sell the decreed property according to the provisions of sub-section- (i) , (ii): & (iv) for realization of unrealized decreetal amount and in the interest of doing so, the Court shall issue a certificate.

(vi) If additional amount is received after selling the property in auction, the said amount so received shall be refunded to the judgment-debtor, and if the amount sold is lesser, further execution suit should be acceptable subject to the provision of section 28.

(vii) In spite of anything contained at sub-section-(iv) & (v) , if the decree-holder is interested to acquire the title of the aforesaid property and submits a petition to the effect in the court, the court shall be desisting from following the process of sub-section (iv) & (v) without hampering the provisions of sub-section-(i) , (ii) , (iii) in any way; and according to the prayer of the decree-holder, the court shall pronounce a decree that the self same property has been vested in favour of the decree-holder and issue a certificate to the effect and the certificate issued in such manner, shall be considered the instrument of right and title and the court shall send a copy of the said certificate .to the local Sub-Registrar for registration.

(viii) Anything contained in any other laws in force, no tax or registration fee shall be recoverable, for issuing the certificate under the provisions of subsection (vii).

(ix) If the possession and ownership of the property is handed over according to the provision of sub-section- (v) or its title is vested according to the provisions of sub-section-(vii) upon the decree-holder, subject to the provisions of Section-xxviii, the said decree shall be treated to be the final disposal of the execution suit.

23. What goes without saying is that strict compliance doctrine would require an Artha Rin Adalat to (1) require every bid, accompanied by 25% of the bid amount, in the form of a bank draft or pay order to be filed before the date fixed for the auction sale. (II) dropage of the bid in the tender box directly along with the bidding documents (or sending the same to the relevant authority by registered post) within the fixed time, (III) attempts must be made to auction sell the property on the schedule date, (IV) if the property cannot be sold in accordance with the provisions in sub-sections (I) (II) & (III), the Court will publish fresh advertisement, this time, at least in two widely circulated national dailies of Bengali vernacular, (IV) if the property cannot be sold after all these efforts, the same shall be vested in the possession of the decree holder who shall hold it for the realisation of the decreed amount.

24. The section also stipulates that the Adalat shall set aside a sale if the price quoted in the bid is exorbitantly low.

25. It is axiomatic that the Adalat concerned has gone nowhere near the principle of strict compliance.

26. Mr Ali's view is that to execute the decree against a debtor, substantial compliance, rather than strict compliance, will do, particularly if such a move does not plunge the debtor to any predicament.

27. No doubt, there are instances where substantial, rather than absolute compliance will suffice. But where legislators contemplates strict or absolute compliance, nothing short of that will pass the test of infallible legality. Which one is to be applied depends on what the legislators intended.

28. In this respect Maxwell's version provides great assistance. In Maxwell's view, "An absolute enactment must be obeyed or fulfilled exactly, but it is sufficient if a directory enactment be obeyed or fulfilled substantially." (Maxwell-Interpretation of Statute, 12th Edition, page 315, also Woodward vs Sarson, 1875 LR 10 C P, Haryana vs PC Wadhwa AIR 1987, SC 1201).

29. The Court of Appeal in London and Clydeside Estat vs Aberdeen District Council (1979 2 All ER 876) went far enough to say that even certain directory provisions are to be followed strictly in order to make the Act valid, adding that strict compliance is not needed in respect to such directory provisions, total noncompliance with which will have no effect on the Act.

30. So, if Maxwell's version be given effect to, absolute compliance would be warranted when the enactment is absolute, as opposed to being, directory.

31. A general misconception prevails amongst many who think that an enactment is directory if no consequence is prescribed for defiance. Although it is true in many cases, it cannot be said to be a rule of thumb for there may be mandatory provisions where consequences are not prescribed.

32. The correct position is that where a statute requires something to be done in a particular manner and the consequence for defiance is prescribed, no problem arises to hold the statutory provision to be mandatory, but even a statute without such prescription can, nevertheless, be mandatory as well if the Parliament actually so intends. It all depends on discovering what the legislators truly intended.

33. The words "shall" and must, which creates new right, privilege or immunity and regulates the manner of such exercise are often deemed to imply mandatory prescription, though such words may also be treated as directory, in other words, the converse is not necessarily, inevitable. There is no general rule of universal application for determining whether an enactment is absolute or directory (Jamshed Khan vs SDM PLD 1987 SC 213).

34. In this regard Lord Penzance observed, "I believe as far as any rule is concerned, you cannot safely go further than that in a case you must look to the subject-matter; consider the importance of the provision that has been disregarded and the relation of that provision to the general object intended to be secured by the Act; and upon a review of the case in that aspect decide whether the matter is what is called imperative or only directory" (Howard vs Bodington 1877 2 PD 203). It all depends upon the construction of the statute concerned.

35. According to a plethora of high preponderant of decisions, to decide whether a statutory provision is absolute or mandatory, the Courts are to asses the true intention of the legislators, by perusing the statute as whole.

36. Lord Campbel in Liverpool Borough Bank vs Turner (1861 30 LJ Ch 379) observed (adopted by the Indian Supreme Court in Bhikra) Jaipuria vs India (AIR 1962 SC 113 and Ramchandra vs Govind AIR 1975 SC 915) no universal rule can be laid down to determine whether a provision is mandatory or directory: it is the duty of the Courts to try to get at the real intention of the legislature by carefully attending to the whole scope of the statute and that the intention of the legislature has to be gathered not only from the phraseology of the provisions but also by considering its nature, design and consequences which would follow from construing it one way or the other.

37. In Abdul Latif Khan vs East Pakistan (PLD 1970, Dacca), Dhaka High Court expressed that the universally accepted view is that it is the duty of the Court to apply the recognised rules of interpretation, and to carefully examine the scope and purpose of the statute and thereby to ascertain the real intention of the law makers in enacting a particular provision.

38. Upon considering the language in the statute, a Special Bench of Dhaka High Court held that time limit for holding a meeting to pass a no-confidence resolution under East Pakistan Local Councils (Vote of No-confidence) Rules, 1963 was mandatory.

39. The Indian Supreme Court in Bhikraj Jaipuria vs India, Supra, and Raza Buland Sugar Co vs Municipal Board (AIR 1965 SC 895) observed that a provision will be construed as mandatory if the object of the enactment will be defeated by holding the provision directory.

40. In Osman Gani vs Moinuddin (27 DLR AD 61) this Division proclaimed that it is a cardinal rule of construction that when statutory restrictions are couched in negative terms they are almost invariably held to be mandatory.

41. The Indian Supreme Court qualified this view by holding that the general rule that negative words usually import mandatory implication is, however, subordinate to the context and the context and the object intended to be achieved by the particular requirement (Bombay Union of Journalists vs Bombay AIR 1978 SC 1617) and, if having regard to the context and that the object of the legislation, provisions of law can be found to be directory notwithstanding negative language.

42. Again, in Atta Mohd Qureshi vs Settlement Commission (PLD 1971 SC 61), Pakistan Supreme Court, before our liberation, held that as a general rule, statutes which enable persons to take legal proceedings under specified circumstances, demand that those circumstances must be accurately obeyed, notwithstanding the fact that the provisions thereof are expressed in merely affirmative language.

43. As pre-liberation Pakistan Supreme Court observed, "In the ultimate analyses it is the intention of the legislature that determines mandatory or directory nature of any enactment and this has to be gathered upon consideration of the whole of the statute (Nawab Bibi vs Rafiq Bano, PLD 1971 SC).

44. This Division is Mujibur Rahman vs Abdul Halim (53 DLR AD 93) observed that the words "shall" or "must" prima facie indicates mandatory nature of a provision, while Pakistan Supreme Court in Mohammad Saleh vs Chief Settlement Commissioner (PLD 1972 SC 326) held that even the words "may" and "shall" in legal phraseology are interchangeable depending on the context in which they are used and are not to be interpreted with the rigidity which is attributed to them in ordinary parlance.

45. In Standard Vacuum Oil Co vs Port of Chittagong (13 DLR 794), the then Dacca High Court expressed that though it would be presumed by the Court that legislature intended to use the words in their natural meaning, if such meaning, however, leads to absurdity, or great inconvenience, or for some other reasons is clearly contrary to the obvious intention of the legislature, the words, which are ordinarily mandatory in nature will be construed as directory and vice versa.

46. Indian Supreme Court in Chandrika Prasad Yadab vs Bihar, (AIR 2004 SC 2036) stated that language used by the legislature is not always decisive, and regard must be had to the context, subject matter and the object of the statutory provision in determining whether the provision is mandatory or directory.

47. The same Court in Mohan Singh vs International Airport Authority (1997 9 SCC 132) observed that though the word "shall" gives an impression that it is intended to be mandatory, yet, it requires to be considered in the light of the legislative intent, carefully attending to the scope of the statute, its nature, design and the consequences that would flow from the construction thereof one way or the other and effect must be given to all the provisions harmoniously to suppress public mischief and to promote public Justice.

48. So far as section 33 of the Ain is concerned, we find little difficulty in holding that the provisions therein arc to be followed absolutely not only because consequences have in fact been prescribed by stipulating that in the event no sale can be conclude as per sub-section (I) (II) (III) or (IV), the Court will make fresh advertisements, and then if even thereafter everything fails, the possession of the property shall be vested in the decree holder, but also because, it becomes abundantly clear, by following the ratio of the above discussed cases, that the legislators really intended absolute compliance, as without - that the safety valves provided by section 33 would end up in total haywire.

49. The High Court Divisions decision in Kohinoor Chemicals Ltd. vs Eastern Shippers and Traders (41 DLR 387) to the effect that time stipulated for doing thing is to be treated to be only directory in the absence of specification of consequences, cannot apply in respect to section 33 of the Ain as consequence when bidds are not submitted within specified time, have actually been spelt out.

50. Moreover, under Lord Penzance's view also the provisions in section 33 of the Ain are to be treated as mandatory because it is clear from the language in that section that the legislators intended full protection of the judgment debtor's interest.

51. In this regard it is also to be kept in mind that auction selling of a person's property is a serious matter, where, even generally, all protective devices must be insulated, scrupulously.

52. The owner's fundamental rights under Articles 31 and 42 must not be kept at the bay. Article 42 speaks of a person's right to property subject to any law. Now, section 33 of the Ain is such a law under which a Person's right to property can be transgressed upon. But so far as he has a fundamental right to property, any law that can impair such right, must be construed strictly.

53. A cannon of statutory, interpretation sermons that statute must be interpreted in a manner that can be conducive to citizens rights as far as possible.

54. Article 31 also requires all concerned to treat everyone in accordance with the law, a right that is inalienable. These constitutional provisions undoubtedly require an Artha Rin Adalat to strictly comply with the dictations as contained in section 33 when it decides to auction sell a judgment debtor's property.

55. As no sale took place on 30-5-2005 and, as the appellants submitted no tender, did not deposit any pay order or bank draft on the said date, but the pay order/bank draft was prepared fixing the bid money at Taka 8,92,000 on the following day, sell on the following day, which was not the scheduled date, and again, out of Court, was obviously in breach of the mandates beamed by section 33 of the Ain.

56. The petitioner filed applications on various dates to have the proceeding of sale stayed and subsequently filed an application under order 21 Rule 90 for setting aside the sell, but that was turned down by the Adalat without making any investigation Artha Rin Ain, 2003 is a special law and the procedure laid down there is to be strictly adhered to and followed mandatorily. No expediency is permissible in dealing with the matter arising out of Artha Rin Suit, particularly in selling the properties of judgment debtors in auction.

57. In the instant case as the Adalat failed to follow the special procedure of auction sale, and to comply strictly with what section 33 Commands, the act of auction selling the properly was certainly devoid of jurisdiction.

58. Thus, we are swayed to the irresistible conclusion that it was not open to the trial Court to deviate by even an inch from what section 33 with all its subsections command and that by failing to follow those strictly, and rather acting in a casual manner, the learned trial Judge acted without lawful authority and, hence, the High Court Division was quite astute in its decision.

59. Now, we must also look at the question involving the propriety of the rejection order that the respondent's Order XXI, rule 90 application, generated'. That necessitates us to scan the text in the said CPC provision, which is hence reproduced below:

"(1) Where any immoveable property has been sold in execution of a decree, the decree-holder, or any person entitled to share in a rateable distribution of assets, or whose interests are affected by the sale, may apply to the Court to set aside the sale on the ground of a material irregularity or fraud in publishing or conducting [or on the ground of failure to issue notice to him as required by rule 22 of this Order", ([Provided (i) that no sale shall be set aside on the ground of such irregularity, fraud or failure unless, upon the facts proved, the Court is satisfied that the applicant has sustained substantial injury by reason of such irregularity, fraud or failure.

(ii) that no sale shall be set aside on the ground of any defect in the proclamation of sale at the instance of any person who after notice did not attend at the drawing up of proclamation or of any person in whose presence the proclamation was drawn up, unless objection was made by him at the time in respect of the defect relied upon.]"

60. What is abundantly clear that this rule empowers a Court to set aside an auction sale of a real property, held in execution of a decree on the application of a decree holder or other persons whose interests have been affected by the sale, on the ground of irregularity or fraud, provided the applicant has substained substantial injury.

61. Competence to prefer such an application does not lie in the exclusive domain of the decree holder, but also extends to anyone else whose interest has been affected.

62. This Division in Antibiotic Stores vs Subordinate Judge, (55 DLR AD 13) held that remedy under this rule is available in an execution case under Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003.

63. It has also been quite cogently held by the High Court Division in Molla Shahidul Islam vs Monsur Rahman (57 DLR 164) that no security deposit has to be made as per section 32 (2) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 to prefer an application for setting aside a sale pursuant to a decree passed by an Artha Rin Adalat, a decision we accord our recognition to.

64. Since the order, by which the respondent's Order XXI, rule 90 application was rejected, was a non-speaking one, it is not discernible to know what made the execution Court to arrive at the decision that the said application lacked maintainability.

65. However, we would re-iterate that whenever an application engaging the said pro-vision of the CPC is filed, it becomes a bounden duty of the Court concerned to explore the question whether any of the reasons specified in Order XXI, rule 90 had or had not actually been flouted. Such an application cannot hence be rejected in limini, without exploring those questions, unless the application, on the face of it, is vexatious. In any event the learned trial Judge ought to have assigned reason for holding against maintainability.

<u>66. This is also to be borne in mind that a proceeding under Order XXI, rule 90 is an original proceeding, and not a proceeding in an execution case. Thus by rejecting, the application in limini, the execution Court acted in breach of what Order XXI, rule 90, dictates.</u>

67. The phrase interest, referred to in this rule mean any kind of interest having some direct and positive relation with the property concerned, which must be a present or an existing interest (Punjab Ali vs Mukarram Hossain, 29 DLR SC 185).

68. Calcutta High Court in Dhirendra vs Kamini (AIR 1924 Cal) held that the term interest in the rule extends to all sorts of interests, recognised by law, such as pecuniary interests, proprietors interests, possessory interests and so on.

69. Hence, the subsequent order, the Adalat passed on 8-6-2005, so far as it relates to the disposal of the Miscellaneous Case Under Order XXI, rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure is concerned, was visibly in abdication of its jurisdiction as it failed to make investigation on the allegations of material irregularities, fraud or illegality etc as per the dictations contained in Order XXI, rule 90.

<u>70. These provisions clearly indicate that the application is to be disposed of after making an investigation and the executing Court has to determine on receiving evidence, whether there has been any material irregularity or whether fraud has been practiced and whether the applicant has sustained substantial injury by reason of such irregularities or fraud.</u>

71. In view of what have been stated above, the sell of the properties on 31-5-2005 is declared to have been illegal and without jurisdiction and the subsequent order made on 8-6-2005 on the Order XXI, rule 90 application, filed by the judgment debtor, is also liable to be struck down.

72. This appeal is, hence dismissed, without, however, any order on cost.

73. In consequence the High Court Division's Judgment and Order, setting aside the auction sale, concluded by the Artha Rin Adalat No.1, Thakoorgaon, in Execution Case No 12 of 2003, dated 20th April, 2005, as well as the Order by which the defendant/respondent's Order XXI, rule 90 application was turned down, stands endorsed, as the High Court Division arrived at a right decision.

Before parting, we are inclined to express that the surrounding facts go a long way to suggest that there may have in fact been some connivance between the appellant and the officials concerned, as suggested by Mr Siddique.

End.

full_judgment:
K. Hossain, C. J:- Bangladesh, the defendant in a suit for declaration, is the appellant before us and the matter arises out of an ex-parte decree, which the defendant attempted to set aside, but failed to get relief in the courts below. The plaintiff-respondents on the basis of annual leases from 1929 till 1950 and on payment of revenue till the acquisition of rent receiving interest on 14-4.56 claimed to have acquired tenancy right under the Government and brought the suit in 1968, for declaration of their tide. More than 254 bighas of land are involved in the suit claimed by different plaintiffs, though they have joined together to bring one suit. The suit was decreed exparte on 7-5-69, though the exparte order was recorded earlier on 7-4-69, and it was found that deficit court fees were required to be paid by the plaintiff. The Government applied for sitting aside the exparte decree and got, it set aside by an exparte order on 8-6-72, and the written statement filed by the defendant was accepted. The respondents then moved the court and got another exparte order setting aside the earlier order which set aside the exparte decree. Thereafter the application for setting aside the exparte decree was heard in presence of both sides and the trial court by its order dated 14-8-74, dismissed the Miscellaneous case by which the Government tried to set aside the exparte decree. The order was affirmed on appeal and revision. Leave was granted to consider two questions; first, whether the exparte decree passed by the trial Court satisfied the legal requirement of a judgment, and second, whether the defendant-Government made out a case for setting aside the exparte decree, in that it had sufficient cause for not appearing on the date of hearing.

2. It is to be observed that this is a deplorable case of laches on the part of the lawyer and officers responsible for the conduct of the case on behalf of the Government, but then the court is to see whether the Government had a case to be considered. It seems that this aspect of the case was not considered by the courts below. Apart from this, if we revert to the first question, we find that the trial Court decreed the suit by two orders and they are produced below:

“7-4-69 Plffs. file hazira. Defdts take no steps and are absent on calls. The suit is taken up for exparte hearing. P. W. 1 Israil Ali is examined. Exts. 1-1 (d), 2-2(b) & 3-3(1) are marked for the puffs, case is proved. No decree can be passed in this suit until ad valorem court fees are paid on the plaint in view of the nature of the suit. To 7-5-69 for paying the same.

"7-5-69, Plffs. file deficit court fees worth Rs. 956/25. Shdr to certify the court fees. Exporter deposition of the plffs. already recorded, but deed. Province prays for time to file W. S. to-day. Prayer be rejected as belated one."

Ordered

“That the suit be decreed exparte without costs. It be hereby declared that the plffs. have jote right in the suit land and that they are entitled to hold the same in such right as tenants under the defdt. Government."

<u>3. It may be mentioned that in an earlier case in the case of Bangladesh v. Abdul Wadud (1) and Nur Jahan Begum v. Girl Gopal Sarker,(2) this Court had the occasion to remark that exparte disposal of suit in the manner set out above is not warranted under the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. It is expected that the courts below should observe the minimum legal requirement in disposing of a suit exparte.</u>

<u>4. If we now revert back to the order, it seems that the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error of procedure in deciding the case exparte, and then giving the plaintiff an opportunity to pay the deficit court fees which he ought to have done prior to the hearing of the matter. Apart from this technical error, the trial court again committed an error of procedure in not complying with the mandatory provision. It has been only stated that P. W. 1 was examined. Exts. 1-1(d), 2-2(b) and 3-3(i) marked and the plaintiff's case proved. This does not at all satisfy the legal requirement, nor is it possible from reading the judgment that the trial court at all applied judicial mind; whether the plaintiff's witnesses and the papers produced proved the plaintiff's case. It seems that the papers reveal that a serious question of law involved is, whether the facts asserted by the plaintiffs, even if proved, confer on them their alleged tenancy right under the Government. On their own statements, they successively took yearly leases till 1950 and paid rent or revenue upto 1956. Could these facts make out a. case of tenancy right alleged by the plaintiffs? It was incumbent on the trial court to see whether such feta confer a legal title on the plaintiffs against the Government. In any event, we do not want to express any opinion on this point, excepting to say that the finding recorded by the trial Court neither satisfy the legal requirements nor from such finding the alleged case of the plaintiffs was proved. In this view of the matter, we allow the appeal with costs; set aside the judgments of the Courts below and send the case back on remand to the trial Court for disposal of the suit in accordance with law and in the light of the observations made above after hearing both the parties.</u>

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 6-5-1999 and 11-5-1999 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Rangpur, in Other Class Appeal No.123 of 1998 reversing the judgment and decree dated 21-7-1998 and 28-7-1998 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, PS Badarganj, District Rangpur, in Other Class Suit No. 50 of 1997 should not be set aside.

2. The plaintiffs-respondents-petitioners instituted a suit for permanent injunction and the short fact of the case is that the suit land has originally belonged to Aminuddin Pramanik and Shaharon Mai Bibi and the CS Khatian was duly recorded in their name. While Amiruddin and Shaharon Mia were in peaceful possession of the suit land by purchase they wanted to sell the land for necessity of money, then Shibran Mohanto, the predecessor of the plaintiff purchased the suit land on 14-11-1942 by a registered deed and became the owner and possessor of the suit land. Subsequently SA Khatian was duly prepared in the name of Shibran Mohanto who died leaving behind his two sons namely, Mohabir and Shukdeb. Thereafter on the death of Shukdeb the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 became his heirs and after the death of Mohabir the plaintiff No. 3 became his heir. They have been possessing the suit land on payment of rent and in some portion of Plot No. 613/1080 they constructed homestead and in Plot No. 614 they planted fruit trees such as mango, jack-fruit, lichi trees, etc. They have been enjoying the property for 55/56 years. On the other hand, the defendants have got no right, title and possession in the suit land. On 12-7-1997 AD the defendants threatened to dispossess the plaintiffs forcibly from the suit land and thereafter on 25-7-1997 they tried to erect some huts in some portion of the suit land but due to strong resistance of the plaintiff they could not erect any hut. The defendant is threatening the plaintiff continuously to dispossess him from the suit land hence the plaintiff was constrained to institute the suit.

3. On the other hand, the defendants-opposite parties contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and stating, inter alia, that Shahar Mai Bibi was the tenant under the original landlord Najargpat Singh and others. Subsequently, Shahar Mai Bibi sold the suit land to Amiruddin Paramanik, the predecessor of the defendants in CS record. That out of 3.28 decimals of land 2.02 decimal was in khas possession of Amiruddin and he made pattani settlement of the remaining land and it was recorded in CS Khatian Nos. 87, 88, 91, 92 and 93 respectively. That Shibran Mohanto, predecessor of the plaintiff, was a borgadar under Amiruddin Paramanik and thereafter SA khatian was wrongly prepared in the name of Amiruddin Paramanik and Shibran Mohanto which Amiruddin did not know in his life time. Since Shibran Mohanto did not give the borga crops regularly, so Amiruddin Paramanik returned back the land in his own possession. Thereafter, when settlement operation for preparing SA record was started the fake right of Shibran Mohanto was cancelled.

4. Thereafter, Amiruddin died leaving behind his widow Shaharon alias Shahar Mai and three daughters namely, Asia Mai, Asron Mai and Nais Mai and one son Sarafuddin. Then Sarafuddin died leaving behind two sons, namely, Aftabuddin and Abu Taleh. Then Asaron Mai died leaving behind two sons Afsar Ali Mondal and Asgar Ali Mondal and a daughter Kandiri Mai. Then Afsar Ali Mondal died leaving behind five sons namely, Mosharraf Hossain, Ashraf, Wares, Golam Moula and Ziauddin and six daughters namely, Amena Khatun, Asma Khatun, Jahanara, Sufia, Shefali and Ayesha Khatun. Thus they remained in ejmali possession of the suit land. Thereafter Alauddin, Abdul Hakim and Halima Khatun sold 80 decimal of land on 7-7-1997 and Wares All sold 10 decimal of land And Azahar Ali sold 5 decimal of land on 17-7-1997 to Alikur Rahman, the defendant No. 3. That the defendant No. 3 got the property by purchase and the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 got the property by way of inheritance and they have erected tin shed and have been living in the suit land and the remaining portion they are possessing by cultivation. The predecessors of the plaintiff have got no title and possession in the suit land and that deed dated 24-11-1942 in favour of the plaintiffs are forged, false and collusive. The plaintiffs have got no possession in the suit land and the suit brought for permanent injunction is liable to be dismissed.

5. During the course of trial the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Rangpur on consideration of the evidence on record, documents and exhibits produced by both the plaintiffs and the defendants to prove their respective cases found that the plaintiff has been able to prove the case successfully. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, Rangpur after perusing documents and exhibits and the connected papers passed the judgment and decree on 21-7-1998 in favour of the plaintiff.

6. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court, the defendants appellants-petitioners preferred the appeal before the learned District Judge, Rangpur which was ultimately heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Rangpur who was pleased to allow the appeal and reversed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court by his judgment and decree dated 6-5-1999.

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree dated 6-5-1999 and 11-5-1999 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Rangpur in Other Class Appeal No. 123 of 1998 the plaintiffs-appellants-petitioners preferred the instant revisional application under section 11.5 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the High Court Division and obtained the present Rule.

8. Mr Alauddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-respondents-petitioners, submits that the plaintiff has been able to prove the case successfully by producing the original title deed dated 24-11-1942 and the certified copy of the CS Khatian, SA Khatian, rent receipts and other connected papers which were proved and exhibited as Exhibit-1, 2, 3, 4 and rent receipts as Exhibits series 5.

9. The plaintiff examined as many as 4 witnesses to prove the possession of the suit land. The plaintiff Ganesh Mohanto was examined as PW 1 who categorically stated in his evidence that the entire case of the plaint was proved and exhibited the original registered deed of the year 1942 as Exhibit 1 and CS Khatian Exhibit 2, SA Khatian Exhibit 3, BCR Exhibit 4 and rent receipts Exhibits 5 series. The PW 2 Abdus Sobhan, PW 3 Sharifuddin and PW 4 Mominuddin were examined to prove and corroborate the PW 1 with regard to the possession of the plaintiff in the suit property. Next, he submits that the learned Additional District Judge, Rangpur did not at all apply his judicial mind in assessment of the evidence of the PWs, particularly the evidence of PW 1 plaintiff and also did not consider the original registered title deed over 55 years old, CS Khatian, SA Khatian, DS Khatian and rent receipts. The observation made by the lower appellate Court that in the CS Khatian the name of Shahar Mai Bibi should not be published along with the name of Amiruddin, because she transferred her share to her husband Amiruddin before publication of CS Khatian. The learned Counsel further submits that this finding of the learned Additional District Judge, Rangpur is manifestly perverse, because it is neither the case of the plaintiff nor the case of the defendant and he has made out a third case of transfer without any basis and no such transferred deed or document was produced before the Court by any parties. Finally, the learned Counsel submits that the cardinal principle of law followed in reversing the finding of the trial Court, the lower appellate Court should reverse the finding with reference to the evidence on record assigning the cogent ground. But the lower appellate Court without applying his judicial mind and without considering the evidence on record and Exhibits i.e. 55 years old original registered title deed, original CS, DS, RS Khatian and series of rent receipts, disbelieved the case of the plaintiff without assigning any cogent reason occasioning failure of justice which is liable to be interfered by this Court. In support of his contention the learned Counsel referred the decision in the case of Shishir Kanti Pal and others vs Noor Muhammad and others reported in 55 DLR (AD) 39 wherein it is stated:

"A registered document carries presumption of correctness of the endorsement made therein—One who disputes this presumption is required to dislodge the correctness of the endorsement".

10. On the other hand, the learned Counsel Mr KZ Alam with Mr Md Firoz Shah, appearing on behalf of the defendants-appellants-opposite parties, submits that the finding of the lower appellate Court is final unless and until it appears to be manifestly perverse. The learned Additional District Judge, Rangpur is absolutely correct and justified in reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court because the plaintiff miserably failed to prove his possession in the suit land. The defendant examined as many as 5 witnesses to prove his possession and as well as produced and exhibited 3 registered title deeds executed by Azizur Rahman, Asgar Ali and Wares Ali, the grandson of Amiruddin Promanik in the name of Atiqur Rahman, the defendant No. 3 who was examined as DW 3. The learned Counsel next submits that the defendants purchased the suit land measuring 95 decimals of land from the heirs of Amiruddin Promanik by 3 registered deeds dated 3-7-1997, 7-7-1997 and 17-7-1997. The DW 2 proved and exhibited the registered deeds and stated in his evidence that since the purchase i.e. from 1997 the defendants have been in possession of the suit land. The learned Counsel further submits that there was no misreading, non-reading and non-consideration of any material evidence by the learned Additional District Judge, Rangpur and he did not commit any error of law in allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. The learned Counsel next submits that in a suit for permanent injunction the factum of possession is a main consideration of the Court and the question of title is a secondary matter. In support of his contention, the learned Counsel referred the decision in the case of Md Kamal and others vs AKM Mohsin and others reported in 10 MLR (AD) 100 wherein it has been held that:

"In a suit for permanent injunction plaintiff must prove his exclusive possession. Court can incidentally, look into the prima facie title.

It is well-settled that in a suit for permanent injunction the plaintiff is required to prove his exclusive possession of the suit land and prima facie title thereto. Court cannot decide title in a simple suit for injunction."

11. The learned Counsel finally submits that the lower appellate Court after proper assessment of the evidence on record and applying his judicial mind came to a correct and justified finding in reversing the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial Court which is not liable to be interfered by this Court, as such, the Rule should be made absolute.

12. On a meticulous examination of the evidence on record, documents, khatian, rent receipts and judgment of both the Courts below and other connected paper, it transpires that the trial Court discussed the evidence and also perused the documents, exhibits and also considered the material evidence on record and made his clear observation in decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiff. The lower appellate Court without applying his judicial mind gave much importance in determining the title of the suit land without considering the prime factor of possession. In the instant case, the plaintiff examined 4 witnesses to prove his title in the suit land and also to prove his possession and all the 4 witnesses categorically stated in their evidence that the plaintiff has been living in the suit land since the purchase of the suit land in the year 1942 i.e. about 55 years. On the other hand, the defendant claimed that they purchased the same suit land in the year 1997 and since then they have been in possession of the suit land but the defendant could not prove any act of possession by adducing cogent evidence. Moreover, it appears from the title deed of the plaintiff that Amiruddin Promanik and his wife Shahar Mai Bibi purchased the suit land by a registered deed on 24-11-1942 and the original document was produced and exhibited by the plaintiff and three other PWs stated in their evidence that the plaintiff has been living in the suit land since long, as such, the plaintiff is in consistent possession of the suit land since purchase. Therefore, the plaintiff has been able to prove his title and possession over the suit land by producing original title deed and by adducing oral evidence proved his possession in the suit land. In this connection, I like to refer the decision in the case of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) vs Md Reazuddin PK and others reported in 5 BLC (AD) 76 section 90 Evidence Act wherein it has been held:

"Once such a document more than 30 years old is produced from proper custody section 30 of the Evidence Act entitles the Court to presume that it is a genuine document."

13. The lower appellate Court while reversing the judgment of the trial Court did not refer to the evidence on record and in reversing the judgment of the trial Court the lower appellate Court should assign a cogent and reasonable ground for doing so. In this connection, I like to rely on the decision in the case of Mohsina Khatun vs Ms Habib Knitting Mills reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 47 wherein it is laid down:

"While reversing the judgment of the trial Court the appellate Court is required to reverse the material findings of the trial Court with reference to the evidence on record."

<u>14. From impugned judgment of the trial Court it transpires that in arriving at its finding the said Court carefully considered the material facts and circumstances of the case and also the material evidence on record, the documents, exhibits, the legal position, and also the act of possession in the suit land. The learned trial Court did not commit any error of law and illegality in arriving at its finding because the plaintiff could be able to prove his title as well as the possession in the suit land by adducing oral and documentary evidence. The lower appellate Court, on the other hand, committed an error of law and came to a wrong and erroneous finding occasioning failure of justice in not believing the 55 years original title deed and the possession of the plaintiff over the suit land which was a prime factor of the suit for a permanent injunction and, as such, committed an error of the law which is liable to be interfered by this Court. In this connection, I like to rely on the case of Hussain Ahmed Chowhdhury alias Ahmed Hussain Chowdhury vs Nurul Amin reported in 47 DLR (AD) 162 wherein it has been held:</u>

<u>"If there is misreading of evidence and non-consideration of some material evidence then it was incumbent on the revisional Court to consider the same and to arrive at a proper finding on the material evidence on record and to finally dispose of the case".</u>

15. In view of the facts and circumstances and the legal position of the case I find that the lower appellate Court is absolutely wrong in reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court as such the judgment and decree passed by the lower appellate Court is liable to be set aside.

16. The discussion made above and the facts and legal position of the case, the impugned judgment and decree dated 6-5-1999 and 11-5-1999 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Rangpur, in Other Class Appeal No. 123 of 1998 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 21-7-1998 and 28-7-1998 respectively passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, PS Badarganj, District Rangpur, in Other Class Suit No. 50 of 1997 is hereby set aside and the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court is hereby affirmed.

17. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to the costs.

18. The order of maintaining status quo issued earlier by this court at the time of issuance of the Rule is hereby vacated.

Lower Court records are sent down at once with a copy of the judgment.

End.
