full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: The petitioners seek Leave to Appeal by way of review of the judgment and order dated 25-6-2005 passed by this Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 329 of 2005 against the impugned judgment and order dated 10-1-2005 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2908 of 2004 discharging the Rule issued against those dated 7-8-2004 of the Additional District Judge, Manikgonj in Civil Revision No. 10 of 2004 affirming the interim order of temporary mandatory injunction dated 30-3-2004 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Manikgonj in Title Suit No. 60 of 2001.

2. The respondent filed the suit for permanent injunction restraining the petitioners from dispossessing him forcibly from the suit property and of taking any possession thereof and also from disturbing him with his peaceful possession therein stating, inter alia, that his father, Abdur Rahman acquired the suit property from the Industrial Corporation Limited on the basis of an agreement dated 24-3-1954 and purchased shares of the company and subsequently the plaintiff's father orally gifted the suit property to the plaintiff and that after the death of Abdur Rahman the plaintiff started a Miscellaneous Case No. 273 of 1974 for setting aside the ex parte decree obtained by one Afseruddin Ahmed in Title Suit No. 99 of 1967 and obtained a decree and in execution thereof got possession of the suit land through Court and since then he has been in exclusive possession of the suit land. The plaintiff constructed a cinema hall on the suit land but as the cinema business was found not profitable, the plaintiff decided to construct a market on the suit land and got a plan passed from Manikgonj Pourashava in 1987 and started construction of wall and completed the first floor and undertook to construct the second floor and let out 31 shops of the first floor keeping some space for his own purpose. According to the plaintiff, some of the defendants gave nadabipatra relinquishing their claims in the suit land and that the defendants have no title or possession in the suit land.

3. After the institution of the suit on 10-6-2001 the plaintiff made a prayer for temporary injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing the plaintiffs forcibly from the suit property and also from disturbing in any way the plaintiff's possession therein.

4. By order dated 10-6-2001 the trial Court directed to issue notices on the defendants asking them to show cause within 10 days as to why the prayer for temporary injunction should not be allowed.

5. The defendant Nos. 2-7, 9 and 11 appeared in the suit on 13-6-2001 and prayed for time to file written objection, which was allowed and 26-6-2001 was fixed for filing written objection. On 26-6-2001 the defendant Nos. 1-11 by filing separate applications prayed for adjournment to file written objection and the plaintiff renewed his prayer for temporary injunction. The trial Court allowed the prayer for adjournment for ends of justice and in consideration of the facts and circumstances of the: case passed, an order of status quo directing the parties to maintain their respective possession as to that nature and character of the suit land. The plaintiff then filed violation Miscellaneous Case No. 28 of 2001 On 5-7-2001 under Order XXXIX, rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure claiming that the defendants attempted to dispossess the plaintiff from the suit property but they were however; resisted. Thereafter, the plaintiff again filed violation Miscellaneous Case No. 32 of 2001 on 23-7-2001 under Order XXXIX, rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure against the defendants alleging that the defendants made an attempt to evict the plaintiffs from the suit property which was, however, resisted. The plaintiff subsequently filed violation Miscellaneous. Case No. 37 of 2001 on 13-8-2001 under Order XXXIX, rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure alleging wrongful attempt to dispossess the plaintiff from the suit property upon violating the order of status quo but ultimately, failed in their attempts. Lastly, the plaintiff filed another violation Miscellaneous Case No. 44 of 2001 on 30-9-2001 under Order XXXIX, rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure alleging a further attempt by the defendants to evict the plaintiff from the suit property. Thereafter, the plaintiff filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of possession of the suit land alleging, inter alia, that the defendants with the help of army personnel arrested the plaintiff and his brothers and with the active help of the police of Manikgonj Police Station took over possession of the suit market in clear violation of the order for status quo passed by the trial Court and have been in occupation of the market upon realising rents from the tenants on threat and duress on and from 1-10-2003. The plaintiff accordingly, prayed for an order on the defendants to restore possession of the suit property including the, suit market, as described in the schedule to, the application to the plaint.

6. The defendants contested the prayer for mandatory injunction by filing a written objection contending amongst others, that the plaintiff has no title or possession in the suit land and that the defendants are in possession of the same and there was no occasion for granting any order of injunction in mandatory form in favour of the plaintiff asking the defendants to restore possession of the suit market to the plaintiff. The contesting defendants therefore prayed for rejecting the application filed under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of possession of the suit market to the plaintiff.

7. The trial Court heard the matter and by order dated 30-3-2004 found that the defendants violated the order of status quo passed by the trial Court and thereby passed an order of eviction of, the plaintiffs front the suit property including the suit market. The trial Court also took notice of few decisions reported in 47 DLR (AD) 6, 20, DLR 501; 35 DLR (AD) 42 and followed the proposition of law laid down in those decisions holding "The state of things existed just at the date of institution of the suit to prevent the defendants from doing any act to defeat the very purpose, in such case may issue an order in mandatory form to demolish the thing done, by the defendant." The trial Court found that the cinema hall situated on the suit land on the basis of a licence in the name of the plaintiff, the payment of holding tax by the plaintiff and payment of income tax by the plaintiff alone including the plan of the market in the plaintiff's name alone and the agreement with the tenants indticting them into possession of several shops in, the suit market including the tenancy agreements with the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 indicated that the plaintiff was in exchisive possession of the suit land and he was dispossessed by the defendants during pendency of the suit with the aid and assistance of the police officers and thus. The defendants are liable to restore possession of the suit land to the plaintiff and accordingly by judgment and order dated 30-3-2004 allowed the prayer for temporary injunction in mandatory form.

<u>8. The contesting defendants then preferred CR No. 10 of 2004 before the District Judge, Manikgonj. The Additional District Judge, Manikgonj who heard the same concurred with the trial Court that the plaintiff was in exclusive possession of the suit land on the date of institution of the suit and at the time of issuance of the order of status quo and the plaintiff was dispossessed during pendency of the suit by the defendants. The Additional District Judge also noticed several decisions of our Courts and held that the Court is empowered to pass order under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure even where the application was made under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 and this can be done for ends of justice and the High Court Division should not interfere against such order under its revisional jurisdiction. The Additional District Judge also noticed the proposition of law as available under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and held that mandatory injunction would be available if dispossession had taken place during the pendency of the suit or during an order of ad interim injunction. The Additional District Judge came to a clear finding that the plaintiff was in possession of the suit land when the order of status quo was passed and that the plaintiff was dispossessed from the suit market during the pendency of the order of status quo. Accordingly, by judgment and order dated 7-8-2004 the Additional District Judge dismissed the revisional application and affirmed the decision of the trial Court allowing the prayer for mandatory injunction.</u>

<u>9. The Rule having been discharged the petitioner moved this Court but the petition for leave to appeal in Civil Petition No. 329 of 2005 was dismissed on merit. Thereafter, the petitioner again moved this Court for review.</u>

<u>10. The review not being an appeal against the impugned judgment or that no fresh or important fact arose for our consideration or that there was any error apparent on the face of the record that has surfaced or that the non-consideration has substantially affected the parties, we do not think that the matters urged before us required to be investigated afresh by way of review.</u>

<u>The review petition is, accordingly, dismissed.</u>

End.

lawyer:
Mohammadullah, Advocate instructed by Nurul Islam, Advocate-on-Record—For the Appellant.

parties:
Afazuddin (Md) ------ Appellant.
Vs.
Md. Ataur Rahman and another ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
MM Ruhul Amin J: This appeal by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 28-1-2002 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3537 of 1999 heard analogously with Civil Revision No. 3536 of 1999 disposing the same with modification.

2. The respondent No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 562 of 1985 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Dhaka against the present appellant and others for Specific Performance of Contract. The suit was subsequently transferred to the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Dhaka and was renumbered as Title Suit No. 3 of 1987.

3. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that the defendant No. 1 entered into an agreement with him to sell the suit property at a consideration of Taka 1,20,000 and on receipt of Taka 5,001 from the plaintiff as earnest money the defendant No.1 executed a bainapatra in favour of the plaintiff on 19-2-1985. There was stipulation that defendant No. 1 after procuring necessary papers would inform the plaintiff and thereafter, on receipt of the balance consideration money within a month from the date of bainapatra, the defendant No. 1 would execute and register the necessary sale deed in favour of the plaintiff. On 2-3-1985 the plaintiff enquired from the defendant No.1 if he had obtained necessary papers for completion of the transaction. The defendant No. 1 replied that he was trying to procure the same. The plaintiff again enquired from the defendant No.1 on 10-8-1985 but the defendant No.1 was found to be indifferent. The plaintiff continued to request the defendant No. 1 for procuring necessary papers but the defendant No. 1 did not pay any heed to it. On receipt of the summons of Title Suit No. 737 of 1985 of the 2nd Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Dhaka, the plaintiff learnt that the defendant No. 1 as plaintiff filed the suit for recovery of khas possession of 1/3rd katha of land of Plot No. 219 of Khatian No. 6, of Mouza Ibrahimpur, PS Dhaka Cantonment, Dhaka against him and his wife as defendants. In spite of repeated reminders the defendant No. 1 did not execute the sale deed on receipt of balance consideration money although the plaintiff was always ready and willing to pay the balance consideration money to the defendant No. 1. The plaintiff was, therefore, constrained to file the suit for specific performance of contract.

4. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement stating that he was ready and willing to execute and register the kabala in favour of the plaintiff after obtaining the balance consideration money. The further case of the defendant No. 1 is that as per terms of the bainapatra the plaintiff agreed to pay the balance consideration money within 1(one) month from the date of bainanama and get the sale deed executed and registered from the defendant No. 1. Since the land was already with plaintiff so it was not written in the bainanama that possession would be given. The plaintiff, thereafter, proposed to the defendant to sell another 3/4th decimals of land of Plot No. 219 but the defendant refused. The plaintiff forcibly encroached 3-3/4 decimals of land and started construction thereon. Accordingly, the defendant No.1 instituted Title Suit No. 737 of 1985 in 2nd Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Dhaka for recovery of khas possession. The said Title Suit No. 737 of 1985 was transferred to the 3rd Court of Sub-ordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Dhaka and renumbered as Title Suit No. 4 of 1987. Title Suit No. 4 of 1987 and Title Suit No. 3 of 1987 were heard analogously in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Dhaka. Title Suit No. 3 of 1987 was dismissed and Title Suit No. 4 of 1987 decreed by judgment dated 23-11-1998. The defendant No. 1 preferred Title Appeal No. 74 of 1999 in the Court of District Judge, Dhaka. On transfer the appeal was heard and disposed of by the learned Additional District Judge, 7th Court, Dhaka along with Title Appeal No. 75 of 1999 and both the appeals were dismissed. Being aggrieved, the plaintiff preferred Civil Revision Nos. 3537 and 3536 of 1999 before the High Court Division. The Rule issued in Civil Revision No. 3537 of 1999 against the judgment and decree passed in Title Appeal No. 74 of 1999 affirming the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 3 of 1987 was disposed of with modification that the plaintiff, Md Ataur Rahman of Title Suit No.3 of 1987 would deposit in the trial court to the credit of defendant No.1, Afazuddin a sum of Taka 1,50,000 as solatium over and above Taka 1,15,000 the balance consideration money within 3(three) months from the date of judgment and on receipt of the amount of both balance consideration money and soletium, the defendant No. 1 would execute and register the sale deed in favour of the plaintiff. It was further directed that if the plaintiff could not deposit the amount within time fixed by the court, the suit shall stand dismissed. The Rule issued in Civil Revision No. 3536 of 1999 was discharged.

5. Leave was granted to consider the submission that the amount of solatium of Taka 1,50,000 is very inadequate which is apparent on its face being clearly against the finding by the High Court Division to the effect that the valuation of the suit land made as on 19-2-1985 after 17 years of the contract has gone up manifold. The price of the suit land has gone up by more than ten times and at the present market value of the suit land will be above Taka 12 lac. The High Court Division has failed to consider that the aforesaid solatium is not commensurate with the present market value of the suit land.

6. We have heard Mr Mohammadullah, the learned Advocate for the appellant and Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel for the respondent and perused the judgment of the High Court Division and other connected papers.

7. It transpires from the record that the bainapatra in question was executed on 19-2-1985 and Title Suit No. 562 of 1985 subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No. 3 of 1987 for specific performance of contract was filed in the same year (1985). After passing of the decree by the trial Court the plaintiff deposited the balance consideration money within time as directed by the Court. After passing of the judgment of the High Court Division in civil revision the plaintiff deposited the solatium amount within time fixed in the judgment. It may be mentioned that the appeal, Civil Revision Case and the Civil Petition for leave to appeal were preferred by the defendant No. 1 appellant.

<u>8. Thus it appears that the plaintiff was always willing and ready to pay the balance consideration money and there is no laches on his part but he could not tender the balance consideration money earlier as upto 1992 income tax clearance certificate was required for the purpose of registration of sale deed. Since the defendant No. 1 did not obtain the same and on enquiry on two occasions as mentioned in the plaint, the defendant No. 1 did not give any satisfactory reply regarding procurement of income tax clearance certificate, the plaintiff did not tender the balance consideration money and get the sale deed executed and registered from the defendant No. 1 for want of necessary income tax clearance certificate to be obtained by the defendant No. 1. Thus it appears that there was rather, laches on the part of the defendant No.1 in the matter.</u>

<u>9. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, and all aspects of the matter, we are of the view that the amount of solatium awarded by the High Court Division is not too inadequate. However, we propose to allow a further sum of Taka 50,000 (fifty thousand) as solatium to defendant No. 1.</u>

<u>The appeal is, accordingly, dismissed with the modification that the respondent would deposit Taka 50,000 (fifty thousand) as further solatium in favour of the appellant within 3(three) months from the date of receipt of the copy of the judgment.</u>

End.

lawyer:
Mohammad Mobarak Hossain—For the Petitioners
Mohammad Abul Kashem Bhuiyan—For the Opposite Party
parties:
Mina Begum and others ------ Plaintiff-Petitioners
Vs.
Joj Miah ------- Defendant-Opposite Party
full_judgment:
This Rule, on an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure (in short, the CPC) at the instance of the plaintiff-petitioners was issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 29-5-2012 and 4-6-2012 respectively passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Brahmanbaria, in Title Appeal No. 62 of 2009 affirming the judgment and decree dated 14-7-2009 and 20-7-2009 respectively passed by the learned Assistant Judge (in-charge) Akhaura, Brahmanbaria in Title Suit No. 69 of 2007 dismissing the suit should not be set-aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule, in short, is that the late plaintiff Mohammad Ali, now being dead, instituted the above suit for declaration of his title into the suit land by adverse possession averring, inter-alia, that 0.15 acres of land appertains to settlement plot No. 209 corresponding to BS plot No. 575 of settlement khatian No. 60 of Noorpur mouza under Akhaura Police Station of Brahamanbaria district originally belonged to the defendant No. 1 who purchased the same from others on 25-6-1975.

3. The defendant No. 1 while in possession of the said land sold the same at a consideration of Taka 20,000 in presence of the common relations of both the parties to the plaintiff in 1981 and from then the plaintiff has possessed the suit land. The defendant No. 1 had been serving in the Bangladesh Army at the relevant time. He had made commitment to the plaintiff that at his convenient time he would execute and register a kabala deed for the suit land in favour of the plaintiff.

4. The plaintiff demanded kabala from the defendant No.1 on many occasions but he taking the plea of his service in the Army was dragging the same. On 1-1-1990 the plaintiff requested the defendant for execution and registration of the kabala deed but the defendant No.1 promising to register the kabala had requested the plaintiff to get the land recorded in his (defendant No.1) name in the ongoing record of right and accordingly the plaintiff in order to maintain the tranquility among them got the land recorded in the name of defendant No.l. Since the defendant denied to execute and register the kabala deed in favour of the plaintiff on 30-8-2006 he (plaintiff) made an allegation on 31-8-2006 before the Chairman of No. 3, Akhaura (south) Union Parishad which was registered as case No. 14 of 2006 in the office of the Union Parishad and pursuant to the said petition filed by the plaintiff, a meeting to resolve the dispute between the parties took place on 28-11-2006 and the meeting took a decision but the defendant ultimately denied to execute the decision of the said compromise meeting and the local Chairman gave a certificate to that effect on 12-2-2007.

5. The defendant filed a petition to the Deputy Commissioner, Brahmanbaria on 3-9-2007 for eviction of the plaintiff alleging, inter-alia, that the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land forcibly and the said petition was sent to the Akhaura Police Station wherein it was registered as GD entry No. 1564 dated 3-9-2007. In the said petition, the defendant No.1 categorically admitted the forcible possession of the plaintiff into the suit land. The plaintiff ultimately denied the sale of the suit land to the plaintiff on 12-10-2007. Hence the plaintiff has been constrained to file the suit.

6. The suit was contested by the defendant No.1 filing written statement wherein he denied the material allegations made in the plaint. The case of the defendant No.1, in short, is that the plaintiff is his step brother and he is the elder brother of the plaintiff, their father died in 1968 and from then, they have been living jointly with their mother. In the war of liberation, the defendant had participated actively whereupon after the war of liberation he joined in the Bangladesh Army and ultimately the plaintiff used to look after the common ancestral properties of the plaintiff and the defendant at their native village.

7. The further case of the defendant is that he had purchased the suit land from his uncle Ali Akbar by a registered deed on 25-6-1975. At the time of preparation of the recent record of right, the defendant handed over the original deed of the suit land to the plaintiff to get his (defendant) name recorded and accordingly the hal record of right has been prepared in the name of the defendant. The plaintiffs taking the advantage of his possession into the suit land on behalf of the defendant and also using the original deed have been claiming the suit land on some false plea. The claim of title of the plaintiff into the suit land is false and frivolous. The defendant did never sell the suit land to the plaintiff a consideration of Taka 20,000. So, the suit is liable to be dismissed with costs.

8. Upon the above pleadings, the trial Court framed as many as 4 issues to dispose of the suit. The plaintiff examined 6 witnesses and submitted some papers which were duly marked as exhibits in the suit while the defendant examined 4 witnesses but did not adduce any documentary evidence. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence on record dismissed the suit and as against the said judgment of the trial Court, the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No. 62 of 2009 in the Court of District Judge, Brahmanbaria and the appeal was ultimately heard by the Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Brahmanbaria who by his impugned judgment and decree affirmed the judgment of the trial Court. The petitioners being the substituted heirs of late original plaintiff moved this Court and obtained the present Rule. The Rule is resisted by the sole defendant-opposite party.

9. Mr Mohammad Mobarak Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners supports the Rule. He submits that though the petitioners have come in this Court against the judgment and decree of affirmance but if the very basis of the concurrent findings of the two Courts below appears to be as misconception or based on no evidence, such concurrent findings cannot claim any immunity from this Court. He also submits that the plaintiff filed the original suit for declaration of his title by way of adverse possession asserting his uninterrupted and continuous possession in to the suit land from 1981 till filing of the suit in 2007. But the Courts below did not at all consider the possession of the plaintiff into the suit land.

10. He further submits that the plaintiff very successfully proved his possession into the suit land and since the suit was for declaration of title by way of adverse possession, the Courts below should have considered the continuous possession of the plaintiff. He taking me through exhibit-3 submits that the defendant filing a petition before the Upazilla Nirbahi Officer, Akhaura, Brahmanbaria had admitted the forcible possession of the plaintiff into the suit land and this admission of the defendant is very much consistent with the case of the plaintiff that the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land forcibly denying the title of the defendant into the suit land. But both the Courts below overlooking the exhibit-3 dismissed the suit and this kind of non-consideration of material evidence by the Courts below is an error of law and when there is error of law in taking decision by the Appellate Court below this Court can interfere into the decision of the appellate Court below.

11. He also submits that both the Courts below took notice of the conciliation meeting held under the leadership of the Chairman of Akhaura Union Parishad (PW 6), but both the Courts below failed to conceive and consider the inherent meaning of the resolution taken by the mediator. The local Chairman under whose leadership the compromise meeting has taken place on 28-11-2006 gave a certificate to the plaintiff on 12-2-2007 which has been marked in the suit as exhibit-2 will go to show that the defendant had admitted the sale of the land to the plaintiff but both the Courts below seriously overlooked the averment of the exhibit-2.

12. The learned Advocate also submits that since the suit was for declaration of title by way of adverse possession the prime consideration of the Courts below should have been whether the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land adversely from 1981 till filing of the suit and though the plaintiff had proved the said facts successfully by the local witnesses but even then the Courts below without considering such evidence very arbitrarily and capriciously dismissed the suit. So, the impugned judgment and decree of the Appellate Court below is liable to be set-aside decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiff.

13. On the other hand, Mr Mohammad Abul Kashem Bhuiyan the learned Advocate appearing for the sole defendant-opposite party opposing the Rule very strenuously contends that the plaintiff filed the suit for declaration of his title by way of adverse possession but the plaint itself discloses that he was admitting the title of the defendant into the suit land till 13-8-2006 and 28-11-2006. In order to succeed in a suit like this, the plaintiff is to prove his adverse possession into the suit land for more than 12 years but if the adverse possession of the plaintiff is counted in this particular suit from 13-8-2006 of 28-11-2006 his such possession appears to be hostile for one year only as against the defendant as the suit was filed in 2007.

14. He very categorically submits that there is no date of any sale and also as to when the plaintiff was inducted into the possession pursuant to his alleged purchase from the defendant. Then the plaint shows that the plaintiff admitting the title of the defendant till 2006 demanded the kabala from him (defendant). So, if it is conceded for a moment that the plaintiff had purchased the suit land in 1981 from the defendant but his (plaintiff) possession from 1981 to 2006 was never a hostile possession against the real owner, the defendant as he had admitted the ownership of the defendant during those period of time.

15. He also submits that it is admitted that the plaintiff and the defendant are step brothers of each other and after the death of their father they were in the same mess and since the defendant has been serving in the Bangladesh Army and since the plaintiff has been living in the native village at Nurpur, all the ancestral properties and the properties owned by the defendant were under the control and management of the plaintiff but the plaintiff taking the said managerial activities claimed his adverse possession into the suit land for some illegal gain.

16. He also submits that in 1990, the field survey for the recent record of right was going on in the locality, as such the defendant handed over the original kabala of the suit land to the plaintiff in the normal course of family business to get his name recorded and accordingly the plaintiff did the same. Had there been any fact of sale in 1981, the plaintiff must not have allowed the defendant to record his name in 1990. So, all these facts reveal that in fact before 1990 there was no any event of sale between the parties. But whenever the plaintiff got the original kabala from his brother for the preparation of the record of right he being misguided unethically claimed his ownership using the said original deed into the suit kind.

17. He also submits that in the plaint it has been averred that in presence of the common relations, the suit land was sold to the plaintiff by the defendant. But the plaintiff though examined 6 witnesses in the suit but could not examine any common relation of the plaintiff and the defendant in order to prove the alleged sale. The Courts below scanning the evidence of both the parties have concurrently found that the plaintiff case is based on surmise and conjecture and they taking into consideration the evidence and other connecter materials on record rightly dismissed the suit. They did not commit any error of law and they did not bypass any evidence in the record. So, the judgment of the Courts below do not call for interference from this Court. So, the Rule is liable to be discharged with costs.

18. I have considered the above submissions and the arguments of the learned Advocates of both the parties with profound attention and have gone through the materials on record including the plaint, written statement, judgment of the Courts below and the evidence both oral and documentary adduced by the parties.

19. In this Rule, it is admitted that the defendant was the owner of the suit land in question and he had purchased it from his uncle on 25-6-1975. The case of the plaintiff is that he had purchased the suit land from his step brother, the defendant and pursuant to the said purchase he has possessed the suit land from 1981. But interestingly it is important to note here that neither in the plaint nor in the evidence of the plaintiff there is any definite date as to when he (plaintiff) was inducted into the possession of the suit land. In the plaint it was averred among other that in presence of the common relations and the witnesses, the plaintiff had purchased the suit land. The plaintiff examined as many as 6 witnesses in the suit but none of them is the witness of the sale in question and both the Courts below considered this fact of the suit in a very right way. In this regard, the learned Advocate for the petitioner argued that since the plaintiff claims title by way of adverse possession, the evidence in order to prove the purchase of the land and the date of possession thereof is immaterial. But I find it difficult to have any substance in this argument. The defendant denied the adverse possession of the plaintiff into the suit land. So, there should have been a definite date from when the plaintiff started to possess the suit land. In the case of Sheikh Farid (Md) and others vs Abdul Wadud Sikdar and others reported in 58 DLR (AD) 248 the appellate division did not rely upon the plea of adverse possession simply for the want of any date of starting time of possession. The Appellate Division observed the said fact in the following manner:

"The plaintiff was required to establish from what particular point of time he started to possess the land in assertion of his title upon denying the title of the real owner i.e. Karuna Moyee Dasi. The evidence from plaintiff's side is totally lacking for establishing the fact that from a particular point of time he started to possess the land asserting his title upon denying the title of the real owner to his knowledge as well as to the knowledge of the others and since that date he was possessing the land for more than 12 years. In our view, there is no evidence that at any particular point of time the plaintiff claimed title in the land in suit on the basis of adverse possession or, -in other words, claimed his title in the land upon denying the title of the real owner." (para 10 of the judgment)

20. The observation made in the reported case has a full manner of application with the case in my hands and it is difficult for me to take any different view from than that of the reported ease.

21. Adverse possession means possession of a person in hostility and adversely against the real owner with the knowledge of the real owner and others and same must be very open and notorious against the real owner also. But surprisingly in the suit I find that the plaintiff had requested the defendant although till 2006 for having a kabala from him and it is in the admission of the plaintiff that on 30-8-2006 on his request the defendant denied to execute and register a kabala in his favour. This fact means and includes that the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land admitting the right and title of the defendant till 30-8-2006. So, if it is conceded for a moment that the plaintiff was in possession of the suit land from 1981 to 2006 how this sort of possession can be considered as adverse possession against the real owner. The possession of the plaintiff can be at best hostile and adverse after 30-8-2006 only when the defendant denied to execute the kabala in favour of the plaintiff. The trial Court and the appellate Court below considering all these facts and circumstances came to a sound conclusion that the possession of the plaintiff was never a hostile and adverse into the suit land against the defendant The Courts below also found that since he was living in the native village of the defendant, he used to look after the joint property of the plaintiff and the defendant including the suit land. I find no illegality in the finding and decisions of the Court below based on proper appreciation of the evidence and other materials on record.

<u>22. In my consideration, the plaint of the plaintiff is sufficient to hold that his possession was never hostile from 1981 to 2006 as within this period he was requesting the defendant to execute and register a kabala admitting his title. The hostile and adverse possession of the plaintiff was started in fact from 30-8-2006 when the defendant denied to execute and register a kabala and within one year of 2006 the suit was filed. So the said one year is not sufficient to consider the claim adverse possession of the plaintiff.</u>

<u>23. Whenever the plaintiff claims title by adverse possession he is under duty bound to prove that his possession was adverse and hostile against the real owner for more that 12 years within the knowledge of the real owner and others. But in this particular case, the plaintiff could not prove that his possession was hostile for more than 12 years against the defendant.</u>

24. The Courts below on proper scrutiny of the evidence on record rightly dismissed the suit. There appears no misreading or non-reading or non-consideration or misconstruction of evidence by the Courts below. In exercising the revisional jurisdiction, this Court can interfere in the concurrent findings of the Courts below when there appears non-consideration of evidence in arriving the decision by the Courts below. But I find that the Courts below have properly scanned the evidence of both the parties and the facts related thereto and thereafter came to a sound conclusion that the possession of the plaintiff was never hostile and adverse possession against the defendant. Thus I find no merit in the Rule.

25. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

Let a copy of this judgment and order along with the lower Courts record be sent down to the Court concerned.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 63 of 2007.
lawyer:
Mahbubey Alam, Senior Advocate, instructed by Chowdhury Zahangir, Advocate-on-Record—For the Petitioners. 
Khan Saifur Rahman, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record—For Respondent No. 1.

parties:
Morium Begum and others ------ Petitioners.
Vs.
Durga Matha & others ------ Respondents.
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 24-8-2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 637 of 2002).
full_judgment:
Md Tafazzul Islam J: This petition for leave to appeal arises out of the judgment and order dated 22 and 24-8-2006 of the High Court Division passed in Civil Revision No. 637 of 2002 discharging the Rule obtained challenging the judgment and decree dated 29-10-2001 of the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Barisal passed in Title Appeal No. 35 of 1995 reversing those of dated 1-3-1995 of the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Barisal Sadar, Barisal passed in Title Suit No. 189 of 1991, decreeing the suit.

2. The respondent No. 1, as plaintiff, filed the above Title Suit No. 189 of 1991 praying for declaration that the suit land mentioned in Ka schedule of the plaint is debottor property and also for declaration that the decree dated 17-5-1971 passed in Title Suit No. 94 of 1971 and another decree passed on 20-1-1972 in Title Suit No. 268 of 1971, both from the 2nd Court of the then Munsif, Barisal in respect of the land mentioned in schedule Ka and Ga to the plaint, are illegal, void, collusive and not binding upon the plaintiff on the averments that the suit land belonged to Kali Ranjan, Beni Madhab, Bhuban Mohan, Mohini Mohan, Amrita Kamuari Debba, Akhoy Kumar, Monoranjan and Subodh Kumar who, on the date of Janmastami Festival of the year 1345 BS dedicated the suit land measuring .092 acres out of plot Nos. 3374 and 3375 in favour of Shree Shree Kali Mata, Shree Shree Durga Mata, Shree Shree Shitala Mata, the Bigraha, and in the suit land two temples and one Puja Mandap were established and the members of Hindu Community have been worshipping therein since 1345 BS, in RS operation the aforesaid dedicated land were wrongly recorded in the name of the aforesaid owners as their residence but however, in the remark column the word "Mandir" was recorded in plot No. 3374; the plaintiff Bigraha has been possessing suit land dedicated to it; but of the original owners Kali Ranjan died leaving behind only daughter the defendant No. 9 who died in Barisal on 28-4-44 and Beni Madhav, who was a government servant left the country before partition and died in West Bengal 25 years ago and Mohini Mohan died in West Bengal in the year 1948; Nefaz Ali Laskar, the defendant No. 1 and Kashem Ali Munshi, the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 2-5 brought Civil Suit No. 268 of 1971 in the Court of the learned Munsif, Barisal for declaration of their title in the suit land on the basis of pattan from the recorded owners made in the month of Chaitra 1349 BS and the above defendant No. 1, in his individual capacity also filed Civil Suit No. 94 of 1971 in the same court for declaration of his title on the land described in Kha schedule of the plaint claiming that all the recorded owners except Kali Ranjan, made pattan of the same in his favour in the month of Baishak 1345 BS but, in fact, no such pattans were ever made and further the properties covered by both the suits being within the municipal area no such pattans could be made; further the summons of the above suits were not served upon defendants of the said suit and the plaintiffs of the above suits, on obtaining a false service returns, managed to get compromise decrees dated 20-1-72 and 17-5-71 though some of the defendants of the above suits also died before filing those suits and some of them became Indian nationals long before; Nafez Ali Laskar as well as Kashem Ali Munshi were never put into possession on the basis of the alleged pattans nor the present defendants are in possession of the suit land; the office-bearers of the Puja Committee, which was constituted for the purpose of conducting Durgapuja, being illegally influenced over by the defend-ants are conspiring to transfer the suit land to the principal defendants; Nidher Kumar Datta who is a Pujari, on 16-11-1991 came to learn about those decrees then he, after obtaining certified copies of the same on 27-1-1991, instituted the instant suit on obtaining permission under Order I, rule 8, CPC. The defendant No. 1 and, Mariam Begum, the defendant No. 41, contested the suit by filing separate written statements contending that Kali Ranjan had been in possession of the suit land which had two huts and a condemned building situated at plot No. 3365 and he, by pattan, settled the same to Nafez Ali Laskar, the defendant No. 1, and Kashem Ali Munshi, the predecessor of defendant Nos. 2-5, in the first part of Chaitra 1349 BS and put them in possession and Nafez Ali Laskar and Kashem Ali Munshi paid rent for more than 12 years and then on amicable partition Nafez Ali Lasker got southern part of plot No. 3365; since the name of Nafez Ali Laskar and Kashem Ali Munshi were not recorded they filed the above Civil Suit No. 268 of 1971 challenging the wrong recorded and the summons of the above suit were duly served upon the defendants of the said suit and the suit was duly decreed on 20-1-72 and then Nafez Ali Laskar mutated his name and then a separate holding was prepared in his name and besides that a municipal holding was also prepared in his name and he also erected new huts after obtaining approval of plan from the municipal authority and then he made a gift of the suit land to his daughter Mariam Begum, the defendant No. 41, by registered deed of heba dated 25-5-1982; the aforesaid Kashem Ali Munshi also made a gift of his portion of the pattani land, described in Ka /Kha schedule to the plaint, in favour of his daughter, the defendant No. 5, by a registered deed of heba dated 13-11-1983 who exchanged the same suit land with Keshabashan on 9-3-1987 and Keshabashan then sold the same to Khokan Kumar, Kartick Chandra and Tultul Mokherjee, the defendant Nos. 42, 43 and 44 respectively, and they are possessing the suit land and in the said exchange dated document Makhan Lal Chowdhury, member of the then Puja Committee of the plaintiff Bigraha, is an attesting witness; the suit land was released from VP List on 25-6-1984; the defendant No. 9, the daughter of Kali Ranjan, inherited nothing by way of inheritance and she also had no possession in the suit land but defendant Nos. 31 and 32 managed to have kabalas from her by way of false representation and then tried to mutate their names but due to objection raised by the defendant Nos. 7-8 they could not be successful and the defendant Nos. 31 and 32 also failed to obtain municipal plan in their favour and the defendant No. 9 also did not put them into possession and the so-called solenama between the plaintiff and the defendant Nos. 31-32/42-44 is false and the defendant No. 41 is in possession of her part in assertion of her title and in exclusion of others for more than 12 years and the plaintiff Bigraha had no title and possession in the said land; further the suit, being a suit simpliciter, is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the suit is also barred by limitation.

3. The defendant Nos. 7-8 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement contending that Boni Madhav, the recorded owner, on 1-2-1944 transferred part of the suit land to the defendant No. 6 and the record of right having not been prepared in his name the defendant No. 6 brought Civil Suit No. 94 of 1971 which was decreed on compromise and then the defendant No. 6 mutated his name in SA Khatian and Nidher Kuiriat Datta the Pujari and the representative of plaintiff, was fully aware of the same and further on 29-64974 the defendant No. 6, with the knowledge of Nidher Kumar Datta, transferred the suit land to defendant Nos. 7 and 8 who are possessing their respective portions by mutating their names and on payment of rents and taxes: Subodh Chowdhury Dey an Advocate of Barisal Bar, got an order of auction sale of the suit land in Execution. Case No. 23 of 1973 but the defendants saved the property from auction by depositing decretal amount and then said Sobudh Chowdhury Dey took an attempt to take lease of the suit land from VP Authority in VP Case No. 1220/68-69 but these defendants released the suit land on 29-12-1979 from Board of Revenue; the husband of defendant No. 8 transferred .033 acre of land to defendant No. 39 and the plaintiff Bigraha had or has no title and possession in the scheduled land. The defendant Nos. 31, 32 filed written statements contending that the plaintiff Bigraha has a temple over suit plot No. 3374 and part of land of plot No.. 3365 and the Hindu Community is using it for the purpose of worshipping and the defendant No. 9, transferred 0.030 acre of land of plot No. 3365 to the defendant Nos. 31 and 32, registered sale deeds dated 6-8-1976 and 13-11-1986 respectively and put them in possession and they are possessing their purchased land. The defendant Nos. 42 and 44 filed a joint written statement contending that Kali Ranjan dedicated his share in Suit Plot No. 3374 but did not make any dedication of his share in plot Nos. 3364 and 3365 and the defendant No. 9, the daughter of said Kali Ranjan, on mutation of her name in plot Nos. 3364 and 3365 transferred 0.03/4 acre of land of plot No. 3364 and 0.045 acre of land of plot No. 3365 to Sufia Begum, the defendant No. 5, who purchased the same in benami of her father Abdul Majid Sharif by a registered deed dated 6-8-1976 and subsequently said Abdul Majid Sharif executed a registered Nadabipattra on 13-11-1976 in favour of the defendant No. 5 and thereafter, defendant No. 5 transferred the same to Keshabashan by a deed of exchange dated 9-3-1987 and Keshabashan transferred the said land to defendant Nos. 42 and 44 by a registered kabala dated 18-11-1987 and 9-10-1991 and during pendency of the suit, the plaintiff Bigraha and defendant Nos. 31-32/44 filed compromise petition wherein the plaintiff admitted the claim of defendant Nos. 31-32/42 and 44.

<u>4. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, after hearing, having found that the plaintiff Bigraha has the temple over the land of Plot No. 3374 and it has no possession over the part of the land of Plot No. 3365 declared title of plaintiff Bigraha to the land of plot No. 3374 only. On appeal the learned Additional District Judge, after hearing, allowed the appeal holding that the defendant No. 1 and Kashem Ali Munshi, the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 2 to 5, having obtained the decree by practicing fraud the subsequent transfer of portion of the suit land made by them on the basis of the said decree is illegal and that the solenama between the plaintiff and defendant Nos. 31, 32/42 and 44 declaring title of the plaintiff in the suit land has been duly made and that the earlier judgment and decree passed in Civil Suit Nos. 94 of 1971 as well as 286 of 1997 are illegal and not binding upon the plaintiff and that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land. As against that the defendant-petitioners moved the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 637 of 2002 and after hearing the High Court Division discharged the Rule holding that the appellate Court duly found that the plaintiff Bigraha is in possession of the suit land and further, the claim of alleged pattan by the defendants in the city of Barisal is hit by the provision under section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act and so the contesting defendant acquired no pattani right in the suit land on the basis of unregistered document. Moreover, the Exhibits showing payment of rent do not show that those were paid in respect of the suit land.</u>

5. We have heard the learned Advocate-on-Record, perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and also other connected papers.

6. As it appears, the High Court Division on proper consideration of the materials on record arrived at a correct decision and there is no illegality or infirmity in the above decision so as to call for any interference.

The petition is dismissed.

End.

full_judgment:
.

Syed Mahmud Hossain J : This appeal by leave by the plaintiffs arises out of the judgment and order dated 13-4-2006 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 206 of 1998 discharging the Rule and affirming the judgment and decree dated 28-7-1977 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Lakshmipur in Title Appeal No. 150 of 1989 allowing the appeal reversing the part decree dated 28-2-1977 passed by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, Additional Court, Noakhali in Title Suit No. 19 of 1972.

2. The facts, leading to this appeal, in brief, are as follows:—

The appellants herein as the plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 19 of 1972 in the Additional Court of Sub-ordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Noakhali for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession in respect of 9.73 acres of land by removing structures therefrom and for recovery of mesne profit.

3. The case of the plaintiffs, in short, is that there was a Niskor Lakhiraj in the name of Ram Raton Sur under Bhulua Zamindari within Tauzi No. 5 of Noakhali Collectorate. The owner of the Niskor was Mohesh Chandra Narayan Chowdhury and subsequently Prasanna Narayan Chowdhury became owner of the Niskor by inheritance. The Niskor was subsequently sold in auction for arrears of cess and one Baksha Ali Mia Baksha Ali Patwary purchased the same in auction and got delivery of possession and sale certificate. The total area of this Niskor was 15 drones covering different mauzas. During the CS operation of 1915-1918 only 100.42 acres of land were recorded in CS Khatian No. 212 in respect of Ander Manik Mouza in the name of Baksha Ali Mia. The other lands of other Mouzas had no existence at that time. After the reformation of the land, the tenants did not return the land nor did they pay rent. Baksha Ali Patwary entered into possession of the entire land. After that, Baksha Ali Patwary made a gift of the entire Niskor land in favour of his two sons, namely, Eskabdor Ali Mia and Najibur Rahman @ Ali Ahmed Mia by a deed of gift dated 21st Bhadra 1320 BS. They gifted 1/3rd land of this Niskor in favour of their brother Sirajuddin Ahmed Mia by a deed of gift dated 21st Chaitra 1334 BS The sorts of Baksha Ali Mia made a settlement of 4 kanis of land of Ander Manik Mouza in favour of Abu Sayed Mohammad Noman by a kabuliyat dated 20th Poush 1358 BS corresponding to 5-1-1952 in respect of estate plot Nos. 17 and 21 of the Estate Map prepared by Elahi Baksha Amin. Abu Sayeed Mohammad Noman subsequently sold those 4 kanis of land to Anowar Ullah and Ahmed Ullah by a deed of sale dated 10-2-1952. Three sons of Baksha Ali Mia again made a settlement of 4 kanis of land of Ander Manik Mouza in favour of Abdur Rob in respect of estate plot Nos. 26 and 27. After that, Abdur Rob also sold those 4 kanis of land to Fazlul Haque and Hafizullah by a deed of sale dated 10-1-1952, and they sold those 4 kanis of land to Sultan Ahmed by a deed of sale dated 28-5-1958. Sultan Ahmed sold his 4 kanis of land to plaintiff No. 1, Zillur Rahim Mia by 2 deeds of sale dated 21-11-1967 and 30-11-1967. Thereafter, Hedayet Hussain, Abdul Kaiam and Anwarullah together sold their total 4 kanis of land to the plaintiffs by two deeds of sale dated 30-12-1967. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 filed Title Suit No. 88 of 1963 in the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge); Noakhali in respect of this suit land but the suit was dis-missed for default. The suit land was recorded during SA operation in Khatian Nos. 822 and 623 in the names of the plaintiffs' vendors. During Diara settlement, the names of the plaintiffs' vendors were recorded upto field stage but subsequently in the final Diara Khatian, the name of defendant No. 1 was recorded in respect of 13 annas and 15 gondas share of the suit land and the remaining 2 annas and 5 gondas share of land were recorded in the names of the plaintiffs. The Diara Khatian in the name of defendant No. 1 is wrong. Defendant No. 1 entered into the suit land as borgadar of the plaintiffs' vendors. Soon after their purchase, plaintiffs got possession in the suit land and possessed the same up to 1376 BS. But the defendants are not allowing the plain-tiffs to enter into the suit land from Ashar, 1377. The defendants have no right, title and interest in the suit land. Hence is the suit.

4. Defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying all the material statements made in the plaint. The case of this defendant, in short, is that Ainuddin Miaji and Omaruddin Hajee were the owners of the land of Taluk Ram Ratan Sur. Ainuddin Miaji died leaving behind his son, Ali Mia and daughter Joynab Banu as his heirs. Ali Mia died leaving behind his son, Sultan Ahmed and Fazlul Haque who became owners of the suit land. Sultan Ahmed and Fazlul Haque sold their shares, that is, 6.64 acres of land to defend-ant No. 1 by two registered deeds of sale dated 3-12-1957 and delivered possession thereof to him. After purchase of defendant No. 1, the land was subsequently increased to 9.73 acres. Since purchase defendant No. 1 has been possessing the same by constructing huts, cook-shed and cowshed etc. and also by excavating a tank and has since been residing there. Defendant No. 1 was never a borgadar under Hedayet Hussain and others who were never the owners of the suit land. This defendant has acquired good title by adverse possession.

5. The trial Court decreed the suit on contest in part and the plaintiffs' title in respect of 3.09 acres of land was declared and khas possession was also allowed by evicting defendant No. 1 therefrom. On appeal by the plaintiffs in Title Appeal No. 115 of 1989, the appellate Court allowed the appeal and decreed the suit in full in respect of 9.73 acres of land and the cross-objection of the defendant was rejected.

6. Against the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court, the heirs of defendant No. 1 filed a revisional application before the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 206 of 1998. The High Court Division discharged Rule by the judgment and order dated 13-4-2006.

7. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with judgment and order dated 13-4-2060 passed by the High Court Division, the defendant-petitioners moved this Division by filing Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1375 of 2006 in which leave was granted on 7-6-2007 resulting in the initiation of Civil Appeal No. 110 of 2007.

8. Mr. Osman Gani, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-appellants, submits that the High Court Division without taking into consideration the propriety of respective claims of the title of the plaintiffs and defendant No. 1 in the suit land concurred with the judgment of the lower appellate Court which decreed the suit in full and that the plaintiffs could neither prove their title to nor possession in the suit land and, as such, the impugned judgment should be set-aside. He further submits that admittedly defendant No. 1 was in possession of the suit land prior to his purchase and the High Court Division without considering this aspect of the case delivered the impugned judgment and, as such, the Impugned judgment should be set-aside.

9. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of respondent Nos. 1-7, submits that the plaintiffs have been able to prove their title to the suit land and that they have filed the suit within twelve years from the date of dispossession and, as such, no interference is called for.

10. Leave was granted on the following submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellants.

"The trial Court decreed the suit in part in respect of 3.09 acres of land out of 9.73 acres of land for which the present petitioners filed cross-objection in appeal on the ground that the char lands added/ increased will be the land of the owner but the appellate Court without considering the cross-objection disallowed the same and, as such, the appellate Court erred in law in disallowing cross objection of the petitioners and the High Court Division also failed to consider that the defendants-petitioners acquired title in the suit land by kabalas which are earlier in point of time than the kabalas of the defendants. The appellate Court failed to consider the finding of the trial Court that the petitioners have been possessing the suit land by constructing their dwelling huts and other huts and excavating tank before purchase of the plaintiffs and, as such, plaintiffs' vendors were not in possession of the suit land for which the plaintiffs did not acquire right, title and possession in the suit land by their alleged purchase; rather the plaintiffs purchased litigation, so the appellate Court and the. High Court Division erred in law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in decreeing the plaintiffs' suit. The appellate Court without adverting to the findings of the trial Court on point of title and possession and without reversing the same, allowed the appeal and the High Court Division also maintained the same and, as such, there has been miscarriage of justice."

11. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates, the impugned judgment and order delivered by the High Court Division and the papers incorporated in the paper book.

12. Admittedly there was a Niskor Taluk in the name of Mohesh Chandra Narayan Chowdhury within Bhulua Zamindary. There is no gainsaying the fact that the suit land is part of Niskor Taluk appertaining to Mouza Ander Manik. The plaintiffs' case is that the suit land appertains to estate plot Nos. 17, 21, 26 and 27 in the Estate Map prepared by Elahi Baksha Amin of Baksha Ali Estate. The defendants claimed that these estate plots attract the diara plot or the suit plots. In paragraph 8 of the written statement, the defendants stated to have purchased 6.64 acres of land of estate plot Nos. 9, 15, 21, 27, 10, 16, 22 and 28 of the Estate Map of the then Talukders. The deeds of sale, Exhibits A and A(1) of defendant No. 1 contain the above mentioned estate plots. Therefore, it appears that the estate plot Nos. 21 and 27 are common in both the lands. The plaintiffs' further case is that Mohesh Chandra Narayan Chowdhury gave an ejara of land of Ander Manik Mouza of the Niskor Taluk to one Ainuddin Patwary for 17 years for collection of rents from the tenants by patta kabuliyat dated 29th Poush 1292 BS marked as Exhibit-3, but before the expiry of this ejara period Mohesh Chandra Narayan Chowdhury created a Sarbapori Kayami Mokarary Taluk in respect of the land of this ejara patta, Exhibit 3, in the name of Baksha Ali Patwary by a patta dated 25th Agrahayan 1298 BS, marked Exhibit-2. The plaintiffs stated the origin of his suit land from Ejara patta dated 29th Poush 1292 BS (Exhibit-3). The plaintiff as PW 2 stated in his deposition that a Taluk, namely, Ainuddin Miajee was mentioned in Exhibit 3. Ainuddin Miajee as stated in the written statement of defendant No. 1 and Ainuddin Miajee as stated in Exhibit-3 is the same person. Exhibit-3 contains several Taluks and there is a mention of Taluk, Ainuddin Miajee and Omaruddin Hajee and from the above fact, it appears that the land contained in the deed of sale of defendant No. 1 got its origin in Exhibit-3. The plaintiff as PW2 in his cross-examination stated that Ainuddin had a son Ali Mia and that Ali Mia had two sons named Fazlul Haque and Sultan Ahmed. Defendant No. 1 stated to have purchased the suit land from Fazlul Haque and Sultan Ahmed by two registered deeds of sale dated 3-12-1957.

13. The trial Court came to a finding that the plaintiffs and the contesting defendant drew the origin of the disputed land from the ejara patta (Exhibit-3) and that it could not be said that the deeds of defendant No. 1 were absolutely bogus. The trial Court also found that the deeds of sale of defendant No. 1 were coupled with possession and that defendant No. 1 had been possessing the suit land from the time of his purchase.

14. The appellate Court having considered the evidence on record both oral and documentary came to a finding that the plaintiffs had been able to prove their title to and possession in 6.64 acres of land out of the suit land. What is important to note here is that the appellate Court did not advert to the findings of the trial Court as regards the title and possession of defendant No. 1 in the suit land.

15. The trial Court came to a finding that defendant No. 1 had been possessing the suit land by erecting khamarghor and by excavating tank before purchase of the plaintiffs and that the plaintiffs did not get possession in the suit land by their alleged purchase; rather the plaintiffs purchased litigation.

16. The High Court Division, however, simply concurred with the decision of the appellate Court. When a revisional application is filed against judgments of reversal, the High Court Division is under the obligation to apply its mind independently before drawing any inference with regard to the conflicting findings of the Courts below and to come to a decision with whose judgment the High Court Division will concur. In the case in hand, this minimum requirement has not been complied with.

17. The description of the schedule given in the plaint is as follows: Revisional Final

২। ১৯৫৯/৬০ ইং সনের  Revisional  জরিপি ৬২২/৬২৩ খাতিয়ানের পূর্বেবাক্ত দাগ হায়ের ভূমি পরিবর্তি ১৯৬৪/৬৫ইং সনের দিয়ারা জরিপী লক্ষীপুরা থানা অন্তর্গত ২৬৮ নং আধার মালিক মৌজার নিম্ন লিখিথ খতিযান ও দাগ হায় Final রেকর্ড হইয়াছে দিয়ারা  Final খতিয়ান।

২৫৭নং

প্রকাশ থাকে যে, অত্র আরর্জিতে কথিত বাদিপক্ষের বায়াগনের বন্দোবস্তীয় ও বাদিগনের খরিদা মোট ৮ কানী জমি ১.২০ ডিং এককানী হিসাবে মোট ৯.৬০ ডিং হয় তাহা জরিপী মাপের ইতর বিশেষে ৯.৭৩ ডিং হইয়াছে।

18. It is curious to note that though the trial Court found that defendant No. 1 had title to and possession in 6.64 acres of land, it is not comprehensible how the trial Court could pass a decree in favour of the plaintiffs in respect of the remaining unidentified suit land measuring 3.09 acres.

19. We have already quoted the schedule appended to the plaint before and from that schedule it is very difficult to curb out 3.09 acres of land. In this connection it is pertinent to quote Rule 3 of Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure as under:—

"Where the subject-matter of the suit is immovable property, the plaint shall contain a description of the property sufficient to identify it, and, in case such property can be identified by boundaries or numbers in a record of settlement or survey, the plaint shall specify such boundaries or numbers and where the area is mentioned, such description shall further state the area according to the notation used in the record of settlement or survey, with or without, at the option of the party, the same area in terms of the local measurement."

20. The above Rule reveals that the immovable property in respect of which relief is prayed for must be identified.

<u>21. A court of law cannot pass a decree in respect of land which is not specified How the trial Court could pass such a part decree in respect of an unidentified land is shrouded in mystery. In a suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession the plaintiffs are not only required to prove their title to the suit land and but also to prove that the suit has been filed within twelve years from the date of alleged dispossession. From the evidence of the PWs, it appears that the plaintiffs could not prove that the suit has been filed within twelve years from the date of dispossession. Admittedly, defendant No. 1 was in possession of the suit land prior to the purchase of the plaintiffs. The part decree passed by the trial Court in favour of the plaintiffs appears to be a gratuitous decree and there is no scope for passing such decree.</u>

22. Having considered the facts and circumstances and evidence on record it appears that the plaintiffs are not entitled even to a part decree.

23. In the light of the findings made before, we find substance in the appeal.

Accordingly the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs and the impugned judgment is set-aside and the suit is dismissed as a whole.

End.
