Ranadhir Sen, J: This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff is directed against the judgment and order dated 1-6-76 of the learned Subordinate Judge, rejecting an application for temporary injunction in a suit for certain declarations namely:

“(ক) নালিশী তফছিল বর্ণিত সম্পত্তির ও তদুপরিস্থিত বসত বাড়ীতে বাদিনীর প্রকৃষ্ট স্বত্ত্ব থাকা প্রচার পাইবার ডিগ্রী দিতে

(খ) পাবনা জেলার সংক্ষিপ্ত সামরিক আদালতের এম, এল,জি, আর ১১/৭৬ নং মোকদ্দমায় নালিশী সম্পত্তি ২নং বিবাদীর নিজস্ব সম্পত্তি বলিয়া যাহা বাজেয়াপ্ত করিয়া ১নং বিবাদীর প্রতি আপিত হইবার আদেশ দিয়াছেন। উক্ত আদেশ ফলে বলাহীন বে-আইনী বেদাড়া null and void ও without  Jurisdiction ও বাদিনীর প্রতি বাধ্যকর নহে বলিয়া ঘোষণা দিতে

(গ) সাকুল্য আদালত ব্যয় ১/২ নং বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধে বাদীনিরকে পাইবার ডিক্রী দিতে

(ঘ) আইন ও ইকুটি মূলে বাদিনী আর যে যে প্রতিকার যে ভাবে পাইতে পারে তাহা ও ডিক্রী দিতে”

2. The plaintiff impleaded Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Pabna as defendant No. 1, Md. Amjad Hossain and his minor son Sajid Hossain as defendant No. 2 and 3. The learned Subordinate Judge did not issue any notice upon the defendants to show cause why the prayer should not be granted within the scope of Order 39 Rule I of the Code of Civil Procedure. The matter was heard ex-parte. The learned Subordinate Judge entered into a question touching the maintainability of the suit and the petition for injunction.

3. For proper appreciation of the questions raised in this appeal, we quote the relevant portions of the impugned judgment:-

"Heard the learned Advocate Mr. M. A. Kashem and perused the affidavit. The said Advocate submits that the property in question has been purchased by the plff, with the earnings of her own income and that she has been accordingly living therein since purchase on 20-2-74 and that her husband Mr. Amzad Hossain has no interest whatsoever in the said property and accordingly the Summary Martial Law Court, Pabna, while' convicting the said Amzad Hossain and awarding punishment has acted illegally by confiscating the property. The plff. has prayed for a declaration that the confiscation of the said property and vesting of the same to the Republic of Bangladesh is illegal, null and void and inoperative upon the plff. It has been prayed by the plff. actioner that the defdt. No. 1 be restrained from ousting the plff. therefrom by an order of ad-interim injunction till disposal of the suit.

From the foregoing submission and fact s it is admitted that the suit property stands already confiscated by a competent forum of adjudication, namely, the Summary Martial Law Court, Pabna. The property in question, therefore, already vests with the state. I have gone through the judgment dated 12th April, 1976 of the said Summary Martial Law Court and on perusal it appears that threadbare discussion has been made on this point in the said judgment where the plff. also appeared as a witness i n order to prove that the property is her and not of her husband's. Her evidence and other evidences at length have been minutely considered and after due deliberation the property has been considered to be the property of Mr. Amzad Hossain purchased benami in the .name of his wife the plff. and his son Sajid Hossain. So long as the suit property remains confiscated it cannot be held that the plff. has any interest in the suit property. This being the position of the puff. vis-a-vis the suit property, the Offish prayer for injunction is not tenable. The prayer for injunction is, therefore, rejected Further to mention that the judgment and decision of the Martial Law Court, in my opinion, cannot be questioned in this forum."

4. Mr. Pal, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the appeal has taken us through the plaint, the petition for injunction and the impugned order. According to the learned Advocate, the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in refusing the plaintiff's prayer for temporary injunction upon a misconception of facts and law. Mr. Pal contends that the plaintiff was not a party to the alleged Martial Law case and the decision in the Martial Law case did not operate against the plaintiff and her right to sue in the competent civil court for the aforesaid reliefs was not taken away under the law.

5. Mr. Sultan Ahmed, the learned Deputy Attorney General appearing on behalf of respondent No. 1 contends with an amount of emphasis that Martial Regulation No. 1 of 1975 did not leave any scope for a suit of the instant nature challenging the decision of a Martial Law Court, to be instituted in a civil court which is otherwise competent to entertain a suit for declaration. The learned Deputy Attorney General has taken us through some of the provisions of Regulation I of 1975. He has specifically drawn our attention to Article 4 of the said Regulation for the purpose of appreciating the question raised in this appeal. Article 4 runs as follows:-

"Review of Proceedings etc. (1) No appeal shall lie from any order, judgment or sentence of a Martial Law Court.

(2) All proceedings of Special Martial Law Courts shall, immediately after the termination thereof, be submitted to the Government for review; and all sentences of death or transportation for life shall have to be confirmed by the President.

(3) All proceedings of Summary Martial Law Courts shall, immediately after the termination thereof, be submitted to the (Sessions Judge) within whose jurisdiction the trials were held, for review.

(4) The Government may, on review, set aside, vary or modify any order, judgment or sentence or make orders for retrial or such other orders as he deems necessary for the ends of justice.

(5) A Sessions judge may, on review, set aside, vary or modify any order, judgment or sentence or Make orders for retrial or such other orders as he deems necessary for the ends of justice.

(6) Subject to, review, all orders, judgment and sentences of a Martial Law Court shall be final.

(7) No order, judgment, sentence or proceedings of a Martial Law Court shall be called in question in any manner whatsoever in, by or before any Court, including the High Court and the Supreme Court.

(8) No Court, including the High Court and the Supreme Court, shall call for the records of the proceedings of any Martial Law Court for any purpose whatsoever.

(9) No lawyer shall appear or plead before the Chief Martial Law Administrator or a Sessions Judge at the time of review of a case".

6. Relying on the above Article, the learned Deputy Attorney General contends that the ouster of jurisdiction of "any Court including the High Court and the Supreme Court" was complete. He has laid particular emphasis on the expression "in any manner whatsoever in, by or before any Court, including the High Court and the Supreme Court" occurring in clause 7 of Article 4 referred to above. Analysing the contention of a total bar, the learned Deputy Attorney General submits that the subject-matter of the suit is the property which was involved in a Martial Law case and the Martial Law Court pronounced judgment in respect of the said property holding that the said property was acquired by the accused Mr. Amzed Hossain in the benami of his wife, the plaintiff and his minor son defendant No. 3. Therefore, in his view, the jurisdiction of a Civil Court including the High Court and Supreme Court to adjudicate a claim in respect of the said property was ousted and such ouster was complete.

<u>7. Mr. Pal, on the other hand, has sought to repel the contention of the learned Deputy Attorney General contending that no right, title or liberty of any person other than that of the accused was specifically taken away under the aforesaid provisions of Regulations I of 1975. In his view, the plaintiff's right remains unaffected notwithstanding the judgment of the Martial Law Court. Evidently, the plaintiff was not a party to the case before the Martial Law Court and she was not convicted for any offence. There was no allegation against her and no charge was framed against her in the matter of acquisition of the property by the accused in her name and in the name of her minor son defendant No. 3. The learned Deputy Attorney General could not refer to any provision in the aforesaid Regulations by or under which the right of person other than a person convicted by a Martial Law Court was taken away. Property is related to person with whom ownership resides along with its incidents. The law, of benami transactions has not been proscribed by the Martial Law Regulations. We have not been taken through any law or authority by or under which the right of the plaintiff to institute a suit in a competent civil court for declaration of her title to the property according to law has been extinguished specifically. We appreciate the difficulty faced by the learned Deputy Attorney General in asserting the proposition of a total ouster of court's jurisdiction. Article 4 of Regulations I of 1975 has not expressly taken away any inherent right of a third person. The scheme of Regulation No. 1 of 1975 indicates the object of the same. It is apparent that the said Regulation was brought into being for the purpose of dealing with certain classes of offences and offenders connected therewith and for punishment specifically mentioned therein. The scope of Article 4 of Regulations No. 1 of 1975 cannot be enlarged to embrace a person other than the person convicted under the Martial Law. Article 4 of the said Regulations applies to a person convicted thereunder. It would be going too far to spell out a meaning that Article 4 of Regulation i of 1975 contemplated a total ouster of civil court's jurisdiction or that such ouster was complete. There are authorities which speak in favour of the inherent jurisdiction of the civil court even under the Martial Law Regulations. Reading clauses 6 and 7 together we do not find any indication to oust the civil court's jurisdiction expressly and/or absolutely. The expression "in any manner whatsoever" must be read with reference to a person who has been convicted under the said Martial Law Regulations. It may be pointed out that the right of-appeal has been expressly taken away by clause I of Article 4. The power of review which has been given under the said Article, rests with the Government or the. Sessions Judge, as the case may be and may be exercised if it is deemed "necessary for ends of justice." The aforesaid provisions of Martial Law Regulations I of 1975 do not, in our opinion, impose a bar to the institution of a suit in a competent civil court for declaration of title to the property in question by the plaintiff who was not a party to the Martial Law case but is a person whose right to property has been affected consequent upon a decision of the Martial Law Court. It may be recalled that the plaintiff was not an accused convicted in the Martial Law case. The concept of confiscation of property is not a novel gift of the Martial .Law Regulations. The alleged order of confiscation did not take away the real owner's right to establish her title to the property under an order of confiscation. In the background of the contentions raised by the learned Advocates we are of the view that the suit as framed is prima facie maintainable in a competent civil court with the reliefs prayed for. We have considered Prima-facie the question of maintainability of the suit as a question of law. We are not to be understood to have expressed any opinion on the merits of the plaintiff's case: which, the plaintiff is required in law to prove in order to succeed in securing the reliefs claimed.</u>

8. The learned Subordinate Judge appears to have taken a misconceived view of facts and law, upon a hazy impression of the subject-matter in suit while rejecting the plaintiff's prayer for temporary injunction.

9. It is not understood on what materials the learned Subordinate Judge held that "it is admitted that the suit property stands already confiscated by a competent forum of adjudication, namely, the Summary Martial Law Court, Pabna." We do not find any foundation in law behind the approach of the learned Subordinate Judge in disposing of the temporary injunction matter relied upon the judgment and order of the Martial' Law Court. The learned Subordinate Judge appears to have noticed "threadbare discussion" and "careful consideration after due deliberation" in the judgment of the Martial Law Court. This indicates that the learned Subordinate Judge failed to apply his mind to the plaintiff's case for injunction in the light of the averments made in the plaint and the petition for injunction. The judgment of the Martial Law Court was not liable to be commented upon by the civil court so far as defendant No. 2 was concerned except for the purpose of review by the competent authority indicated by Article 4 clause 3 and 4. The learned Subordinate Judge appears to have overlooked the scope of his jurisdiction under Order 39 Rule I of the Code of Civil Procedure. It appears from the affidavit-in-opposition filed in C.R. No. 964(fm) of 1976 that "on 18.7.76 the petitioner vacated the entire suit property" and that on 21.7.76 a magistrate took over vacant possession of the entire property on behalf of the State. It, therefore, follows that the plaintiff was in possession of the suit property on the date of institution of the suit and on the date the impugned order was passed. The learned Subordinate Judge appears to have completely overlooked the fact of plaintiffs possession while rejecting the plaintiff's prayer for temporary injunction. The plaintiff appears to have been allegedly dispossessed during the pendency of the suit. She may have appropriate remedy in law if she so choses. Since we have found that the suit as framed is prima facie maintainable, we remit the matter to the learned Subordinate Judge for disposal of the injunction matter according to law.

10. For the reasons stated above the appeal is allowed. The judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge are set aside and the matter is remitted to the learned Subordinate Judge for disposal according to law and in the light of observations made above. We do not make any order as to costs.

11. The connected Rule being C.R. No. 964(fm)/1976 is discharged in view of the order passed in the appeal. There will be no order as to costs.

12. In the interest of a proper disposal of the injunction matter we do not express our views in the matter of injunction. The learned Subordinate Judge will dispose of the injunction matter on consideration of the plaintiff's prima-facie case, the balance of convenience and inconvenience and the question of irreparable loss and in accordance with law.

End.

full_judgment:
This Application under section 115 of the Code of Civil procedure is direction against judgment dated 25-8-2002 and decree dated 29-8-2002 passed by the learned joint District judge, 1st Court Rajbari in Title Appeal No. 90 of 2002 allowing the Title Appeal and reversing the judgment dated 23-4-2002 and decree dated 28-4-2002 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Rajbari in Title Suit No. 35 of 1999 in decreeing the Title suit.

2. The plaintiffs Respondents petitioners filed Title Suit No. 35 of 1999 against the Defendant Appellant-Opposite party No. 1 for declaration of title to and khas possession of the suit land. The plaintiffs stated that the suit jote of the scheduled lands situated under Mouza Khankhanapur, PS and District Rajbari in RS Khatian No.419 and SA Khatian No. 464 belonged to a family of owners in possession consisting of Amir Mridha, Mohiuddin Mridha, Khatoon Jahiran Bibi and Amena Khatoon who as RS recorded tenants hold the lands in ejmali. It transpired that the co-sharer tenant Amir Mridha died unmarried leaving behind his brother Mohiuddin Mridha, sisters Hazu Khatoon and Jahiran Bibi, and mother Amena Khatoon as his nears and successors. Hazu Khatoon and Jahiran Bibi sold 97 decimals and 13 decimals of land to their brother Mohiuddin on 12-2-1949 by registered Kabala and handed over possession to him. Mohiuddin Mridha sold 30 decimals of land which Mohiuddin got by inheritance through registered Kabala on 14-10-1950 to Shandari Nessa wife of Nazar Ali Pramanik and handed over the possession of the same to her Shandari Nessa possessing 30 decimals of lands through her husband Nazar Ali Pramanik died before the SA Operation leaving her only son Abdul Khaleque Pramanik and her husband Nazar Ali Pramanik as her heirs and successors. Upon Nazar Ali's death, Abdul Khaleque Pramanik inherited his father's share later selling his lands to Shushil Kumar Bhokta through registered kabala on 14-2-1975 only to buy back Shushil Kumar's lands through registered kabala on 18-2-1978. Subsequently, Abdul Khaleque Pramanik being the owner in possession of the lands sold the same on 18-2-1993 by kabala Deed No. 8817 registered on 18-12-1993 to the plaintiff Nos. 1-2 and handed over possession to them. It is against this backdrop that the Defendant filed Title suit No. 155 of 1990 which was dismissed for default. The plaintiffs filed case No. 30 of 1994 in the Union , Parishad against the Defendant No. 1 for having cut away bamboos from plot No. 5567 by force, thereafter taking possession of and erecting a house thereon, which was not contested by the Defendant and the plaintiffs got an ex parte order of compensation. The Defendant also forcibly took possession of some lands that were initially subject of a wrong entry in the BS records that was subsequently corrected in the plaintiffs" favour upon an objection filed by them That notwithstanding, the Defendant, thereafter proving unwilling to give up possession of the suit lands on, one plea or the other at the plaintiff's request and on 6-3-1999 the Defendant having refused to remove his house there from, the plaintiffs filed the Title suit praying for declaration of Title and for his possession.

3. In contesting the suit the Defendant No. 1 in deviation from the plaintiff's account of the history of title of the suit lands contended that Mohiuddin Mridha never parted with the suit lands as stated by the plaintiffs but instead died owning and possessed of the suit lands leaving his three sons the defendant No. 1 Shahjahan Mridha, Malek Mridha, and Selim Mridha and his first wife Jandran Nessa and daughter Beauty Khatoon. It was also stated that the Defendant No. 1, therefore, appropriately has a dwelling house on a suit land paying taxes to the Union Parishad. In this regard, the Defendant No. 1 claimed that the documents relied upon by the plaintiffs not being genuine and consequentially not acted upon, the plaintiffs have no right, title and interest to and possession of the suit lands.

4. The petitioners contend that the learned Assistant judge having aptly found on both questions of title and possession in the plaintiff's favour and accordingly decreed the suit, the learned Joint District Judge allowed the appeal of the Defendant appellant reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court without considering and examining relevant oral and documentary evidence. This contention is based on the Ground that upon Mohiuddin Mridha, the father of the Opposite party No. 1, having transferred his property by sale to Shundari Nessa in 1950, he had no subsisting interest, thereafter, to pass on to the opposite party No. 1 or indeed to any of his other heirs. The petitioners also contend that had the lower appellate Court property considered all relevant evidence adduced by both parties, it would correctly comprehend the petitioners' case. The petitioners also contend that the lower appellate Court did not attach significance to the history of litigation between the parties that was duly considered by the trial Court.

5. Heard the learned Advocates for the plaintiff petitioners and the Defendant Opposite party, perused the Application and the judgments and decrees of the Courts below.

The case involves disputed questions of title, possession, and dispossession, thereby leading this Court to consider the extent to which one party has been better able to prove its claim to title and possession in relation to the other. This was the exercise under taken by the learned Assistant judge in Title suit No. 35 of 1999 in examining another ran go of available documentary evidence in conjunction with corroboration Statements of relevant witnesses.

6. It is noticed that the deed dated 14-10-1950 has being kabala No. 2855 effecting a sale transfer of those it land by Mohiuddin Mridha in favour of Shandari Nessa, constitutes the main point of divergence in the cases of the plaintiffs Respondents petitioners and the Defendant Appellant opposite party No. 1 The opposite party No. 1 contends, it only by reason of the Kabala not being produced in its original as Exhibit-7 before the trial Court, that the absence of any primary evidence to prove the kabala and the sale manifests the petitioners failure to establish a crucial what in the chain of title by which they claim title by purchase from 18-12-1993 onwards. Accordingly, it is further contended that in the absence of this link crucial to the chain of title claimed by the petitioners, the title of the Opposite party No. 1 by with of a prior deed of Heba of 1990 as well as a claim by inheritance from his father to the suit land shall invariably take precedence over the petitioners claim to the land. In this regard, this Court has carefully considered that part of the trial Courts judgment involving an unscrambling by the learned Assistant Judge of the factual and legal context of the case before him. In that process the learned assistant Judge apply and duly considered the history of litigation pertaining to the suit land that bore upon the questions of the title and possession before the trial Court. It is that Courts view that the learned Assistant Judge's consideration in particular of Exhibits-52, 3 and 4 properly and adequately guided the trial Court in resolving the disputed crucial issues at hand. Exhibit-2 as pertains to a partition suit in Civil case No. 155 of 1990 filed by the Opposite party on 5-8-1990 against the predecessor in interest of the petitioners i.e Shundari Nessa and/or her heirs appeared crucial to the learned Assistant Judge in ascertaining the petitioners chain of title. A perusal of the plaint filed by the present opposite party No. 1 as petitioner in Civil case No. 155 of 1990 reveals that it was accepted as a given that at least on the date that the Civil case was filed the opposite party No. 1 held land as co-sharer by virtue of inheritance and the Heba dated 10-7-1990 with Shundari Nessa and/or her heirs who came to be on the land from 14-10-1950. It is further evident from the plaint in civil case No. 155 of 1990 that recognizing Shundari Nessa's title and interest in the suit land, the opposite party No. 1 sought merely to delimit his interest vis-a-vis that of Shundari Nessa and her heirs, by virtue of the partition suit so filed. It is also evident that the case was dismissed for default on 8-7-1992 being thereby in evidence of the Opposite party No. 1 having for the reason or the other, apparently abandoned his claim and case as petitioner. Incidentally, and as submitted by the learned counsel for the opposite party No. 1, the draft publication of BS Khatian No.1899 had already been prepared on 26-2-1992 showing the entitlement of the opposite party No. 1 to approximately 5 decimals of the suit land.

7. It is against this backdrop that this Court, like the trial Court below, has had to consider the issue of dispossession raised by the petitioners as is said to have occurred on 5-5-1994. It is not disputed that the suit land was sold to the petitioners on 18-12-1993. The petitioners claim that soon thereafter the opposite party No. 1 actively dispossessed the petitioners constraining them to filed case No. 30 of 1994 with the concerned Union Parishad arbitration form praying for an for an order and direction on the opposite party No. 1 remove all obstacles to the petitioners possession of the land and to restore and compensate as necessary. It has been submitted by the learned Advocate for the Opposite party No.1 that this case was filed on 7-5-1994 and disposed of on 16-2-1995 without any notice to the opposite party No.1. The accuracy of this submission is suspect as relevant records of the proceedings as found in the Exhibit-3 series show that the opposite party No.1 having put in an appearance on 9-6-1994, thereafter, remained absent in the two years following the filing of the case leading thereby to an exparte disposal of the same on 16-2-1995 with the arbitration form having taken notice on 19-1-1995 of the sustained failure on the part of the opposite party No.1 to appear despite repeated notices. The order and direction given in that case on 16-2-1995 reads thus—

“বিবাদীগণ আগামী ত্রিশ দিনের মধ্যে বাদীর জবরদখলকৃত সম্পত্তির দখল ত্যাগ করিয়া উত্তোলনকৃত ঘর অপসারন করিয়া লইয়া যাইবে এবং বাশ কাটার ক্ষতিপূরণ বাবদ ৫০০ (পাঁচশত) টাকা বিবাদীগণ বাদীর অনুকুলে আগামী ত্রিশ দিনের মধ্যে পরিশোধ করিবে।

অদ্য ১৬-২-১৯৯৫ ইং তারিখে আমার সহি ও সীল মোহর যুক্ত অত্র রায় প্রকাশ করা হইল।”

স্বাঃ এ, কে, এম ইকবাল হোসেন

চেয়ারম্যান

সালিশী আদালত

৬ নং খানখানাপুর ইউনিয়ন পরিষদ

This order was found by the learned Assistant Judge to be in evidence of both the petitioner's possession of and dispossession from the suit land. A perusal of the Exhibit 3 documents pertaining to case No. 30 of 1994 reveals no ground for this Court to disagree with that finding by the learned Assistant Judge. The next stage of the legal battle was fought out in the petitioners Objection case No. 498 of 1995 challenging the earlier entry in the draft Record of rights of 1992 in favour of the opposite party No. 1. This case, as is evident in the Exhibit-4 judgment dated 2-11-1997, was filed under the relevant provisions of the state Acquisition Rules, 1951 read with those of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Proceeding on the disputed claims to the property by the petitioner and the opposite party No. 1 and referring to the history of litigation pertaining to the sale as evident in particular in Civil Case No. 155 of 1990, the judgment found against the correctness of the entry favour in the opposite party No. 1 in the draft Record of rights and found for entering the petitioners names instead. This in this Court view, also further bolstered the petitioners claims as adjudicate upon in case No. 30 of 1994. It is asserted, that an appeal as ostensibly preferred by the opposite party No. 1 against this judgment awaiting disposal, therefore, leading the opposite party No. 1 to question the very maintainability of the petitioners suit. This Court finds that the question of a pending appeal arises in the statement made by the opposite party No.1 upon cross-examination in somewhat vague terms and appears not to have been substantiated by evidence by the opposite party No. 1 of there before the trial Court or the lower appellate Court. This Court, upon a perusal of all relevant documents, finds that no attempt was made by the opposite party No. 1 to prove further the filing or the pendency of such appeal.

8. In light of the above, it is this Court's view that the trajectory of litigation pertaining to the disputed land, and as aptly appreciated by the learned Assistant Judge upon examining evidence, has been one of confirmation in various legal forums of the chain of title commencing in 1950 and continuing uninterruptedly to culminate in the acquisition of title by the petitioners in 1993. The issues of possession, title and dispossession that has loomed large in this case, have been settled in at least three different legal forums in Civil case No. 155 of 1990 case No. 30 of 1994 and objection case No. 498 of 1996 (Exhibits 2, 3 and 4 respectively). There is nothing on record that goes to show that in any such legal forum the title of the opposite party No. 1 by inheritance and gift was formally established on its own terms or with a view to dislodging in any way the claims to title and possessions put forward by the petitioners.

<u>9. It is in this context that this Court is now laced with impugned judgment of the learned joint District Judge which in reversing the trial Court's judgment came to a finding, inter alia, that though the prima facts title of the petitioners predecessors in interests could be proven before the trial Court there is the outstanding question of actual and uninterrupted possession of the land by the petitioners which thereby proved fatal to the petitioners case at the appellant stage. It is not clear to this Court as to how and why the learned District Judge came to take issue with the question of possession, given the fact that the judgment of the trial Court amply discussed the issue and disposed of the same with an express finding upon a consideration of the evidence on record as corroborated by the PWs. That difficulty, in the view of this Court, stems primarily from the lack of discussion of evidence, oral and documentary, by the lower appellate Court to support its finding in this regard. In other words, that judgment is not ably served by definite and specific findings supported by reasoned consideration of evidence. In the absence of cogent reasoning or of clear findings on any issue of fact and law in the impugned judgment, this Court in revision has been hard pressed to best understand the correctness or general drift and gist of the impugned judgment. This Court finds that in that regard the impugned judgment fails far short of the standard in Order 41, rule XXXI of the Code. Considering the specificity of the findings of the trial Court based on full consideration of facts and evidence, this Court fails to see why the impugned judgment or reversal is so marked by its back of elaboration to any level of satisfaction of the reasons no reversing the trial Court's judgment. Moreover, and on the basis of this Court's reading of relevant facts, and oral and documentary evidence, this Court also finds that the learned joint District Judge came to an incorrect decision in reversing the trial Court's judgment. There is brother in the facts or evidence to show or justify the issue taken by the lower appellate Court with the Court with the petitioners possession or the lack of it of the suit land at all material times and their dispossession there from and in that regard, the learned joint District Judge is found to have erred in law in reaching an erroneous decision to reverse the trial Court's judgment. The learned joint District Judge failed to no to that the petitioners having been better able to prove their title and possession in the suit land as compared to the opposite party No.1 and that the trial Court properly and sufficiently adjudged the matter in favour of the petitioners.</u>

10. In light of the above, this Court finds substance in the Rule. Accordingly, the impugned judgment dated 25-8-2005 and decree dated 29-8-2002 are hereby set aside.

11. In the result the Rule is made absolute.

12. There is no Order as to costs.

Send down the Lower Court Records at once.

End.

KM Kamrul Kader J: This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff is directed against the judgment and decree dated 25-7-2010 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 162 of 2009, rejecting the plaint under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure filed by the defendant-respondents.

2. The material facts in short are that, the appellant as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 162 of 2009 before the Court of learned Joint District Judge, 5'h Court, Dhaka stating inter alia that R. Zaman & Company Ltd is a Private Ltd. Company, it is incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913, on 8-4-1984 under the defendant No. 1 and the plaintiff is the Managing Director of the said Company. Its authorized capital is Taka 1,25,00,000 only (one crore twenty-five lakhs), divided into 1 lac 25 thousand shares, each share worth Taka 100 (one hundred) only and paid up capital was Taka 10 lakhs as per balance sheet dated 30-6-2005, subscribed by the 13 shareholders.

3. The Company has purchased a denationalized and privatized industry namely Kuliarchar Ground Nut Mills Ltd. at a price of Taka 1,00,24,000 only, under an agreement dated 18-6-1987, executed by the Government and the Company. Thereafter, on 4-11-1994 a deed of financing was executed in between the plaintiff and the company for becoming Managing Director of the Company with Payment of Taka 55,00,000 (fifty-five lakhs) in share subject to the approval of the Ministry of Industries, which was accorded on 12-1-1995.

4. Next, on 1-4-1995 a meeting of the Board of Directors of the Company was held under the Chairmanship of Defendant No. 2 and in that meeting the plaintiff was appointed as the Managing Director of the Company and the company handed over 400 shares in his name, which was duly approved by defendant No. 10. Thereafter, the plaintiff was re-elected twice as Managing Director of the company for a period of 5(five) years each on 15-9-1999 and 30-10-2004 respectively. Next, on 30-5-2004, the defendant Nos. 2-6 expressed their intention to sell their 600 shares at a price of Taka 1, 20,000,00 only and the plaintiff agreed to purchase their shares and accordingly a deed of agreement was executed and the plaintiff paid an amount of Taka 42, 00,000 only to the defendants nos. 2-6. Thereafter, the defendant Nos. 3-5 served a notice on 10-6-2005 demanding payment of the balance amount, after receiving the said notice the Plaintiff gave a reply on 27-6-2005 expressing his willingness to make payment of the rest/balance amount provided that they will execute prescribed instruments to transfer the said shares in the name of the plaintiff, but they did not pay any heed to it.

5. Due to non-payment of the balance amount government charged penal interest, the plaintiff filed a title suit being No. 9 of 1999 (re-numbered) before Joint District Judge, Dhaka against the defendant No. 10 for a declaration that the excess amount of money demanded by the government is wrong, unlawful and not binding upon the company. After conclusion of trial learned Additional Joint District Judge, Dhaka decreed the suit of the plaintiff. During pendency of the said suit, the defendants removed the plaintiff from the post of Managing Director on 22-3-1997, which was challenged by the plaintiff by filing a Writ petition being No. 1834 of 1997, before this Hon'ble Court and after hearing the parties, the Rule was made absolute by the judgment and order dated 5-8-2007.

6. The plaintiff filed an application on 23-10-2005 to the defendant No. 10 to make payment of rest of the installment, amounting Taka. 24,01,815.97 only (Taka twenty-four lakhs one thousand eight hundred fifteen and ninety seven paisa) by October, 2005. Subsequently,the plaintiff made payment of rest of the amount on 23-1-2006 and filed Title Suit No. 1449 of 2008 for specific performance of contract against the defendant No. 10.

7. In the meantime, the defendant No. 2 received some money from a third party with a condition to sale of shares of the said Company, without any approval from the board of directors. Mr Rashiduzzaman and Mr. Khurshid-uz-zaman sold their 280 shares to Mr. Shafiqul Islam, Mr. Rafiqul Islam and Mr. Saiful Islam and they were shown as the directors of the company on 30-3-2006. The defendant No. 2 in collusion with defendant Nos. 3-6 created some false documents to misappropriate the properties of the Mill. The plaintiffs post as Managing Director was shown vacant under section 110 of the Companies Act and the defendant No, 2 was shown as the Managing Director in a meeting held in the Kuliarchar Ground Nut Mill, wherein, defendant Nos. 2-6 were shown present in that meeting and passed the said resolution, though the defendant Nos. 3-5 were out of Bangladesh at the relevant period. On getting that information the plaintiff filed a General Diary entry on 14-8-2006 to the Kuliarchar Police Station and a copy of the said GD was sent to the defendant No. 1, after receiving the same the defendant No. 1 passed an order upon the plaintiff and defendant No. 2 to settle the matter amicably. Later, the plaintiff filed a Writ Petition No. 9278 of 2006 against the aforesaid order before this Hon'ble Court and after hearing the parties their Lordships was pleased to make the Rule Nisi absolute on 18-8-2008 and declared that the impugned letter dated 8-8-2006 has been issued without lawful authority and directed the Registrar of Joint Stock-Companies and Firms to hold an enquiry in respect of the return as submitted by the company M/s R. Zaman & Company through writ petitioner and the counter return, under the authority as availed to him under the provision of Section 193 of the Companies Act. 1994. The plaintiff after obtaining the certified copy of the aforesaid judgment and order sent it to defendant No. 1 on 24-5-2009, unfortunately, he without considering the said Judgment and order, passed an order which needs to be declared to have been passed unlawfully and hence not binding upon the plaintiff.

8. The defendant No. 2 in collusion with defendant Nos. 2-6 sold out stock and other articles of the said Mill amounting to over Tk. 2,00,00,000 (two crore), for depriving of the plaintiff from his due share as major shareholder of the company. The defendant Nos. 2-6 collected rents from the tenants of the Mill, at the rate of Taka 12,000 per month, which is illegal and unauthorized. The plaintiff is the Managing Director of the Company. But the defendant No. 1 most illegally approved the appointment of the defendant No. 2 as Managing Director of the Company, which is illegal and void. Further, the defendant Nos. 2-6 tried to misappropriate the properties of the company. The cause of action of the suit arose on 24-5-2009. The plaintiff brought this suit for declaration praying for 7 reliefs, which read as follow:

“অতএব প্রার্থনা এই যে,

১। আর, জামান এন্ড কোং লিঃ এর ব্যবস্খাপনা পরিচালক হিসাবে বাদীর নিযুক্তি বৈধ ঘোষণার ডিক্রি প্রদানে;

২। আর, জামান এন্ড কোং লিঃ এর ব্যবস্খাপনা পরিচালক হিসাবে বাদীকে অব্যহতি দান অবৈধ মর্মে ঘোষণার ডিক্রি প্রদানে;

৩। আর, জামান এন্ড কোং লিঃ এর ব্যবস্খাপনা পরিচালক হিসাবে ২নং বিবাদীর নিযুক্তি অবৈধ মর্মে ঘোষণার ডিক্রি প্রদানে;

৪। বিগত ১৮-৬-১৯৮৭ ইং তারিখে চুক্তিমুলে ক্রয়কৃত ক তফছিল বর্ণিত কলিয়ারচর গ্রাউন্ড নাট মিলের ক্রেপস (অস্থাবর সম্প্ত্তি) ২নং বিবাদী কর্তৃক বিক্রয় ক্ষমতা বর্হিভূত এবং বিক্রয়লব্দ অর্থ উক্ত মিলেব ব্যাংকের হিসাবে জমা দানের ডিক্রি প্রদানে;

৫। বাদীকে অবৈধভাবে অব্যাহতি দানের পর মিলের হিসাবে যে আয় হয়েছে তাহা মিলের হিসাবে জমা দানের জন্য ২নং বিবাদীর বিরূদ্ধে ডিক্রি প্রদানে;

৬। বিগত ২৪-৫-২০০৯ ইং তারিখে ১ নং বিবাদী কর্তৃক আদেশ আইনানুগভাবে প্রদান করা হয় নাই মর্মে ঘোষণার ডিক্রি প্রদানে;

৭।বাদী অদ্যবধি কোম্পানীর হিসাবে শেয়ার কেনা বাবদ ৯৭০০০০ (সাতানব্বই লাখ) টাকা এবং মিল খরিদের লক্ষ্যে বিগত ১৮-৬-১৯৮৭ ইং তারিখের চুক্তির বিপরীতে বরাবরে টাকা ২৪০০০০০(চব্বিশ লাখ) জমাদানে কোম্পানীর শেয়ার কেনার বিপরীতে করা হইয়াছে মর্মে ঘোষণার ডিক্রি প্রদান; এবং

৮। আইন ও ইকুইটি মতে বাদী আর যে প্রতিকার পাওয়ার হকদার উহার আদেশ দানে মর্জি হউক।

9. During pendency of the suit the plaintiff filed an application under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restraining the defendant No. 2 from discharging duties as Managing Director of the Company and after hearing the party, learned Joint District Judge passed an Order of ad-interim injunction on 5-7-2009 and restrained the defendant No. 2 to act as Managing Director of the said Company till filing of the written objection.

10. The defendant No. 2 made appearance by filing a written objection against the application for temporary injunction. After submission of written objection the plaintiff filed an application along with a prayer not to accept the vokalatnama and the written objection as the same was filed by a fake person and to take necessary step in accordance with law. Thereafter, on 25-8-2009 the plaintiff filed another application along with prayer to submit the passport of the defendant No. 2.

11. Next, the defendant No. 2 on 2-9-2009 filed an application under Order VII Rule 11 praying for rejection of the plaint. In the mean-time, the defendant No. 10 entered appearance upon filing a written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint. Thereafter, on 3-6-2010, the defendant No. 10 filed an application for rejection of the plaint, under Order VII rule 11(a) and (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In both the applications under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Criminal Procedure the defendants alleged that the suit is barred by law and civil court has no jurisdiction to try this suit as the relief claimed by the plaintiff attract the provision of the section 3 and 43 of the Companies Act, 1994. The plaintiff on 25-10-2009 filed a written objection contending interalia that on 18-6-2009 the plaintiff filed an application along with a prayer not to accept the vokalatnama and the written objection as the same was filed by a fake person and to take necessary step in accordance with law and the same is still pending before the Court. It was necessary to resolve this matter first, before considering the application for Rejection of plaint. The learned Joint District Judge 5th Court, Dhaka, kept the application dated 18-6-2009 filed by the plaintiff in abeyance while allowed the application filed by the defendants under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and rejected the plaint by his judgment and order dated 25-7-2010. 12. Challenging the said judgment and order dated 25-7-2010, which amounts to a decree the instant appeal has been preferred by the plaintiff appellant.

13. Mr Md Nur Hussain Chowdhury the learned counsel appearing on behalf of the appellant having taken us through the entire material on record including the impugned order submits that the plaintiff filed a Title Suit No. 162 of 2009 in the court of learned Joint District Judge. 5th Court, Dhaka, under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, praying for 7 (seven) reliefs, but on misconstruction of law and facts learned Joint District Judge rejected the plaint under order VII, rule 11(a) and (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure and holding that the suit is barred by law and the instant suit is not maintainable according to the provision of section 3 and 43 of the Companies Act, 1994 said finding is erroneous, if the Companies Act, the Rule and Rulings are read together, impugned order is not sustainable in law. He further submits that there is no provision in the Companies Act to file any declaratory suit under which the plaintiff could seek reliefs he claimed in the suit and these reliefs are only available under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and, as such, the impugned order and decree is not sustainable in law.

14. The learned Counsel for the appellant submits that section 9 of the Civil Procedure Code gives Jurisdiction to the Civil Court to try all civil disputes unless they are expressly or impliedly barred. Sections 3 and 43 of the Companies Act have not barred the jurisdiction of the Civil Court in this matter. He further contended that the relief claimed by the petitioner cannot be grounded on any provision under the Companies Act. To substantiate his submission he placed reliance on the decisions of the cases of Messrs Chalna Fibre Company Ltd. Khulna vs Abdul Jabbar and 9 others reported in 20 DLR (SC) 335 and Md Shamsuzzaman Khan vs MS Islam, 28 DLR 976.

15. The learned Counsel lastly submits that the appellant as plaintiff filed this declaratory Suit before the court of learned Joint District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka praying for 7 reliefs, these reliefs are not simple one in nature for adjudication in summary manner and need be adjudicated after taking both oral and documentary evidence and should not be decided in this summary proceeding under section 43 of the Companies Act. Reliance was placed on a decision in the case of Nurun Nahar Zaman vs Sea Pearl Lines Ltd. 11 BLC (2006) 111.

16. Mr AKM Badrudduza, the learned counsel appearing on behalf of the respondents submits that the learned Joint District Judge after carefully considering the plaint, relevant laws and other materials on record rejected the plaint and dismissed the suit of the plaintiffs. The learned Advocate for the respondents argued that the reliefs claimed by the Appellant fall under the jurisdiction of the High Court Division as company matter, under section 43 of the Companies Act, according to the provision of Rule 9 of the Companies Rule 2000. The learned Advocate for the respondents also submits that adequate remedies were provided for settlement of such dispute under the Companies Act. He has relied in this connection on section 43 of the Companies Act. The learned Counsel for the respondents further submits that the Court of Joint District Judge had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit as the reliefs claimed therein were in substance for reliefs under the provision of section 43 of the Companies Act and these reliefs could only be granted by the High Court Division under Rule 9 of the Companies Rules, 2000, which alone had exclusive jurisdiction in the matter under section 3 of the Companies Act. The affairs of the Company should be regulated in accordance with the law that has been provided by the Companies Act itself. In the case of any breach the grievances can only be addressed before a Company court according to the provision of the section 3 of the Companies Act. The judgment and decree passed by the learned Joint District Judge is well reasoned in terms of law, facts and the materials on record, there is no reason to interfere with it.

17. With a view to appreciate the submission made by the learned Advocates from both sides, we have to consider the plaint of the instant suit and the principles of law as laid down in the Civil Procedure Code and the Companies Act. According to the provision of section 9 of the Civil Procedure Code gives Jurisdiction to the Civil Court to try all civil disputes unless they are expressly or impliedly barred. Expressly barred means barred by' any enactment passed by legislature and impliedly barred means the remedy is available in the statute itself for the right or obligation it has created and, as such, same remedy cannot be sought in a civil court. In the cases of Messrs Chalna Fibre Company Ltd. Khulna vs Abdul Jabbar and 9 others reported in 20 DLR (SC) 335 it was held that: "It is a well settled rule that the ouster of jurisdiction of a civil Court in respect of a civil suit is not to be readily inferred. Unless that jurisdiction has been either expressly or impliedly taken away by some other law it will continue to vest in the civil Court."

18. According to the provision of the section 2(d) of the Companies Act, 1994, the court means the court having jurisdiction under this Act. Section 3 of the Companies Act provides that the Court having jurisdiction under this Act shall be the High Court Division provided that the Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette and subject to such restrictions and conditions as it thinks fit empower any District Court to exercise all or any of the jurisdiction by this Act conferred upon the Court, and in that case such District Court shall, as regard the jurisdiction so conferred, be the court in respect of all companies having their registered office in the district.

19. The learned Advocate for the respondents argued that the reliefs claimed by the Appellant fall under the jurisdiction of the High Court Division as company matter, under section 43 of the Companies Act according to the provision of Rule 9 of the Companies Rule 2000. Rule 9 of the Companies Rule 2000, provides that:

"In all courts having jurisdiction under this Act shall be kept and maintained a book called "the Register of Company Matters" in which shall be entered and numbered serially all application made under sections 13, 15, 41, 43, 59, 71, 81, 82, 85, 89, 115, 151, 153, 111, 175, 176, 193, 203, 228, 229, 230, 231, 233, 245, 248, 251, 253, 255, 258, 259, 261, 262, 263, 264, 265, 293, 294, 296, 299, 300, 301, 302, 303, 305, 309, 311, 312, 314, 316, 326, 328, 331, 333, 338, 339, 340, 342, 346, 349, 395, 396, and any other original proceeding under the Act in relation to a company.

20. According to provision "of Rule 9 an aggrieved person can file an application under section 43 of the Companies Act, to rectify the register of members of a company. This Section provides that: 43. Power of Court to rectify register:-

(1) If- (a) the name of any person is without sufficient cause entered in or omitted from the register of members of a company; or (b) default is made or unnecessary delay takes place in entering on the register the fact of any person having become or ceased to be, a member, the person aggrieved, or any member of the company, or the company, may apply to the Court for rectification of the register.

(2) The Court may either refuse the application, or may order rectification of the register and payment by the company of any damage sustained by any party aggrieved and may also make such order as costs as it may consider proper.

(3) On any application under this section the Court may decide any question relating to the title of any person who is a party to the application to have his name entered in or omitted from the register whether the question arises between members or alleged members or between members or alleged members on the one hand and the company on the other hand and generally may decide any question necessary or expedient to be decided for rectification of the register and may also deckle any issue involving any question of law.

21. We also consider the submission placed by the learned Counsel for the appellant that the reliefs claimed by the Appellant are not only for rectification of share register, there are allegation of fraud against the defendants and adequate relief cannot be provided under the aforesaid section. Further, there is no provision in the Companies Act to file any declaratory suit under which the plaintiff could seek reliefs he claimed in the suit and these reliefs are only available under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

22. In the present suit, the plaintiff praying for following reliefs to the court, according to the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, to the effect that a decree be passed declaring that (a) the plaintiff is legally appointed Managing Director of the R. Zaman and Company Limited and (b) the removal of the plaintiff from the post of Managing Director of the Company is illegal and without jurisdiction and (c) a decree be passed to the effect that the appointment of the defendant No. 2 as Managing Director of the Company is illegal and other reliefs prayed by plaintiff with regard to the properties of the company and to deposit the same or equivalent money to the company's account. All that had been done, according to the plaint that his fictitious removal from the post of the Managing Director of the Company had been accepted by defendant No. 1. The plaintiff alleged that the defendant No. 2 in collusion with defendant Nos. 3-6 created some false documents to transfer shares of company to the 3rd parties and the defendant Nos. 2-6 in collusion with each other sold out stock and other articles of the said Mill amounting to Taka 2,00,00,000 (two crore), for depriving of the plaintiff from his due share as major shareholder of the company, all these had been done fraudulently and illegally. He also alleged that the defendant No. 2-6 tried to misappropriate the properties of the Mill and he had been illegally and fraudulently removed from his office of Managing Director and that he could only be restored to his said office, if he obtained a declaration from a competent court that his removal was illegal.

23. We also noticed that the plaintiff alleged, some forged documents have been created to deprive him from the properties and assets of the company, he also seeks reliefs with regard to the assets of the company, these reliefs are not simple in nature for adjudication in summary manner and need be adjudicated after taking both oral and documentary evidence and should not be decided in summary proceeding for rectification of the share register, according to the provision of section 43 of the Companies Act.

<u>24. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the principle of law as laid down it appears that the nature of the dispute is entirely a civil dispute and it can only be resolved by a competent civil court. There is no provision in the Companies Act to file any declaratory suit under which the plaintiff could seek reliefs he claimed in the suit and these reliefs are only available under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.</u>

25. In view of submission made above, we find substance in this appeal.

26. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed and the judgment and decree dated 25-7-2010 passed by learned Joint District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 162 of 2009 is hereby set-aside and the connected Civil Rule being No. 489(F)/2010 is hereby discharged.

27. No order as to costs. Send down the lower Court's records along with a copy of this judgment at once.

End.
